tabs.Nurses' Notes: 0730: 76-year-old client, postoperative day 2 following open sigmoid colectomy for perforated diverticulitis. Drowsy but arousable; oriented to person, place, and time, though less engaged than yesterday and intermittently restless. States, "I just feel off today." Midline abdominal incision edges approximated with a small amount of serosanguineous drainage on the dressing; skin around the incision warm with a faint spreading redness. Reports incisional pain 4/10, relieved to 2/10 with scheduled analgesia. Abdomen softly distended, hypoactive bowel sounds in all quadrants. Indwelling urinary catheter draining dark amber urine, 20 mL/hr for the past 2 hours. Tolerating sips of clear liquids.
tabs.Vital Signs:
2000 (previous day): T 37.6 C (99.7 F), HR 88/min, RR 18/min, BP 126/74 mm Hg, SpO2 97% on room air.
0730: T 38.4 C (101.1 F), HR 102/min, RR 22/min, BP 108/62 mm Hg, SpO2 94% on room air.
tabs.Labs: 0800: WBC 14,800/mm3 (was 11,200/mm3 on postoperative day 1) with 9% bands. Hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL. Glucose 148 mg/dL (client is not diabetic). Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL (preoperative baseline 0.9 mg/dL). Lactate ordered, result pending.

tabs.Nurses' Notes: 1015: 58-year-old client walks into triage reporting chest pressure that began about 45 minutes ago while mowing the lawn. Describes it as "an elephant sitting on my chest," radiating to the left jaw and left arm, rated 8/10. Skin cool and diaphoretic; nauseated, vomited once on the way in. Took two doses of an antacid at home with no relief. History of hypertension and hyperlipidemia; smokes 1 pack per day and has for 30 years. Placed immediately in a treatment room on the cardiac monitor.
tabs.Vital Signs: 1020: T 37.0 C (98.6 F), HR 104/min, RR 24/min, BP 156/94 mm Hg, SpO2 95% on room air. Pain 8/10.
tabs.Diagnostics: 1025: 12-lead ECG shows 3-mm ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in leads I and aVL. 1030: High-sensitivity troponin I drawn; result pending.

tabs.Nurses' Notes:
0710: 68-year-old client, postoperative day 2 following right total hip arthroplasty. Up to the chair with physical therapy yesterday; removed the sequential compression devices overnight, stating they were "too hot." Hip dressing dry with a small amount of serosanguineous drainage; surgical pain 3/10 with movement.
0718: While being assisted back to bed, client suddenly grips the chest and states, "I cannot catch my breath." Respirations rapid and shallow; client anxious and restless. Reports sharp chest pain that worsens with inspiration. Breath sounds present bilaterally with no adventitious sounds. Provider paged.
tabs.Vital Signs:
0700: T 37.1 C (98.8 F), HR 84/min, RR 16/min, BP 128/76 mm Hg, SpO2 96% on room air.
0718: T 37.2 C (99.0 F), HR 122/min, RR 30/min, BP 102/68 mm Hg, SpO2 86% on room air.
tabs.Medication Record: Enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously once daily for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis: dose refused yesterday evening; client stated, "Those shots leave bruises." Oxycodone-acetaminophen 5/325 mg orally every 6 hours as needed for pain, last given 0600. Docusate sodium 100 mg orally twice daily.

tabs.Nurses' Notes: 0945: 19-year-old client with type 1 diabetes mellitus brought to the emergency department by a roommate. Client reports 2 days of nausea, vomiting, and "flu-like" symptoms and states she stopped taking her insulin yesterday "because I wasn't eating anything." Reports diffuse abdominal pain, extreme thirst, and frequent urination. Client is drowsy but arousable and oriented x3. Deep, rapid respirations noted with a fruity odor to the breath. Mucous membranes dry; skin turgor poor. Voided 400 mL dilute urine on arrival.
tabs.Vital Signs: 0950: Temperature 100.9 F (38.3 C) oral; heart rate 124/min; respirations 32/min, deep and regular; blood pressure 98/60 mm Hg; SpO2 99% on room air. Weight 60 kg.
tabs.Labs: 1000: Glucose 540 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.12, PaCO2 24 mm Hg, HCO3 9 mEq/L. Sodium 130 mEq/L, potassium 5.6 mEq/L, chloride 97 mEq/L, anion gap 24 mEq/L. BUN 28 mg/dL, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL. Serum ketones: large. Urinalysis: glucose 4+, ketones 3+.

tabs.Nurses' Notes: 0910: 68-year-old client brought to the emergency department by spouse. Spouse reports that at breakfast at 0830 the client suddenly developed a right facial droop, slurred speech, and weakness of the right arm; the client was completely well before that. History of hypertension and hyperlipidemia; takes lisinopril and atorvastatin. No anticoagulants, no recent surgery, no history of bleeding. On exam: right facial droop, speech slurred but understandable, right arm drifts downward within 10 seconds when raised. NIHSS score 12. Stroke alert activated.
tabs.Vital Signs: 0915: Temperature 98.4 F (36.9 C); heart rate 92/min, irregularly irregular; respirations 18/min; blood pressure 168/94 mm Hg; SpO2 96% on room air. Capillary glucose 118 mg/dL. Weight 82 kg.
tabs.Diagnostic Results: 0935: CT head without contrast — no intracranial hemorrhage, no early infarct changes. 0940 labs: INR 1.0, platelets 240,000/mm3, glucose 116 mg/dL. 12-lead ECG: atrial fibrillation, rate 90s, no acute ST changes.

tabs.Nurses' Notes: 1040: 62-year-old client presents to the emergency department reporting 2 days of black, tarry, foul-smelling stools and dizziness when standing. Reports 3 months of epigastric burning that is worse between meals. Takes ibuprofen 800 mg three times daily for osteoarthritis of the knees; denies alcohol use. Skin pale and cool; client appears fatigued. Abdomen soft with mild epigastric tenderness, no rigidity. No bright red rectal bleeding.
tabs.Vital Signs: 1045: Lying — blood pressure 112/70 mm Hg, heart rate 96/min. Standing — blood pressure 88/58 mm Hg, heart rate 122/min; client reports dizziness on standing. Respirations 20/min; SpO2 97% on room air; temperature 98.2 F (36.8 C).
tabs.Labs: 1100: Hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL (13.9 g/dL at a visit 6 months ago); hematocrit 24%. BUN 42 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. Platelets 310,000/mm3, INR 1.1. Stool guaiac: positive.

tabs.Nurses' Notes: 0800: 34-week primigravida admitted from the clinic reporting a headache for 8 hours unrelieved by acetaminophen, "spots" in her vision, and right upper quadrant pain rated 6/10. Face and hands visibly edematous; 2+ pitting edema of the lower extremities. Deep tendon reflexes 3+ with 1 beat of ankle clonus. Urine dipstick 3+ protein. Fetal movement reported as normal. Continuous fetal monitoring applied; provider notified.
tabs.Vital Signs: 0800: BP 168/112 mm Hg, HR 92/min, RR 18/min, Temp 37.1 C (98.8 F), SpO2 98% on room air. 0815 (repeat, left lateral position): BP 172/114 mm Hg. FHR baseline 140/min, moderate variability, no decelerations.
tabs.Labs: 0830: Hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL, Hematocrit 38%, Platelets 98,000/mm3, AST 88 units/L, ALT 76 units/L, Creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, Uric acid 7.2 mg/dL, Urine protein/creatinine ratio 0.9.

tabs.Nurses' Notes: 0230: G4P4 delivered a 4,420-g (9 lb 12 oz) infant vaginally at 0200 after a precipitous 3-hour labor. Fundus boggy, midline, 1 cm above the umbilicus; firms briefly with massage, then relaxes. Peripad and underpad saturated with lochia rubra and several large clots within 15 minutes of placement. Client states, "I feel dizzy and cold." Skin pale and cool. Provider notified; prescriptions received.
tabs.Vital Signs: 0200: BP 118/72 mm Hg, HR 84/min, RR 16/min. 0230: BP 96/58 mm Hg, HR 118/min, RR 22/min, Temp 36.8 C (98.2 F), SpO2 97% on room air.
tabs.Labor Flow Sheet: 2300: Admitted at 6 cm in spontaneous labor. 0148: Complete and pushing. 0200: Spontaneous vaginal birth; second stage 12 minutes; infant 4,420 g. No laceration or episiotomy. 0210: Placenta delivered intact. Estimated blood loss at delivery 350 mL. Oxytocin 20 units in 1,000 mL lactated Ringer solution infusing at 125 mL/hr.

tabs.Nurses' Notes: 1300: G2P1 at 41 weeks admitted for oxytocin induction for late-term pregnancy. Cervix 5 cm dilated, 90% effaced, 0 station. Membranes ruptured artificially at 1130 with clear fluid. Epidural infusing with adequate pain relief. Oxytocin infusing at 12 milliunits/min. Client resting in bed, oriented, denies nausea.
tabs.Labor Flow Sheet: 1300: Contractions every 2.5 minutes, lasting 80-90 seconds, strong to palpation; FHR baseline 140/min, moderate variability, accelerations present, no decelerations (Category I). 1335: Six contractions in 10 minutes, each lasting 95 seconds, with a firm uterine resting tone; FHR baseline 145/min, minimal variability, recurrent late decelerations to 110/min with slow return to baseline (Category II).
tabs.Vital Signs: 1300: BP 108/64 mm Hg, HR 82/min, Temp 37.0 C (98.6 F). 1335: BP 102/60 mm Hg, HR 88/min, SpO2 98% on room air.

tabs.Nurses’ Notes: 0915: 9-month-old brought to the emergency department by a parent for 3 days of vomiting and 8-10 watery stools per day. Several children at day care have had similar symptoms. Infant is listless but cries when disturbed; cry produces no tears. Anterior fontanelle sunken. Mucous membranes dry and sticky. Lips cracked. Skin turgor: fold remains tented for 3 seconds over the abdomen. Extremities cool, capillary refill 4 seconds. Parent reports only one scant wet diaper in the past 12 hours and that the infant vomits within minutes of every bottle offered.
tabs.Vital Signs: 0920: Temperature 37.9°C (100.2°F) axillary. Heart rate 178/min. Respirations 44/min, unlabored. Blood pressure 84/52 mm Hg. SpO2 98% on room air. Breath sounds clear bilaterally.
tabs.Growth Chart / Weights: Well-child visit 2 weeks ago: 8.2 kg. Today, 0910 (bare weight, same scale type): 7.4 kg — a loss of 0.8 kg, approximately 10% of body weight.

tabs.Nurses’ Notes: 1740: 4-year-old carried into triage by a parent. Child was well this morning, then developed a sore throat and a fever that rose abruptly over the past 4 hours. Child is sitting upright on the parent’s lap, leaning forward on both arms with the chin thrust out and mouth open. Drooling continuously and refusing to swallow. Voice is muffled ("hot potato" quality). Inspiratory stridor audible without a stethoscope. No cough noted. Child appears anxious and very still, eyes wide. Weight 16.5 kg.
tabs.Vital Signs: 1745: Temperature 39.8°C (103.6°F) temporal. Heart rate 148/min. Respirations 36/min with suprasternal retractions. SpO2 93% on room air. Blood pressure deferred to avoid agitating the child.
tabs.History: No chronic illnesses. No known allergies. Immunization record: hepatitis B birth dose only; parents declined all subsequent vaccines, including Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) series.

tabs.Nurses’ Notes:
2200: 58-year-old, postoperative day 1 after open colon resection. Reports incisional pain 7/10; pressing PCA button frequently. History of obstructive sleep apnea; home CPAP not brought in. Spouse at bedside states, "I press the button for him whenever he grimaces in his sleep so he can rest."
0200: Entered room for rounds. Client snoring deeply, then apneic pauses noted. Respirations 6/min and shallow. Pupils pinpoint bilaterally. Does not open eyes to name; arouses only briefly to sternal rub (POSS sedation score 4). Rapid response called, PCA button removed from spouse’s reach.
tabs.Vital Signs:
2000: RR 14/min, SpO2 96% room air, BP 128/76, HR 82.
2300: RR 11/min, SpO2 93% room air, BP 118/70, HR 76.
0130: RR 8/min, SpO2 89% room air, BP 108/64, HR 68.
0200: RR 6/min shallow, SpO2 84% room air, BP 102/60, HR 64.
tabs.Medication Administration Record: Hydromorphone PCA started 1400: demand dose 0.2 mg IV, lockout 10 minutes, no basal rate, 4-hour limit 3 mg. Pump history 2200-0200: 38 demand attempts, 22 doses delivered (4.4 mg total). Ondansetron 4 mg IV at 2100. Naloxone 0.4 mg IV PRN respiratory depression on the standing postoperative order set.

items.stem: A client is receiving a continuous IV heparin infusion for a pulmonary embolism. Which laboratory result indicates to the nurse that the infusion is within the therapeutic range?
options: aPTT of 65 seconds with a control of 32 seconds
aPTT of 30 seconds with a control of 32 seconds
INR of 2.5
Platelet count of 250,000/mm3
items.rationale: Heparin therapy is monitored with the aPTT, and a therapeutic value is roughly 1.5 to 2 times the control, so 65 seconds against a control of 32 is therapeutic. An aPTT equal to the control means the client is not anticoagulated. The INR monitors warfarin, not heparin, and a platelet count reflects risk for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia rather than the anticoagulant effect.

items.stem: A client receiving IV heparin develops significant bleeding, and the provider prescribes the reversal agent. Which medication does the nurse prepare to administer?
options: Vitamin K
Protamine sulfate
Naloxone
Acetylcysteine
items.rationale: Protamine sulfate binds heparin and neutralizes its anticoagulant effect, making it the antidote for heparin overdose. Vitamin K reverses warfarin, naloxone reverses opioids, and acetylcysteine is the antidote for acetaminophen toxicity.

items.stem: The nurse is teaching a client who is starting warfarin therapy at home. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Use a soft-bristled toothbrush for oral care.
Shave with an electric razor instead of a blade.
Report black, tarry stools or blood in the urine right away.
Avoid aspirin and NSAID pain relievers unless the provider approves them.
Double the next dose if a dose is missed.
Expect frequent nosebleeds as a normal part of therapy.
items.rationale: Warfarin increases bleeding risk, so clients should minimize trauma with a soft toothbrush and electric razor, report signs of internal bleeding, and avoid aspirin and NSAIDs, which further impair clotting. A missed dose should never be doubled because that raises the INR unpredictably, and frequent nosebleeds indicate excessive anticoagulation that must be reported, not an expected effect.

items.stem: Before administering the morning dose of metoprolol, the nurse finds the client's apical heart rate is 52 beats/min. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Give the medication and reassess in 30 minutes
Give half of the prescribed dose
Withhold the dose and notify the prescriber
Encourage the client to ambulate, then give the dose
items.rationale: Beta blockers slow the heart rate, so a dose is typically withheld and the prescriber notified when the pulse is below 60 beats/min to prevent symptomatic bradycardia. Giving the full or a partial dose could dangerously lower the rate further, and the nurse may not alter a prescribed dose independently.

items.stem: A client who began taking lisinopril three weeks ago reports a persistent dry, hacking cough. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: "This cough means you are having an allergic reaction; stop the drug immediately."
"A dry cough is a known effect of this medication; I will notify your provider, who may change your prescription."
"Take an over-the-counter cough syrup and continue the medication."
"The cough is a sign your blood pressure is too low."
items.rationale: ACE inhibitors such as lisinopril commonly cause a persistent dry cough related to bradykinin accumulation, and the provider often switches the client to an ARB, which does not have this effect. The cough is not an allergic reaction, so the client should not simply stop the drug abruptly, and masking it with cough syrup does not address the cause. It is unrelated to the blood pressure reading.

items.stem: The nurse is reviewing a client's new prescriptions. Based on the drug name alone, which medication does the nurse identify as an angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB)?
options: Atenolol
Omeprazole
Valsartan
Atorvastatin
items.rationale: The suffix "-sartan" identifies angiotensin II receptor blockers such as valsartan. The suffix "-olol" indicates a beta blocker, "-prazole" a proton pump inhibitor, "-statin" a cholesterol-lowering agent, and "-pril" would indicate an ACE inhibitor.

items.stem: A client is starting nifedipine for hypertension. Which beverage should the nurse instruct the client to avoid?
options: Grapefruit juice
Orange juice
Skim milk
Cranberry juice
items.rationale: Grapefruit juice inhibits the intestinal enzyme that metabolizes many calcium channel blockers, which raises the serum drug level and can cause profound hypotension. Orange juice, milk, and cranberry juice do not have this interaction with nifedipine.

items.stem: The nurse is preparing to administer digoxin to an adult client with heart failure. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Auscultate the apical pulse for one full minute
Check the radial pulse for 15 seconds and multiply by four
Give the dose with a full glass of orange juice
Place the client in high Fowler position
items.rationale: Digoxin slows conduction through the AV node, so the apical pulse must be counted for a full minute before each dose and the dose withheld with the prescriber notified if the rate is below 60 beats/min in an adult. A brief radial count is not accurate enough to detect an irregular or slow rhythm, and the other actions do not address the cardiac risk.

items.stem: The nurse suspects digoxin toxicity in a client with heart failure. Which findings support this suspicion? Select all that apply.
options: Loss of appetite
Hypertension
Nausea and vomiting
Increased appetite
Yellow-green halos around lights
Apical heart rate of 48 beats/min
items.rationale: Anorexia, nausea, and vomiting are classic early signs of digoxin toxicity, while visual changes such as yellow-green halos and bradycardia or other dysrhythmias reflect more advanced toxicity. Digoxin toxicity suppresses rather than increases appetite, and it causes rhythm disturbances, not hypertension.

items.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with stable angina about sublingual nitroglycerin. Which instruction should the nurse include?
options: Sit or lie down before placing the tablet under the tongue
Swallow the tablet with a full glass of water
Chew the tablet thoroughly for faster relief
Take the tablet only with food to prevent stomach upset
items.rationale: Nitroglycerin causes vasodilation that can produce sudden hypotension and dizziness, so the client should sit or lie down before taking a dose to prevent falls. The tablet must dissolve under the tongue for rapid absorption; swallowing or chewing it destroys much of the effect, and food is irrelevant to the sublingual route.

items.stem: Before administering a scheduled dose of IV furosemide, the nurse reviews the morning laboratory results. Which value requires the nurse to contact the prescriber before giving the dose?
options: Sodium 138 mEq/L
Potassium 2.9 mEq/L
Glucose 108 mg/dL
Chloride 100 mEq/L
items.rationale: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that wastes potassium, and giving it when the level is already below the normal range of 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L risks dangerous dysrhythmias, so the prescriber must be notified first. The sodium, glucose, and chloride values listed are all within or near normal limits and do not contraindicate the dose.

items.stem: A client with heart failure is prescribed spironolactone. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?
options: "I will report muscle weakness or an irregular heartbeat."
"I will use a potassium-based salt substitute instead of table salt."
"I will have my blood drawn for electrolyte levels as scheduled."
"I will take this medication at the same time every day."
items.rationale: Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic, so adding potassium-based salt substitutes can cause hyperkalemia; this statement shows a knowledge gap. Reporting signs of electrolyte imbalance, keeping laboratory appointments, and taking the drug consistently all reflect correct understanding.

items.stem: The nurse administers regular insulin subcutaneously at 0730 with breakfast. During which time frame should the nurse monitor the client most closely for hypoglycemia?
items.rationale: Regular insulin peaks approximately 2 to 4 hours after injection, so a 0730 dose exerts its strongest glucose-lowering effect during the late morning, when hypoglycemia is most likely. Fifteen to thirty minutes after injection corresponds to onset rather than peak, and the later time frames fall after the peak has passed.

items.stem: The nurse is preparing to draw up regular insulin and NPH insulin in the same syringe. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Withdraw the prescribed dose of regular (clear) insulin.
Perform hand hygiene and gently roll the NPH vial between the palms.
Withdraw the prescribed dose of NPH (cloudy) insulin.
Inject air equal to the NPH dose into the NPH vial and remove the needle without withdrawing insulin.
Inject air equal to the regular insulin dose into the regular vial.
items.rationale: After hand hygiene, the NPH suspension is rolled to mix it, air is injected into the NPH vial first (without drawing medication), then air is injected into the regular vial and the regular insulin is withdrawn before the NPH. Drawing clear before cloudy prevents the longer-acting NPH from contaminating the regular insulin vial and altering its rapid action.

items.stem: A client with type 1 diabetes received insulin two hours ago. Which findings suggest the client is experiencing hypoglycemia? Select all that apply.
options: Fruity odor to the breath
Cool, clammy, diaphoretic skin
Shakiness and tremor
Increased urination and thirst
Palpitations with a rapid heart rate
Sudden confusion and irritability
items.rationale: Hypoglycemia triggers a sympathetic response producing cool diaphoretic skin, tremor, and tachycardia, and the glucose-starved brain becomes confused and irritable. A fruity breath odor and polyuria with polydipsia are findings of hyperglycemia and diabetic ketoacidosis, not low blood glucose.

items.stem: A client who takes metformin daily is scheduled for a CT scan with IV iodinated contrast this afternoon. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Give the metformin with a sip of water as scheduled
Contact the provider, anticipating that metformin will be withheld around the time of the contrast study
Double this morning's dose because the client will miss the evening dose
Administer the metformin intravenously instead of orally
items.rationale: Iodinated contrast can impair renal function, and metformin that accumulates in renal impairment increases the risk of lactic acidosis, so the drug is typically withheld at the time of the study and for about 48 hours afterward until renal function is confirmed. Giving, doubling, or changing the route of the dose would all increase the client's risk.

items.stem: The nurse is providing teaching for a client newly prescribed phenytoin for a seizure disorder. Which client statement indicates correct understanding?
options: "I will brush and floss carefully every day and see my dentist regularly."
"I can stop the medication once I have been seizure-free for a month."
"I should skip my dose on days I feel drowsy."
"Bleeding gums mean the medication is working."
items.rationale: Phenytoin commonly causes gingival hyperplasia, so meticulous oral hygiene and routine dental care help limit gum overgrowth. Anticonvulsants must never be stopped abruptly or skipped because doing so can precipitate seizures, and gum changes are an adverse effect to manage, not a sign of effectiveness.

items.stem: Two days after starting haloperidol, a client develops painful twisting of the neck to one side and upward deviation of the eyes. Which medication should the nurse prepare to administer?
options: Benztropine
A second dose of haloperidol
Lithium
Ondansetron
items.rationale: Torticollis and oculogyric crisis are acute dystonic reactions, an extrapyramidal effect of typical antipsychotics that is treated promptly with an anticholinergic such as benztropine (or diphenhydramine). Giving more haloperidol would worsen the reaction, and lithium and ondansetron have no role in treating dystonia.

items.stem: A client taking fluphenazine is brought to the emergency department. Which findings support a diagnosis of neuroleptic malignant syndrome? Select all that apply.
options: Temperature of 40.1 C (104.2 F)
Severe "lead-pipe" muscle rigidity
Hyperactive reflexes with clonus
Rapidly fluctuating blood pressure with tachycardia
Profuse diaphoresis
Pinpoint pupils
items.rationale: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a life-threatening reaction to antipsychotics marked by very high fever, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability with labile blood pressure and tachycardia, and profuse sweating. Hyperreflexia with clonus points to serotonin syndrome rather than NMS, and pinpoint pupils suggest opioid effect.

items.stem: A client who takes lithium for bipolar disorder reports two days of vomiting and diarrhea and now has a coarse hand tremor and an unsteady gait. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Administer the next lithium dose with food
Encourage the client to rest and reassess in four hours
Withhold the lithium, notify the provider, and anticipate a stat serum lithium level
Give an antidiarrheal medication and continue the current regimen
items.rationale: Coarse tremor, ataxia, and persistent gastrointestinal symptoms indicate lithium toxicity, especially after fluid losses, because dehydration and sodium depletion cause the kidneys to retain lithium. The drug must be held, the provider notified, and a stat level drawn; the maintenance range is only about 0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L. Continuing doses or merely treating symptoms allows the level to climb further.

items.stem: A client taking phenelzine is selecting foods from the dinner menu. Which selection indicates the client needs further dietary teaching?
options: Grilled chicken breast with rice
Aged cheddar cheese and salami tray
Scrambled eggs with toast
Fresh fruit salad
items.rationale: Phenelzine is an MAOI, and tyramine-rich foods such as aged cheeses and cured or fermented meats can precipitate a hypertensive crisis because the enzyme that breaks down tyramine is inhibited. Fresh meats, eggs, grains, and fresh fruit are low in tyramine and safe to eat.

items.stem: A client taking sertraline was recently started on tramadol for pain. Which findings should the nurse recognize as manifestations of serotonin syndrome? Select all that apply.
options: Agitation and restlessness
Hypothermia
Hyperactive deep tendon reflexes
Diaphoresis with fever
Flaccid muscle tone
Tachycardia
items.rationale: Combining an SSRI with another serotonergic drug such as tramadol can cause serotonin syndrome, which presents with agitation, hyperreflexia and clonus, fever with sweating, and autonomic changes such as tachycardia. The syndrome produces hyperthermia rather than hypothermia and increased neuromuscular activity rather than flaccidity.

items.stem: Following a procedure with IV midazolam, a client is difficult to arouse with a respiratory rate of 7 breaths/min. Which medication should the nurse anticipate administering?
options: Naloxone
Flumazenil
Protamine sulfate
Calcium gluconate
items.rationale: Flumazenil is the reversal agent for benzodiazepines such as midazolam and is used for oversedation with respiratory depression. Naloxone reverses opioids, protamine reverses heparin, and calcium gluconate is given for magnesium toxicity or certain calcium channel blocker effects.

items.stem: A client using a morphine PCA pump is found somnolent with pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 6 breaths/min. The nurse stops the infusion and stimulates the client, who remains minimally responsive. Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Administer naloxone as prescribed
Request a prescription for flumazenil
Reduce the PCA basal rate by half and continue monitoring
Recheck the respiratory rate in 15 minutes
items.rationale: Somnolence, pinpoint pupils, and a respiratory rate of 6 indicate opioid-induced respiratory depression, which is reversed with the opioid antagonist naloxone. Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, not opioids, and simply lowering the rate or waiting to reassess leaves the client hypoventilating and at risk for respiratory arrest.

items.stem: A client has been receiving IV gentamicin for five days. Which client report is most important for the nurse to communicate to the provider?
options: "I have ringing in my ears."
"I feel hungry between meals."
"My IV site itched briefly yesterday."
"I had one soft stool this morning."
items.rationale: Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin are toxic to cranial nerve VIII, and tinnitus is an early sign of ototoxicity that can progress to permanent hearing loss if the drug continues. The nurse also monitors BUN, creatinine, and trough levels for nephrotoxicity. Hunger, a resolved itch, and a single soft stool are not signs of aminoglycoside toxicity.

items.stem: A client has taken oral prednisone daily for six months for rheumatoid arthritis. Which instruction is most important for the nurse to emphasize?
options: Do not stop taking this medication abruptly
Take the medication on an empty stomach
Avoid all dairy products while on this medication
Skip the dose on days when joint pain is mild
items.rationale: Long-term corticosteroid use suppresses the adrenal glands, so stopping abruptly can cause acute adrenal insufficiency; the dose must be tapered under provider direction. Prednisone should be taken with food to reduce gastric irritation, dairy is not restricted, and doses should never be skipped based on symptoms.

items.stem: A client with asthma is prescribed both an albuterol inhaler and a beclomethasone inhaler for use at the same time. Which instruction should the nurse give?
options: Use the beclomethasone first, then the albuterol
Use the albuterol first, wait a few minutes, then use the beclomethasone
Alternate which inhaler is used first each day
Use only one of the inhalers per day, never both
items.rationale: Albuterol is a rapid-acting bronchodilator; using it first opens the airways so the inhaled corticosteroid can reach deeper lung tissue and work more effectively. Reversing the order reduces steroid delivery, and both medications are intended to be used as prescribed, not alternated or omitted.

items.stem: A client taking theophylline for chronic lung disease calls the clinic with new symptoms. Which report should the nurse recognize as a possible early sign of theophylline toxicity?
options: Nausea, restlessness, and a racing heart
Drowsiness and constipation
Weight gain and ankle swelling
Hoarseness and a dry cough
items.rationale: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic range of about 10 to 20 mcg/mL, and early toxicity typically presents with gastrointestinal upset, restlessness, and tachycardia, which can progress to seizures and serious dysrhythmias. Sedation with constipation, fluid retention, and hoarseness are not characteristic of theophylline toxicity.

items.stem: The nurse administers IV ondansetron to a client 30 minutes before the first dose of chemotherapy. The nurse understands the purpose of this medication is to achieve which outcome?
options: Prevent nausea and vomiting
Increase the effectiveness of the chemotherapy
Prevent an allergic reaction to the chemotherapy
Reduce chemotherapy-related fatigue
items.rationale: Ondansetron is a serotonin (5-HT3) receptor antagonist given prophylactically before chemotherapy because prevention of nausea and vomiting is more effective than treating it after it starts. It does not enhance the chemotherapy itself, prevent hypersensitivity reactions, or treat fatigue.

items.stem: The nurse is preparing to administer morning medications. Which actions demonstrate safe medication administration practice? Select all that apply.
options: Confirm the client's identity using two identifiers before giving the medication.
Compare the medication label with the medication administration record when obtaining, preparing, and giving the drug.
Leave the medication at the bedside for the client to take later.
Ask the client about allergies before administering a first dose.
Prepare medications for several clients at the same time to save steps.
Document the medication immediately after the client takes it.
items.rationale: Safe administration includes verifying the right patient with two identifiers, performing three label checks against the record, screening for allergies, and documenting promptly after the dose is taken. Leaving medications unattended means the nurse cannot verify they were taken, and preparing doses for multiple clients at once invites mix-ups and wrong-patient errors.

items.stem: A client has taken oral amiodarone for atrial fibrillation for 6 months. Which laboratory tests does the nurse expect to be monitored periodically because of this medication?
options: Serum potassium and magnesium levels
Complete blood count and platelet count
Thyroid and liver function tests
Blood urea nitrogen and creatinine
items.rationale: Amiodarone contains iodine and can cause both hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism, and it is also hepatotoxic, so thyroid function and liver enzymes are followed throughout therapy. Electrolytes, blood counts, and renal function are not the labs most affected by amiodarone. Periodic chest imaging and eye examinations are also indicated because of pulmonary and corneal effects.

items.stem: A client who has taken amiodarone for a year reports a new dry cough and increasing shortness of breath with activity. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Reassure the client that a dry cough is an expected effect of the medication.
Notify the provider because these findings may indicate pulmonary toxicity.
Instruct the client to take the medication with food to reduce the cough.
Encourage increased fluid intake and an over-the-counter cough suppressant.
items.rationale: A nonproductive cough and progressive dyspnea in a client on long-term amiodarone suggest pulmonary fibrosis or pneumonitis, the most dangerous toxicity of the drug, and the provider must be notified so imaging and pulmonary testing can be done. These symptoms are never an expected effect to be reassured away. Taking the drug with food, adding fluids, or suppressing the cough would mask a potentially fatal complication without addressing it.

items.stem: Immediately after the nurse gives rapid IV adenosine for supraventricular tachycardia, the cardiac monitor shows a flat line lasting several seconds. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Begin chest compressions immediately.
Administer atropine from the emergency cart.
Defibrillate the client at 200 joules.
Continue observing the monitor for return of an organized rhythm.
items.rationale: Adenosine briefly blocks conduction through the AV node, so a short period of asystole lasting a few seconds is an expected effect while the rhythm resets, and the nurse should keep watching the monitor. Compressions, atropine, or defibrillation are not indicated for a transient, anticipated pause. Emergency equipment should already be at the bedside in case the pause does not resolve, but intervening during the expected pause is premature.

items.stem: The nurse is preparing to administer IV adenosine to a client in stable supraventricular tachycardia. Place the steps in the order the nurse should perform them.
options: Flush the line immediately with 20 mL of normal saline.
Confirm the rhythm and ensure emergency equipment is at the bedside.
Depress the plunger rapidly over 1 to 2 seconds.
Attach the adenosine syringe to the IV port closest to the heart.
Observe the monitor for a brief pause followed by rhythm conversion.
items.rationale: The nurse first verifies the rhythm and readies emergency equipment because adenosine can cause profound transient bradycardia or asystole. Because the half-life of adenosine is only seconds, it must be given through the port nearest the heart, pushed over 1 to 2 seconds, and followed instantly by a rapid saline flush so the drug reaches the myocardium before it is metabolized. Monitoring for the expected pause and conversion comes after administration; giving the drug slowly or flushing later would render it ineffective.

items.stem: A client has a heart rate of 38 beats per minute, reports dizziness, and has a blood pressure of 82/50 mm Hg. Which medication should the nurse prepare to administer?
options: Atropine
Adenosine
Metoprolol
Digoxin
items.rationale: Atropine is an anticholinergic that blocks vagal tone and is the first-line drug for symptomatic bradycardia with hypotension and dizziness. Adenosine slows conduction and is used for supraventricular tachycardia, not bradycardia. Metoprolol and digoxin both slow the heart rate further and would worsen this client's condition.

items.stem: During a resuscitation, the code team confirms the client is in asystole. Which medication does the nurse prepare to administer first?
options: Atropine
Amiodarone
Epinephrine
Sodium bicarbonate
items.rationale: Epinephrine 1 mg IV, repeated every 3 to 5 minutes, is the first medication for asystole because its vasoconstriction improves coronary and cerebral perfusion during compressions. Atropine is used for symptomatic bradycardia with a pulse, not asystole. Amiodarone is reserved for shock-refractory ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia, and sodium bicarbonate is not a routine first-line code drug.

items.stem: A client in pulseless ventricular fibrillation remains in the rhythm after defibrillation and a dose of epinephrine. Which medication does the nurse anticipate administering next?
options: Atropine
Amiodarone
Adenosine
Calcium gluconate
items.rationale: Amiodarone is the antidysrhythmic of choice for ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia that persists after defibrillation and epinephrine. Atropine treats bradycardia and adenosine treats supraventricular tachycardia, so neither applies to a pulseless ventricular rhythm. Calcium is reserved for specific situations such as hyperkalemia or calcium channel blocker toxicity.

items.stem: A client develops hives, facial swelling, and wheezing minutes after a bee sting. By which route should the nurse administer the prescribed epinephrine?
options: Subcutaneously into the abdomen
By slow IV push over 5 minutes
Intradermally into the forearm
Intramuscularly into the vastus lateralis
items.rationale: For anaphylaxis, epinephrine is injected intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh because this route gives rapid, reliable absorption. Subcutaneous injection absorbs too slowly during shock, and the intradermal route is only for testing, not treatment. IV epinephrine is reserved for profound cardiovascular collapse under continuous monitoring, not the first-line response to anaphylaxis on a unit.

items.stem: A client receiving the first dose of an IV antibiotic develops hives, wheezing, and falling blood pressure. Place the nursing actions in priority order.
options: Administer epinephrine intramuscularly as prescribed.
Give the prescribed antihistamine and corticosteroid.
Stop the antibiotic infusion.
Apply high-flow oxygen and assess the airway.
Document the reaction and continue close monitoring of vital signs.
items.rationale: The offending infusion is stopped first so no more allergen enters the client. The airway and oxygenation are then supported because airway compromise kills fastest, followed immediately by intramuscular epinephrine, the definitive drug that reverses bronchospasm and vasodilation. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are secondary medications that blunt the ongoing response, and documentation with continued monitoring comes only after the client is stabilized.

items.stem: Norepinephrine is infusing through a peripheral IV line, and the nurse finds the site pale, cool, and swollen. After stopping the infusion, which medication does the nurse prepare to infiltrate into the site?
options: Phentolamine
Protamine sulfate
Phenylephrine
Naloxone
items.rationale: Norepinephrine is a vesicant, and extravasation causes intense local vasoconstriction that can lead to tissue necrosis; phentolamine, an alpha-adrenergic blocker, is injected into the area to dilate the vessels and restore perfusion. Protamine reverses heparin and naloxone reverses opioids, so neither helps here. Phenylephrine is itself a vasoconstrictor and would worsen the ischemia.

items.stem: The nurse discovers that a vesicant vasopressor has extravasated at a peripheral IV site. Place the nursing actions in the order they should be performed.
options: Notify the provider and obtain a prescription for the antidote.
Stop the infusion immediately.
Elevate the extremity and monitor the site frequently.
Inject phentolamine into the affected tissue as prescribed.
Disconnect the tubing and aspirate any residual drug from the catheter.
items.rationale: Stopping the infusion first limits how much vesicant enters the tissue, and aspirating through the catheter before removal pulls back any drug remaining in the line. The provider is then notified so the antidote can be prescribed and phentolamine infiltrated into the ischemic area to counteract vasoconstriction. Elevation and ongoing site assessment support venous return and detect worsening injury; performing them first would delay the actions that actually stop tissue damage.

items.stem: A client in septic shock is receiving a norepinephrine infusion. Which finding best indicates the infusion is achieving the desired effect?
options: Heart rate of 132 beats per minute
Capillary refill of 5 seconds
Mean arterial pressure of 72 mm Hg
Blood pressure of 82/44 mm Hg
items.rationale: Norepinephrine is titrated to maintain a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mm Hg, so a MAP of 72 mm Hg shows the drug is restoring perfusion pressure. A heart rate of 132 and a capillary refill of 5 seconds indicate continued shock and poor peripheral perfusion. A blood pressure of 82/44 mm Hg produces a MAP well below goal, meaning the infusion has not yet achieved its purpose.

items.stem: The nurse is caring for a client receiving a dopamine infusion through a peripheral IV line. Which finding requires immediate action?
options: Urine output of 60 mL over the past hour
Coolness and swelling at the IV insertion site
Mean arterial pressure of 70 mm Hg
Heart rate that has decreased from 118 to 98 beats per minute
items.rationale: Dopamine is a vesicant, so coolness and swelling at the site signal extravasation, which can cause tissue necrosis and requires the nurse to stop the infusion at that site immediately. A urine output of 60 mL per hour and a mean arterial pressure of 70 mm Hg are desired responses to the drug. A heart rate settling from 118 to 98 reflects improvement rather than a complication.

items.stem: The provider selects a dobutamine infusion rather than high-dose dopamine for a client with acute decompensated heart failure. The nurse understands this choice is based on which action of dobutamine?
options: It produces strong peripheral vasoconstriction to raise blood pressure.
It lowers the heart rate to reduce myocardial oxygen demand.
It directly removes excess fluid volume from the circulation.
It increases myocardial contractility with little vasoconstriction.
items.rationale: Dobutamine stimulates beta-1 receptors, strengthening contractility and improving cardiac output without the significant alpha-mediated vasoconstriction seen with high-dose dopamine, so the failing heart is not forced to pump against higher resistance. It does not vasoconstrict strongly, and it tends to raise rather than lower heart rate. Fluid removal is the role of diuretics, not inotropes.

items.stem: The nurse is reviewing situations in which digoxin immune fab is indicated for a client with digoxin toxicity. Which findings support administering the antidote? Select all that apply.
options: Life-threatening ventricular dysrhythmias attributed to digoxin
Serum potassium of 5.8 mEq/L in the setting of acute toxicity
A serum digoxin level slightly above the therapeutic range without symptoms
Ingestion of a massive acute digoxin overdose
An apical heart rate of 88 beats per minute with a therapeutic level
Nausea that resolves after one held dose
items.rationale: Digoxin immune fab binds free digoxin and is reserved for serious toxicity: life-threatening dysrhythmias, hyperkalemia above about 5 mEq/L in acute poisoning, and massive overdoses. Hyperkalemia in acute toxicity reflects poisoning of the sodium-potassium pump and predicts mortality. A mildly elevated level without symptoms, a normal apical rate, or transient nausea managed by holding a dose are handled with monitoring and dose adjustment, not the costly antidote.

items.stem: A client has received IV heparin for 6 days, and the platelet count has fallen from 240,000/mm3 to 85,000/mm3. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Stop all heparin, including line flushes, and notify the provider.
Administer the next scheduled heparin dose and recheck the count in the morning.
Prepare to transfuse platelets.
Request a prescription for enoxaparin to replace the infusion.
items.rationale: A platelet drop of more than 50 percent beginning around days 5 to 10 of heparin therapy suggests heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, an immune reaction that paradoxically causes clotting, so every source of heparin including flushes must be stopped and the provider notified. Continuing heparin risks limb- and life-threatening thrombosis. Platelet transfusion is avoided because it can fuel clot formation, and enoxaparin cross-reacts with the responsible antibodies, so it cannot substitute.

items.stem: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is suspected in a client on a heparin infusion. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Discontinue all heparin products, including catheter flushes.
Anticipate a prescription for a non-heparin anticoagulant such as argatroban.
Prepare to substitute enoxaparin for the heparin infusion.
Monitor the client for new signs of arterial or venous thrombosis.
Transfuse platelets prophylactically before the count falls further.
Ensure heparin-coated catheters are removed as prescribed.
items.rationale: Managing heparin-induced thrombocytopenia requires eliminating every heparin exposure, including flushes and heparin-coated devices, and continuing anticoagulation with a direct thrombin inhibitor such as argatroban because the disorder causes intense clotting. Ongoing assessment for new thrombosis is essential since clots, not bleeding, are the main danger. Enoxaparin is contraindicated because the antibodies cross-react with low-molecular-weight heparin, and prophylactic platelet transfusion is avoided because it can worsen thrombosis.

items.stem: The nurse observes a graduate nurse administering subcutaneous enoxaparin. Which action requires the nurse to intervene?
options: Injecting into an abdominal skinfold 2 inches away from the umbilicus
Leaving the air bubble in the prefilled syringe
Massaging the injection site after withdrawing the needle
Omitting aspiration before injecting the medication
items.rationale: Massaging the site after a low-molecular-weight heparin injection increases bruising and local bleeding, so the nurse must stop this action. The lateral abdomen at least 2 inches from the umbilicus is the preferred site, the air bubble in the prefilled syringe is intentionally retained to clear the needle and seal the drug in the tissue, and aspiration is correctly omitted because it can cause tissue trauma and hematoma.

items.stem: The nurse is administering subcutaneous enoxaparin from a prefilled syringe. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Pinch up a fold of skin and insert the needle at a 90-degree angle.
Withdraw the needle and release the skinfold without massaging the site.
Verify the prescription and perform hand hygiene.
Inject the medication slowly without aspirating or expelling the air bubble.
Select a site on the lateral abdomen at least 2 inches from the umbilicus.
items.rationale: Safe administration starts with verifying the prescription and performing hand hygiene, then choosing the recommended abdominal site away from the umbilicus. The skin is pinched and the needle inserted at 90 degrees so the drug deposits in subcutaneous fat, the medication is injected without aspirating and with the air bubble retained, and the needle is withdrawn without massage. Aspirating or rubbing the site afterward promotes bruising and hematoma formation, which is why those techniques are deliberately avoided.

items.stem: A client with atrial fibrillation is switched from warfarin to apixaban and asks whether the weekly blood tests will continue. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: "Yes, the INR must still be checked weekly with the new medication."
"Routine INR testing is not needed because apixaban has a predictable effect."
"The aPTT will now be checked weekly instead of the INR."
"Blood tests are only needed if you eat foods high in vitamin K."
items.rationale: Apixaban is a direct oral anticoagulant with predictable dosing that does not require routine INR or aPTT monitoring, which is a major advantage over warfarin. The INR is specific to warfarin therapy, and the aPTT tracks heparin, so neither test is used to manage apixaban. Vitamin K intake affects warfarin, not apixaban, so dietary vitamin K does not drive testing.

items.stem: A client arrives with symptoms of an acute ischemic stroke, and thrombolytic therapy is being considered. Which information is most important for the nurse to obtain first?
options: The time the client was last known to be at neurologic baseline
The family history of stroke
The most recent hemoglobin A1c value
Whether the client takes a daily multivitamin
items.rationale: Eligibility for alteplase depends on treating within a narrow window, generally 3 to 4.5 hours from when the client was last known well, so establishing that time is the critical first step. If the time of onset is unknown or outside the window, the thrombolytic is contraindicated because the bleeding risk outweighs the benefit. Family history, glycemic control, and vitamin use do not determine thrombolytic eligibility.

items.stem: The nurse is screening a client with an acute ischemic stroke for alteplase therapy. Which findings contraindicate the thrombolytic? Select all that apply.
options: Active gastrointestinal bleeding
Stroke symptoms that began 90 minutes ago
Major abdominal surgery performed 1 week ago
Blood pressure of 128/78 mm Hg
A history of hemorrhagic stroke
Suspected aortic dissection
items.rationale: Alteplase dissolves clots throughout the body, so active bleeding, recent major surgery, any history of intracranial hemorrhage, and suspected aortic dissection all create an unacceptable risk of catastrophic bleeding and exclude the client. Symptom onset 90 minutes earlier is actually within the treatment window and supports giving the drug. A blood pressure of 128/78 mm Hg is well below the exclusion threshold of about 185/110 mm Hg.

items.stem: A client has just completed an alteplase infusion for a massive pulmonary embolism. Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Avoid intramuscular injections and unnecessary venipunctures.
Monitor neurologic status frequently for signs of intracranial bleeding.
Apply prolonged pressure to any puncture sites.
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter to track output precisely.
Test stools, urine, and emesis for occult blood.
items.rationale: After a thrombolytic, every intervention centers on preventing and detecting hemorrhage: invasive sticks are avoided, existing puncture sites receive extended pressure, body fluids are checked for occult blood, and frequent neurologic checks watch for intracranial bleeding, the most lethal complication. Inserting a urinary catheter is an avoidable invasive procedure that could cause urethral trauma and bleeding, so it is not added simply for convenience of measurement.

items.stem: During an alteplase infusion for an ischemic stroke, the client suddenly reports a severe headache and becomes drowsy. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Administer the prescribed PRN acetaminophen.
Lower the head of the bed and reassess in 15 minutes.
Slow the infusion rate and continue routine monitoring.
Stop the infusion and notify the provider immediately.
items.rationale: A sudden severe headache with declining alertness during thrombolytic therapy is the classic presentation of intracranial hemorrhage, so the infusion must be stopped at once and the provider notified for emergency imaging. Treating the headache with acetaminophen or merely slowing the drip allows the bleeding source to continue receiving thrombolytic. Waiting 15 minutes to reassess wastes the window in which intervention could limit the bleed.

items.stem: A client taking clopidogrel after coronary stent placement receives a new prescription for omeprazole. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Administer both medications together with breakfast.
Teach the client to take the omeprazole at bedtime to avoid problems.
Contact the provider to discuss the interaction between the two drugs.
Hold the clopidogrel until the reflux symptoms resolve.
items.rationale: Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by the CYP2C19 enzyme, and omeprazole inhibits that enzyme, which can blunt the antiplatelet effect and raise the risk of stent thrombosis, so the prescriber should be consulted about an alternative such as pantoprazole. Separating the administration times does not prevent enzyme inhibition. Holding clopidogrel after recent stenting is dangerous because it invites acute stent occlusion.

items.stem: A client taking atorvastatin calls the clinic reporting aching muscles and dark, tea-colored urine. Which instruction should the nurse give?
options: "Increase your fluids and continue the medication as prescribed."
"Hold the next dose and come in today for laboratory testing."
"Take the medication with food to reduce the muscle aches."
"Move the dose to the morning and monitor for improvement."
items.rationale: Muscle pain combined with dark urine suggests rhabdomyolysis, in which muscle breakdown releases myoglobin that can cause acute kidney injury, so the statin is held and a creatine kinase level checked promptly. Continuing the drug while symptoms progress risks renal failure. Changing the timing or taking it with food does not address muscle injury, and increasing fluids alone leaves the cause in place.

items.stem: The nurse is teaching a client who takes simvastatin daily. Which beverage should the nurse instruct the client to avoid?
options: Grapefruit juice
Cranberry juice
Low-fat milk
Decaffeinated coffee
items.rationale: Grapefruit juice inhibits the CYP3A4 enzyme that metabolizes simvastatin, allowing drug levels to climb and greatly increasing the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Cranberry juice interacts with warfarin rather than statins. Milk and decaffeinated coffee have no meaningful effect on statin metabolism.

items.stem: A client asks why the provider recommended taking simvastatin in the evening. Which explanation by the nurse is correct?
options: "Evening dosing prevents the muscle aches this drug can cause."
"The medication would keep you awake if taken during the day."
"Nighttime dosing protects the liver from injury."
"The body makes most of its cholesterol at night, so the drug works best then."
items.rationale: Hepatic cholesterol synthesis peaks overnight, so short-acting statins such as simvastatin are most effective when taken in the evening. The timing has no effect on the risk of myopathy or liver injury, which are monitored with symptom reporting and liver enzymes regardless of when the dose is taken. Statins are not stimulants and do not interfere with sleep.

items.stem: The nurse is teaching a client who is starting rosuvastatin. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Report new muscle pain, tenderness, or weakness promptly.
Expect periodic blood tests of your liver enzymes.
Continue the medication even after cholesterol levels improve.
Take the medication with an antacid to prevent stomach upset.
Large amounts of grapefruit juice can raise the drug level in your blood.
Stop the medication for one week each month to rest the liver.
items.rationale: Statin teaching emphasizes reporting muscle symptoms, which may herald myopathy, and clients should know that liver enzymes are checked at baseline and when symptoms suggest hepatotoxicity. Therapy is long term, because stopping when numbers improve allows cholesterol to rise again, and grapefruit juice can raise levels of several statins. Routine antacid co-administration is not part of statin teaching, and planned monthly interruptions have no basis and undermine the lipid-lowering effect.

items.stem: A client starting high-dose niacin for dyslipidemia reports intense facial warmth and redness shortly after each dose. Which response by the nurse is appropriate?
options: "Stop the medication immediately, because this is an allergic reaction."
"Take the medication with a hot beverage to reduce the reaction."
"Flushing is expected, and taking aspirin about 30 minutes before the dose can lessen it."
"Skip the next two doses, then restart at a higher amount."
items.rationale: Niacin causes prostaglandin-mediated cutaneous flushing that is uncomfortable but harmless, and pretreatment with aspirin about 30 minutes before the dose reduces it. The reaction is not an allergy, so the drug does not need to be stopped. Hot beverages and alcohol taken near the dose intensify flushing, and skipping doses then escalating would worsen rather than prevent the effect.

items.stem: A client takes lisinopril and spironolactone daily for heart failure. Which laboratory value requires the nurse to contact the provider?
options: Sodium 138 mEq/L
Potassium 5.9 mEq/L
Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL
Potassium 3.6 mEq/L
items.rationale: ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone and spironolactone blocks it directly, so the combination predisposes to potassium retention, and a level of 5.9 mEq/L is dangerous hyperkalemia that can trigger lethal dysrhythmias. The sodium and creatinine values listed are normal, and a potassium of 3.6 mEq/L is within range. Clients on this combination are also taught to avoid potassium-containing salt substitutes.

items.stem: A client with coronary artery disease states, "I felt fine, so I stopped taking my metoprolol two days ago." Which complication is the priority concern for the nurse?
options: Rebound tachycardia with angina or myocardial infarction
Fluid retention from loss of a diuretic effect
Hypoglycemia now that the medication is stopped
A hypertensive response to tyramine-containing foods
items.rationale: Chronic beta blockade up-regulates beta receptors, so abrupt withdrawal exposes the heart to a surge of catecholamine stimulation that can precipitate tachycardia, unstable angina, or infarction in a client with coronary disease. Metoprolol is not a diuretic, so fluid retention is not the issue, and stopping a beta blocker removes the masking of hypoglycemia rather than causing it. Tyramine reactions occur with MAOI therapy, not beta blockers.

items.stem: The nurse is teaching a client who takes oral clonidine for hypertension. Which statement indicates the teaching was effective?
options: "I can stop this medicine once my home readings are normal for a week."
"If I miss a dose, I should take three tablets the next morning."
"This medicine will speed up my heart, so I should rest often."
"I should never stop this medicine suddenly, because my blood pressure could spike."
items.rationale: Abrupt discontinuation of clonidine causes a surge of sympathetic outflow with severe rebound hypertension, so the drug must be tapered under provider guidance. Normal home readings mean the drug is working, not that it can be stopped. Missed doses are never tripled, and clonidine slows rather than speeds the heart rate through its central sympatholytic action.

items.stem: A client who has taken hydralazine for a year reports new joint pain, fatigue, and a rash across the cheeks. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Recommend an over-the-counter analgesic for the joint pain.
Explain that these effects fade as the body adjusts to the drug.
Report the findings to the provider as possible drug-induced lupus.
Advise the client to take the medication at bedtime instead.
items.rationale: Long-term hydralazine can trigger a lupus-like syndrome, and the triad of arthralgia, fatigue, and a malar rash should be reported so antinuclear antibody testing can be done and the drug reconsidered. These findings are not a transient adjustment effect, and symptomatic analgesia or a timing change would mask an autoimmune reaction that resolves only when the drug is withdrawn. Nurses also monitor hydralazine clients for reflex tachycardia, a separate common effect.

items.stem: The nurse is preparing a nitroprusside infusion for a client in hypertensive crisis. Which observation requires the nurse to discard the solution?
options: The pharmacy has covered the container with an opaque sleeve.
The solution has developed a blue discoloration.
The freshly mixed solution has a very faint brownish tint.
The medication is diluted in 5% dextrose in water.
items.rationale: Nitroprusside degrades when exposed to light, and a blue color indicates the drug has broken down and may release cyanide, so the solution must be discarded. Protecting the container from light with an opaque covering is correct practice, a faint brownish tint is characteristic of a properly prepared solution, and dextrose 5% in water is the standard diluent. Only the color change signals a dangerous solution.

items.stem: A client has received a high-dose nitroprusside infusion for 3 days. Which findings should the nurse recognize as possible cyanide or thiocyanate toxicity? Select all that apply.
options: New confusion and restlessness
Metabolic acidosis on arterial blood gas results
Tinnitus and blurred vision
Blood pressure rising above the preinfusion baseline
Urine output of 60 mL per hour
A brisk drop in blood pressure when the infusion starts
items.rationale: Cyanide accumulation blocks cellular oxygen use, producing altered mental status and an unexplained metabolic acidosis, while thiocyanate buildup causes neurologic complaints such as tinnitus, blurred vision, and confusion, especially with prolonged high-dose infusions or renal impairment. A rising blood pressure reflects inadequate dosing rather than toxicity. Adequate urine output is a normal finding, and an immediate fall in pressure is the intended effect of this rapid vasodilator.

items.stem: A client has a serum potassium of 2.8 mEq/L, and a coworker draws up undiluted potassium chloride to give by IV push. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Intervene immediately, because potassium is never given by IV push.
Suggest pushing the dose slowly over at least 5 minutes.
Verify the dose and assist with the injection.
Recommend giving the undiluted dose through a central line instead.
items.rationale: Concentrated potassium given by IV push causes cardiac arrest, so it must always be diluted and infused with a pump at a controlled rate, and the nurse must stop the coworker before any harm occurs. Slowing the push does not make it safe, and a central line changes only where the drug enters, not the lethal effect of a bolus. Assisting with the injection would make the nurse a participant in a fatal medication error.

items.stem: The nurse is preparing to administer IV potassium chloride diluted in 1,000 mL of fluid to a client with hypokalemia. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Administer the infusion using an electronic infusion pump.
Verify that urine output is adequate before and during the infusion.
Give part of the dose by slow IV push because the level is critically low.
Place the client on a cardiac monitor for infusion rates above 10 mEq per hour.
Assess the peripheral IV site frequently for burning or phlebitis.
Add extra potassium to the hanging bag to avoid starting a second infusion.
items.rationale: IV potassium always runs through a pump so the rate cannot exceed safe limits, urine output must be adequate because potassium is renally excreted, rates above about 10 mEq per hour require continuous cardiac monitoring, and the irritant solution demands frequent site checks. Potassium is never pushed regardless of the serum level because a bolus stops the heart. Medication is never added to an already hanging bag, since it pools and can deliver a concentrated column of drug.

items.stem: A client receiving diluted potassium chloride through a peripheral vein reports burning along the vein, but the site shows no redness or swelling. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Discontinue potassium replacement for this admission.
Apply a warm compress and increase the rate to finish the infusion sooner.
Reassure the client that burning always means the vein has infiltrated.
Slow the infusion rate and contact the provider about further dilution.
items.rationale: Potassium is irritating to peripheral veins, and burning without signs of infiltration is managed by slowing the rate and asking the provider about greater dilution or central access. Stopping replacement entirely leaves the hypokalemia untreated, and speeding the infusion intensifies the irritation and raises cardiac risk. Burning alone does not prove infiltration, which is identified by swelling, coolness, and sluggish flow.

items.stem: A client with preeclampsia is receiving a continuous IV magnesium sulfate infusion. Which medication should the nurse keep immediately available?
options: Protamine sulfate
Potassium chloride
Calcium gluconate
Flumazenil
items.rationale: Calcium gluconate is the antidote for magnesium toxicity and must be at the bedside so respiratory depression or cardiac effects can be reversed quickly. Protamine reverses heparin and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, so neither applies to magnesium. Potassium chloride is an electrolyte replacement, not an antidote, and giving it here would add no protection.

items.stem: The nurse is assessing a client receiving a continuous IV magnesium sulfate infusion. Which findings indicate magnesium toxicity? Select all that apply.
options: Absent deep tendon reflexes
Respiratory rate of 10 breaths per minute
Urine output of 20 mL per hour
Deep tendon reflexes graded 2+
Facial flushing and warmth as the infusion begins
New lethargy with slurred speech
items.rationale: Rising magnesium levels progressively depress the neuromuscular system, so lost deep tendon reflexes, a respiratory rate below 12, and increasing sedation with slurred speech all signal toxicity, and oliguria matters because magnesium is cleared by the kidneys and low output allows accumulation. Reflexes of 2+ are normal and reassuring. Transient flushing and warmth are expected effects of the infusion, not signs of toxicity.

items.stem: A client who took a large overdose of verapamil is bradycardic and hypotensive. Which medication does the nurse anticipate administering?
options: Adenosine
IV calcium gluconate
Oral potassium chloride
Metoprolol
items.rationale: Calcium channel blocker overdose causes profound bradycardia, hypotension, and impaired contractility, and IV calcium helps overcome the receptor blockade by raising extracellular calcium available to the myocardium. Adenosine and metoprolol both depress conduction further and would deepen the collapse. Potassium plays no role in reversing calcium channel blockade, and high-dose insulin therapy may also be used for severe cases.

items.stem: A client in diabetic ketoacidosis has prescriptions for IV fluids and a continuous regular insulin infusion. The serum potassium result is 2.9 mEq/L. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Hold the insulin infusion and notify the provider of the potassium level.
Start the insulin infusion at the prescribed rate.
Give the insulin subcutaneously instead of by infusion.
Double the IV fluid rate and then begin the insulin.
items.rationale: Insulin drives potassium into cells, so starting the infusion with a serum potassium below about 3.3 mEq/L can produce lethal hypokalemic dysrhythmias; potassium must be replaced first. Beginning the insulin as prescribed, by any route, ignores the dangerous level, and the subcutaneous route does not remove the potassium-lowering effect. Increasing fluids alone does not correct the deficit before insulin exposure.

items.stem: The nurse is caring for a client admitted with diabetic ketoacidosis. Place the prescribed interventions in the order they should occur.
options: Begin the continuous regular insulin infusion.
Add dextrose to the IV fluids when the glucose approaches 250 mg/dL.
Infuse a bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride.
Transition to subcutaneous insulin once the anion gap closes and the client can eat.
Confirm the serum potassium is adequate for insulin administration.
items.rationale: Treatment begins with isotonic saline because profound dehydration is the most immediate threat, and potassium is verified next since insulin shifts potassium into cells and can cause fatal hypokalemia if started too soon. The insulin infusion then corrects hyperglycemia and ketosis, dextrose is added near 250 mg/dL so insulin can continue clearing ketones without causing hypoglycemia, and subcutaneous insulin replaces the drip only after the acidosis resolves. Starting insulin before fluids and potassium, or stopping it as soon as glucose normalizes, leaves the ketoacidosis untreated.

items.stem: The nurse is preparing a continuous IV insulin infusion. Which insulin is appropriate for intravenous administration?
options: Insulin glargine
NPH insulin
Insulin detemir
Regular insulin
items.rationale: Regular insulin is the only insulin among these that is given intravenously, which is why it is used for infusions in diabetic ketoacidosis and other critical situations. Glargine and detemir are long-acting basal insulins for subcutaneous use only, and NPH is a cloudy intermediate-acting suspension that must never enter a vein. Administering a subcutaneous-only insulin IV could cause unpredictable and dangerous effects.

items.stem: A client who overdosed on propranolol remains severely bradycardic and hypotensive after atropine. Which medication does the nurse anticipate the provider will prescribe next?
options: Naloxone
Flumazenil
Glucagon
Protamine sulfate
items.rationale: Glucagon raises heart rate and contractility through its own receptor, bypassing the blocked beta receptors, which makes it the agent of choice for beta-blocker overdose that does not respond to atropine. Naloxone reverses opioids, flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, and protamine reverses heparin, so none of them addresses beta blockade. The nurse should also monitor glucose, because glucagon transiently raises it.

items.stem: The nurse is teaching family members how to respond when a client with diabetes is found unresponsive at home with suspected severe hypoglycemia. Place the actions in the correct order.
options: Turn the client onto the side.
Offer a carbohydrate snack once the client wakes and can swallow safely.
Confirm the client cannot be roused and must not be given anything by mouth.
Notify the provider that the episode occurred, or call emergency services if there is no response.
Inject the prescribed glucagon into a large muscle.
items.rationale: The family first confirms the client is truly unresponsive, because oral glucose is unsafe for anyone who cannot swallow and could be aspirated. Positioning the client on the side protects the airway since glucagon frequently causes vomiting, and the injection is then given into a large muscle. Once the client awakens and can swallow, carbohydrates are given to restore glycogen and prevent recurrence, and the provider or emergency services are contacted to follow up on the episode.

items.stem: A client with bleeding esophageal varices is started on a continuous octreotide infusion. The nurse understands the medication is prescribed for which purpose?
options: To dissolve clots that are obstructing the portal vein
To reduce blood flow in the portal circulation and slow the bleeding
To raise the systemic blood pressure during the hemorrhage
To neutralize gastric acid and protect the varices from erosion
items.rationale: Octreotide is a somatostatin analog that constricts splanchnic vessels and lowers portal pressure, which decreases blood flow through the bleeding varices. It has no thrombolytic action and is not a systemic vasopressor. Acid suppression is provided separately with proton pump inhibitors, and the nurse should monitor glucose because octreotide alters insulin and glucagon release.

items.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with central diabetes insipidus who is starting intranasal desmopressin. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Weigh yourself daily and report sudden weight gain.
Report headache, confusion, or nausea right away.
Expect your urine output to decrease and the urine to look more concentrated.
Drink at least 4 liters of fluid every day while on this medication.
Take an extra dose whenever urination increases.
items.rationale: Desmopressin replaces antidiuretic hormone, so falling urine output with more concentrated urine shows the drug is working, and daily weights detect the water retention that precedes overt toxicity. Headache, confusion, and nausea are warning signs of water intoxication with hyponatremia and must be reported immediately. Forcing 4 liters of fluid invites water overload, and doses are never self-adjusted; increased urination should instead be reported to the provider.

items.stem: The nurse is reviewing laboratory results for a client taking levothyroxine for hypothyroidism. Which value is primarily used to determine whether the dose is correct?
options: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level
Serum calcium level
Fasting blood glucose level
Serum sodium level
items.rationale: The TSH level reflects how well levothyroxine is replacing thyroid hormone: a persistently high TSH indicates underreplacement, while a suppressed TSH suggests the dose is too high. Calcium relates to parathyroid rather than thyroid replacement, and glucose and sodium do not guide levothyroxine dosing. Clients should also report palpitations, tremor, or heat intolerance, which suggest excessive dosing.

items.stem: The nurse is teaching a client about newly prescribed levothyroxine. Which instruction about timing is correct?
options: Take the tablet at bedtime with a small snack.
Take the tablet with breakfast and your calcium supplement.
Take the tablet at whatever time is convenient, varying with your schedule.
Take the tablet in the morning on an empty stomach, 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast.
items.rationale: Levothyroxine is best absorbed on an empty stomach, so it is taken in the morning 30 to 60 minutes before food at a consistent time each day. Food, calcium, and iron all bind the drug and sharply reduce absorption, which is why taking it with breakfast or a supplement is incorrect. Varying the time or pairing it with a bedtime snack produces inconsistent hormone levels.

items.stem: The nurse is providing teaching for a client who takes levothyroxine daily. Which statements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Take the medication at the same time every day.
Separate the dose from calcium or iron supplements by at least 4 hours.
Plan to take this medication for the rest of your life.
Stop the medication once your energy level returns to normal.
Report a rapid or pounding heartbeat to the provider.
Double the dose on days when you feel more fatigued.
items.rationale: Consistent daily timing keeps hormone levels stable, calcium and iron bind levothyroxine and must be separated by several hours, and hypothyroidism usually requires lifelong replacement. Palpitations or a racing heart suggest the dose is too high and should be reported. Stopping the drug when symptoms improve allows hypothyroidism to return, and doses are never self-adjusted based on daily fatigue.

items.stem: A client taking methimazole for hyperthyroidism calls the clinic. Which report requires the most immediate attention by the nurse?
options: Mild nausea shortly after doses
A weight gain of 1 pound over the past week
A sore throat and fever
Feeling more tired at bedtime
items.rationale: Methimazole and propylthiouracil can cause agranulocytosis, and a sore throat with fever is often its first sign, so the client needs an immediate white blood cell count and must stop the drug if the count is low. Mild nausea is a common and manageable effect. Slight weight gain and improved ability to rest can simply reflect the intended slowing of an overactive thyroid.

items.stem: A client who has taken prednisone daily for 2 years is scheduled for major abdominal surgery. Which prescription does the nurse anticipate for the perioperative period?
options: Discontinuing the prednisone 48 hours before surgery
Supplemental IV corticosteroid doses around the time of surgery
Reducing the prednisone to half the usual dose on the day of surgery
Replacing the prednisone with an NSAID until the incision heals
items.rationale: Long-term corticosteroid therapy suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, leaving the adrenal glands unable to mount the cortisol surge that major stress demands, so stress-dose steroids are given perioperatively to prevent adrenal crisis with vascular collapse. Stopping or halving the drug before surgery invites exactly that crisis. NSAIDs provide no glucocorticoid activity and add bleeding and ulcer risks.

items.stem: The nurse is teaching a client who will take prednisone long term for an autoimmune disorder. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Take the medication with food.
Never stop the medication abruptly.
Report fever, sore throat, or other signs of infection.
Check your blood glucose more often if you have diabetes.
Expect weight loss and increased muscle mass while on this drug.
Take the daily dose at bedtime to improve sleep.
items.rationale: Corticosteroids irritate the gastric mucosa, so doses are taken with food, and therapy must be tapered rather than stopped abruptly because the suppressed adrenal glands cannot immediately resume cortisol production. Steroids mask and promote infection, making early reporting essential, and they raise blood glucose, so clients with diabetes need closer monitoring. The drug actually causes weight gain and muscle wasting, and morning dosing mimics the natural cortisol rhythm while bedtime dosing worsens insomnia.

items.stem: A client taking weekly oral alendronate calls the clinic. Which report requires the nurse to notify the provider immediately?
options: New pain or difficulty when swallowing
Occasional mild nausea on the dosing day
A dull muscle ache during the first week of therapy
Constipation relieved by increasing dietary fiber
items.rationale: New dysphagia or pain with swallowing in a client on an oral bisphosphonate suggests esophagitis or esophageal ulceration, a serious complication that requires the drug to be held and the client evaluated. Mild nausea, transient early muscle aches, and manageable constipation are common minor effects that call for routine follow-up. Clients should also report new thigh or groin pain and jaw pain, which can signal atypical fracture or osteonecrosis of the jaw.
