If removing the trigger does not lower the pressure, the provider is notified and a rapid-acting antihypertensive is given to prevent stroke or seizure.

items.stem: Twelve hours after a T3 spinal cord injury, the nurse assesses the client for spinal shock. Which findings are consistent with spinal shock? Select all that apply.
options: Flaccid paralysis below the level of the injury
Absent deep tendon reflexes below the injury
Spastic hyperreflexia of the lower extremities
Urinary retention with bladder distention
Pounding headache with a blood pressure of 220/110 mm Hg
Loss of sensation below the level of the injury
items.rationale: Spinal shock is the temporary loss of all reflex, motor, sensory, and autonomic activity below the injury that begins shortly after cord trauma, so flaccid paralysis, areflexia, urinary retention, and absent sensation are expected. Spasticity and hyperreflexia appear later, and their return signals that spinal shock is resolving. A pounding headache with severe hypertension describes autonomic dysreflexia, which occurs only after spinal shock has resolved.

items.stem: The nurse cares for a client wearing a halo fixation device with a vest after a cervical fracture. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Keep the correctly sized wrench attached to the vest at all times
Turn the client in bed by grasping the metal frame of the halo
Inspect the skin under the vest liner every day for pressure areas
Perform pin-site care as prescribed and report loose pins or drainage
Loosen the vest at bedtime so the client can sleep comfortably
Teach the client to scan the environment by moving the eyes, since the head cannot turn
items.rationale: The wrench stays with the vest so the anterior portion can be removed immediately if cardiopulmonary resuscitation is needed. Daily skin inspection under the liner and prescribed pin-site care prevent breakdown and infection, and because the halo rigidly fixes the head, the client must learn to scan with the eyes and turn the whole body. The device is never used as a handle for turning, and the vest is never loosened without an order because both actions can disrupt cervical alignment.

items.stem: A client with a suspected thoracic spinal injury must be repositioned using the logrolling technique. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: On the leader's count, turn the client as one unit, keeping the spine in straight alignment.
Position pillows behind the back and between the legs to keep the spine aligned after the turn.
Gather at least two other staff members to assist with the turn.
Have the client fold the arms across the chest and place a pillow between the knees.
items.rationale: Logrolling requires a coordinated team of at least three people so the head, shoulders, and hips move together without twisting the injured spine. Crossing the arms and padding between the knees prepares the body to move as a unit, the synchronized turn on the leader's count keeps the vertebral column in a straight line, and pillows then hold the achieved alignment. Any rotation or flexion during the turn could convert an unstable fracture into a cord injury.

items.stem: The nurse monitors a client with a severe traumatic brain injury. Which set of vital sign changes should the nurse report immediately as a sign of brainstem compression?
options: Blood pressure 92/70 mm Hg, heart rate 122, rapid shallow respirations
Blood pressure 196/58 mm Hg, heart rate 46, irregular respirations
Blood pressure 138/86 mm Hg, heart rate 98, regular respirations
Blood pressure 110/74 mm Hg, heart rate 88, deep sighing respirations
items.rationale: A rising systolic pressure with a widening pulse pressure, bradycardia, and an irregular respiratory pattern make up the Cushing triad, a late and ominous sign that intracranial pressure is compressing the brainstem and herniation is imminent. Hypotension with tachycardia suggests hemorrhage elsewhere in the body rather than rising intracranial pressure. Recognizing the triad demands immediate provider notification and preparation for emergency measures to lower the pressure.

items.stem: A client with a basilar skull fracture has thin, clear fluid dripping from the nose. Which instruction should the nurse give the client?
options: Blow the nose gently to keep the airway clear
Do not blow the nose, sneeze with the mouth open, and let the fluid drain onto a loose pad
Pack the nostril firmly with sterile gauze to stop the leak
Sniff the drainage back and swallow it until the provider arrives
items.rationale: Clear nasal drainage after a basilar skull fracture may be cerebrospinal fluid, which can be checked for a halo or ring sign on gauze and tests positive for glucose. Nose blowing, packing, suctioning, or sniffing can force organisms upward through the torn dura and cause meningitis, so the fluid is allowed to drain freely onto a loose absorbent pad and the finding is reported. The client should also avoid straining and should sneeze with the mouth open to limit pressure on the fracture site.

items.stem: A softball player was briefly knocked unconscious by a line drive to the temple, then woke up alert and now insists on returning to the game. Why must this client still be monitored closely?
options: A lucid interval can precede rapid deterioration from an arterial epidural hematoma
Repeat loss of consciousness is impossible once the client has fully awakened
Slow venous bleeding always produces symptoms within the first five minutes
Temporal impacts cause only scalp injuries and never intracranial bleeding
items.rationale: An epidural hematoma classically follows a temporal blow that tears the middle meningeal artery, and the client may lose consciousness briefly, awaken to a deceptively normal lucid interval, and then deteriorate rapidly as arterial blood collects. This makes continued neurologic observation and imaging essential even when the client feels well. A subdural hematoma, by contrast, is usually venous and develops more slowly over hours to weeks.

items.stem: A head-injured client opens the eyes only to painful stimuli, makes incomprehensible moaning sounds, and withdraws from pain. Which Glasgow Coma Scale score should the nurse document?
items.rationale: Eye opening to pain scores 2, incomprehensible sounds score 2 on the verbal scale, and withdrawal from pain scores 4 on the motor scale, for a total of 8. A score of 8 or less generally defines severe brain injury and coma, so this client needs airway protection and intensive monitoring. Accurate serial scoring matters more than any single number because a drop of two or more points signals deterioration.

items.stem: A coworker reports that a client suddenly stopped mid-conversation, stared blankly, smacked the lips, and picked at the bed linens for about a minute, and now remembers none of it. Which type of seizure does this describe?
options: Absence seizure
Focal seizure with impaired awareness
Generalized tonic-clonic seizure
Myoclonic seizure
items.rationale: Automatisms such as lip smacking and picking at clothing, combined with impaired awareness and amnesia for the event, characterize a focal seizure with impaired awareness, previously called a complex partial seizure. Absence seizures cause brief staring but typically last only seconds without automatisms and occur mostly in children. Tonic-clonic seizures involve bilateral convulsive movements, and myoclonic seizures are sudden brief muscle jerks.

items.stem: A hospitalized client's generalized tonic-clonic seizure has just ended. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.
options: Reorient the client to the surroundings.
Turn the client to a side-lying position.
Document the seizure characteristics and its duration.
Suction the oropharynx if secretions are present.
Assess vital signs and check the client for injuries.
items.rationale: In the postictal period the priority is a patent airway, so the client is turned to the side first to let saliva drain and prevent aspiration, with suction used if secretions pool. Vital signs and an injury check follow because the airway takes precedence over assessment. Clients are typically confused and drowsy after a seizure, so quiet reorientation comes next, and documentation of what was observed and how long it lasted completes the response.

items.stem: A client has been seizing continuously for six minutes. The client is side-lying with oxygen applied and suction at the bedside. Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Administer the prescribed intravenous lorazepam
Insert an oral airway between the clenched teeth
Obtain a stat electroencephalogram before giving any medication
Give the prescribed maintenance dose of oral levetiracetam
items.rationale: A seizure lasting five minutes or longer is status epilepticus, a medical emergency that causes hypoxia and neuronal injury, and an intravenous benzodiazepine such as lorazepam is the first-line drug to stop it. Nothing is forced between the teeth during a seizure because it can break teeth and obstruct the airway. Diagnostic studies and oral maintenance drugs do not address the immediate emergency of ongoing seizure activity.

items.stem: A client arrives with ischemic stroke symptoms that began 90 minutes ago and is being evaluated for intravenous alteplase. Which finding in the history would exclude the client from receiving the drug?
options: Blood glucose of 130 mg/dL on arrival
A gastrointestinal hemorrhage two weeks ago
A blood pressure of 160/90 mm Hg
Daily low-dose aspirin use for the past year
items.rationale: Recent active internal bleeding such as a gastrointestinal hemorrhage is an absolute contraindication to thrombolytic therapy because alteplase dissolves protective clots everywhere, not just in the cerebral artery. A glucose of 130, a pressure below 185/110, and prior antiplatelet use do not exclude treatment. Hemorrhagic stroke on computed tomography, recent intracranial surgery, and presentation beyond the treatment window are other key exclusions the nurse helps screen for.

items.stem: A client is rushed to the emergency department with sudden right-sided weakness and slurred speech. Place the steps of the stroke thrombolytic workflow in the correct order.
options: Confirm the blood pressure is below 185/110 mm Hg and review the exclusion criteria.
Perform frequent neurologic and blood pressure checks while monitoring for bleeding.
Establish the exact time the client was last known to be at baseline.
Administer the alteplase bolus followed by the continuous infusion.
Obtain a stat noncontrast computed tomography scan of the head.
items.rationale: The last-known-well time is established first because eligibility for alteplase depends on treating within 3 hours, extended to 4.5 hours for selected clients. A noncontrast head scan must then rule out hemorrhage, since giving a thrombolytic into a bleeding brain is lethal, and the remaining exclusion criteria and blood pressure limit are verified before the bolus and infusion are given. Afterward the client is monitored closely with frequent neurologic and blood pressure checks because bleeding is the major complication.

items.stem: A client with left homonymous hemianopsia after a stroke is startled when staff seem to "appear out of nowhere" on the left. The client is aware of the deficit. Which intervention should the nurse teach?
options: Turn the head deliberately toward the left to scan the entire environment
Keep all personal items on the left side to force use of that visual field
Wear a patch over the left eye during waking hours
Rely on family members to describe everything on the left side
items.rationale: Homonymous hemianopsia is loss of the same visual half-field in both eyes, and because this client is aware of the deficit, teaching a conscious head-turning scanning technique restores a full view of the environment. Placing needed items on the blind side is unsafe early on, and patching an eye does not correct a field cut that exists in both eyes. This differs from unilateral neglect, in which the client is unaware the affected side exists and must first be protected and then gradually cued to attend to it.

items.stem: A client with expressive aphasia after a stroke becomes frustrated while trying to speak. Which approach by the nurse is best?
options: Finish the client's sentences to reduce the frustration
Give the client unhurried time to respond and offer a picture board as an alternative
Speak loudly and slowly so the client can understand better
Limit conversation until speech therapy has restored fluent speech
items.rationale: In expressive aphasia the client understands language but struggles to produce words, so the nurse allows generous time, asks questions that can be answered briefly, and offers alternatives such as picture boards, writing, or gestures. Finishing sentences increases frustration and dependence, and raising the voice does not help because hearing and comprehension are intact. Continued communication attempts should be encouraged rather than avoided.

items.stem: A client with Guillain-Barré syndrome has weakness that began in the feet and has now reached the thighs and hands. Which assessment is the nurse's priority?
options: Serial measurement of vital capacity and respiratory effort
Hourly deep tendon reflex testing of the arms
Pupil size and reaction to light every two hours
Bladder scanning after each voiding
items.rationale: Guillain-Barré syndrome causes ascending paralysis that can reach the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, so serial vital capacity and respiratory assessments detect impending failure before the client stops ventilating, allowing elective intubation rather than a crisis. Reflexes are already absent or diminished and pupil checks are not the central concern in this peripheral nerve disorder. Treatment with plasmapheresis or intravenous immunoglobulin is most effective when started early, and autonomic instability also requires cardiac monitoring.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the history and assessment of a client with suspected Guillain-Barré syndrome. Which findings support this diagnosis? Select all that apply.
options: Symmetric weakness that began in the legs and is moving upward
A respiratory or gastrointestinal infection within the past few weeks
Tingling and numbness of the hands and feet
Sudden facial droop with weakness on only one side of the body
New confusion and memory loss that preceded the weakness
items.rationale: Guillain-Barré syndrome is an immune-mediated demyelination of peripheral nerves that typically follows a recent viral or bacterial infection and produces symmetric ascending weakness with paresthesias. The disorder spares the brain, so cognition remains intact throughout the illness. Sudden unilateral face and arm weakness suggests a stroke and calls for an entirely different emergency response.

items.stem: A client newly diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis asks the nurse what to expect. Which point should the nurse include in early planning?
options: Memory and thinking will decline before the muscles weaken
While speech is still strong, decide on a communication method and discuss wishes about mechanical ventilation
Sensation in the arms and legs will be lost before movement is affected
Symptoms typically flare and then go into remission for months at a time
items.rationale: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis progressively destroys motor neurons while cognition and sensation are generally preserved, so the client will eventually lose the ability to speak and to breathe independently. Establishing an alternative communication system and documenting advance directive decisions about ventilation while the client can still express wishes are early priorities. A relapsing-remitting pattern describes multiple sclerosis, not the steady progression of this disease.

items.stem: A client with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis asks which activity to avoid to reduce the chance of worsening symptoms. Which activity should the nurse identify?
options: Swimming laps in a cool indoor pool
Soaking in a hot tub after exercise
Taking a short walk in the early morning
Doing gentle stretching before bedtime
items.rationale: Heat slows conduction in demyelinated nerves, so hot tubs, hot baths, saunas, and exercising in hot weather can temporarily worsen or trigger multiple sclerosis symptoms. Cool-water swimming is actually encouraged because it provides exercise while dissipating body heat. Infection, stress, and fatigue are other common triggers of exacerbations the client should learn to manage.

items.stem: The nurse plans mealtime care for a client with trigeminal neuralgia. Which intervention is appropriate?
options: Serve foods lukewarm and have the client chew on the unaffected side
Offer iced drinks to numb the painful area before meals
Massage the affected cheek briskly before each meal to relax the muscles
Position a fan to blow gently across the client's face while eating
items.rationale: Trigeminal neuralgia produces excruciating facial pain triggered by light touch, chewing, temperature extremes, and drafts, so lukewarm food and chewing on the unaffected side minimize stimulation of the nerve. Iced drinks, facial massage, and moving air are all classic triggers that can set off a paroxysm of pain. Carbamazepine is the usual first-line medication, and clients may also need reminders to perform oral hygiene, which they often avoid because of the pain.

items.stem: A client with Bell palsy cannot completely close the right eye. Which instruction should the nurse provide?
options: Rinse the eye with tap water each morning to remove crusting
Instill lubricating eye drops during the day and patch or tape the eye shut at night
Avoid all facial movement until the paralysis resolves
Prepare for the facial weakness to be permanent in most cases
items.rationale: When the eyelid cannot close, the cornea dries and can ulcerate, so artificial tears during the day and patching or taping the lid closed at night protect the eye. Most clients with Bell palsy recover substantially within weeks to months, and gentle facial exercises and chewing on the unaffected side are encouraged during recovery. Tap water is not sterile and does not provide the sustained lubrication the cornea needs.

items.stem: The nurse plans care for a client with Parkinson disease who has episodes of freezing while walking. Which interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Administer carbidopa-levodopa at the exact times scheduled
Teach the client to rock gently from side to side to initiate movement when frozen
Remove throw rugs and clutter from walking paths at home
Encourage the client to hurry through doorways to avoid freezing in them
Give each levodopa dose with a high-protein snack to prevent nausea
Instruct the client to step over an imaginary line when the feet feel stuck to the floor
items.rationale: Levodopa has a short duration of effect, and even slightly late doses can leave the client suddenly rigid and unable to move, so on-time administration is essential. Rocking side to side and visualizing a line to step over are proven strategies for breaking a freezing episode, and clearing walkways reduces the fall risk that freezing and festinating gait create. Rushing increases falls, and high-protein intake taken with levodopa competes with its absorption and reduces its effect.

items.stem: The adult child of a client with Huntington disease asks the nurse about the chance of developing the disease. Which response is accurate?
options: Only sons inherit the gene from an affected parent
Each child of an affected parent has a 50 percent chance of inheriting the gene
The disease skips a generation before appearing again
A person who has no symptoms by age 30 did not inherit the gene
items.rationale: Huntington disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, so every child of an affected parent, regardless of sex, has a 50 percent chance of receiving the gene, and inheriting it means the disease will eventually develop. Symptoms most often begin between ages 30 and 50, so being symptom-free at 30 is not reassuring. Presymptomatic genetic testing exists, and the nurse should offer referral to genetic counseling before any testing decision.

items.stem: The nurse assesses a college student with a severe headache and fever for possible bacterial meningitis. Which findings support this concern? Select all that apply.
options: A stiff neck that resists flexion
Flexion of the hips and knees when the neck is bent forward
Pain and resistance when the knee is straightened while the hip is flexed
Photophobia with the severe headache
Bilateral pitting edema of the ankles
Twitching of the cheek when the face is tapped
items.rationale: Nuchal rigidity, a positive Brudzinski sign in which neck flexion causes the hips and knees to flex, and a positive Kernig sign in which knee extension with a flexed hip causes pain and resistance all reflect meningeal irritation, and photophobia with headache and fever completes the classic picture. Ankle edema relates to fluid status, not meningitis. Facial twitching when the cheek is tapped is the Chvostek sign of hypocalcemia.

items.stem: A client is admitted with suspected meningococcal meningitis. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.
options: Administer the first dose of the prescribed intravenous antibiotic.
Place the client in a private room on droplet precautions.
Work with the health department to identify close contacts who need prophylactic antibiotics.
Assist with the lumbar puncture and collection of blood cultures.
items.rationale: Meningococcal disease spreads by respiratory droplets, so isolating the client in a private room on droplet precautions immediately protects staff and other clients. Cultures of blood and cerebrospinal fluid are obtained before antibiotics whenever possible so the organism can be identified, but the first antibiotic dose must follow promptly because delays worsen mortality. Household members and other close contacts then receive prophylaxis such as rifampin or ciprofloxacin, and droplet precautions can be discontinued after 24 hours of effective therapy.

items.stem: The nurse assists with a lumbar puncture for a client with suspected meningitis. Place the nursing responsibilities in the correct order.
options: Position the client side-lying with the knees drawn toward the chest.
Have the client empty the bladder.
Keep the client lying flat and encourage oral fluids.
Verify that informed consent has been obtained.
Support the client in remaining still while the needle is inserted and specimens are collected.
items.rationale: Consent is verified before any invasive procedure begins, and an empty bladder makes the positioning more comfortable and prevents interruption. The side-lying fetal position bows the back and widens the spaces between the lumbar vertebrae for needle insertion, during which the nurse helps the client hold completely still. Afterward the client lies flat to reduce the chance of a spinal headache, and fluids help replace the cerebrospinal fluid that was withdrawn.

items.stem: The nurse cares for a client with an external ventricular drain in place for intracranial pressure monitoring. Which action is correct?
options: Level the drainage system at the tragus of the ear and re-level it whenever the head of the bed changes
Keep the drain open to gravity while transporting and repositioning the client
Flush the ventricular catheter toward the brain each shift to maintain patency
Lower the collection chamber to the floor to speed drainage of cerebrospinal fluid
items.rationale: The transducer and drip chamber are leveled at the tragus, which approximates the foramen of Monro, and must be re-leveled after every change in head-of-bed position because the height of the chamber controls how much cerebrospinal fluid drains. The drain is typically clamped briefly per protocol during transport or repositioning so sudden position changes do not cause rapid overdrainage. Flushing toward the brain risks infection and pressure spikes, and dropping the chamber to the floor would siphon fluid and collapse the ventricles.

items.stem: An 82-year-old client who fell at home has severe right hip pain. The right leg appears shorter than the left and is rotated outward. Which injury should the nurse suspect?
options: A fractured hip
A deep vein thrombosis
Trochanteric bursitis
Sciatic nerve compression
items.rationale: Shortening with external rotation of the affected leg after a fall is the classic presentation of a hip fracture, because muscle spasm pulls the fragments out of alignment. The client should not bear weight, and the limb is kept aligned while surgical repair is arranged; skin traction such as Buck traction is sometimes applied before surgery to reduce painful muscle spasm. Thrombosis, bursitis, and nerve compression do not shorten or rotate the limb.

items.stem: The nurse cares for a client in balanced skeletal traction for a fractured femur. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Ensure the weights hang freely without touching the floor or the bed
Remove the weights briefly whenever the client is repositioned
Inspect the pin sites each shift for redness, drainage, or loosening
Keep the ropes in the pulley grooves with knots positioned away from the pulleys
Add or remove weight according to the client's pain rating
Perform neurovascular checks of the affected extremity at regular intervals
items.rationale: Traction is effective only when the prescribed pull is continuous, so the weights must hang freely, the ropes must ride in the pulley grooves without obstruction from knots, and skeletal traction weights are never lifted or removed by the nurse. Pin sites are portals for infection and are inspected and cared for as prescribed, and regular neurovascular checks detect circulatory or nerve compromise early. Only the provider changes the amount of weight applied.

items.stem: The nurse provides home instructions to a client with a new arm cast. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Report pain that keeps worsening despite elevation and the prescribed analgesic
Slide a padded coat hanger under the cast to scratch itchy skin
Keep the casted arm elevated above heart level for the first day or two
Report a painful warm spot on the cast or a foul odor coming from beneath it
Cover the cast with plastic and submerge the arm while bathing
Report numbness, tingling, or fingers that become pale or cold
items.rationale: Pain unrelieved by elevation and analgesics, along with numbness, tingling, pallor, or coolness of the fingers, can signal compartment syndrome and must be reported immediately. A hot spot on the cast or a foul odor suggests infection developing beneath it, and elevation during the first 24 to 48 hours limits swelling inside the rigid cast. Nothing is ever inserted under a cast because it can break the skin and start an infection, and a covered cast may be protected from splashes but never submerged. Rough cast edges can be padded, or petaled, with tape to protect the skin.

items.stem: It is the second day after a client's above-the-knee amputation. Which positioning intervention should the nurse implement?
options: Keep the residual limb elevated on two pillows at all times
Assist the client to lie prone for 20 to 30 minutes several times a day
Encourage the client to sit in a chair for most of the day
Place a large pillow under the hip and knee whenever the client is supine
items.rationale: During the first 24 hours the residual limb may be elevated to control edema, but after that continued elevation and prolonged sitting keep the hip flexed and can create a flexion contracture that prevents successful prosthetic fitting. Lying prone several times daily extends the hip and stretches the flexor muscles. Pillows under the hip or knee promote the same harmful flexed position the prone periods are designed to prevent.

items.stem: A client whose left leg was amputated a week ago reports burning, cramping pain in the left foot that is no longer there. Which response by the nurse is appropriate?
options: Explain that pain is impossible because the foot has been removed
Administer the prescribed analgesic, because phantom limb pain is real pain
Tell the client the sensation is imaginary and will stop with distraction
Withhold analgesics so the client does not become dependent on them
items.rationale: Phantom limb pain arises from severed nerve pathways that continue to send signals the brain interprets as coming from the missing limb, so the pain is physiologically real and is treated as such. Dismissing it as imaginary damages trust and leaves the pain unmanaged. Analgesics and adjuvant medications such as anticonvulsants or antidepressants, along with mirror therapy, are legitimate treatments, and the sensations usually diminish over time.

items.stem: A client is being discharged to home with a peripherally inserted central catheter for treatment of osteomyelitis of the tibia. Which statement indicates the teaching was effective?
options: "I will need intravenous antibiotics for several weeks and must finish the entire course even if I feel better."
"One week of antibiotic pills should clear this bone infection completely."
"I can stop the antibiotics as soon as the leg pain goes away."
"The infection is cured now, so the catheter is just a precaution."
items.rationale: Bone has limited blood supply, so osteomyelitis requires four to six weeks or more of intravenous antibiotics, and stopping early allows surviving organisms to produce chronic infection that is far harder to eradicate. Symptom relief comes long before the organism is eliminated, so pain resolution is not a signal to stop therapy. The client also needs teaching on catheter site care and on reporting fever or increasing pain.

items.stem: The nurse reviews assessment data for a client with joint pain. Which finding suggests rheumatoid arthritis rather than osteoarthritis?
options: Morning stiffness lasting over an hour with warm, swollen joints in both hands and fatigue
Stiffness that resolves within 15 minutes of getting out of bed
Aching in one knee that worsens with use and improves with rest
Bony enlargement of the finger joints without warmth or redness
items.rationale: Rheumatoid arthritis is a systemic autoimmune disease producing symmetric, warm, swollen joints, prolonged morning stiffness, and constitutional symptoms such as fatigue and low-grade fever. Osteoarthritis is localized wear of cartilage, so it causes brief stiffness, pain that follows activity and eases with rest, and hard bony nodes without inflammation. Distinguishing the patterns matters because rheumatoid disease is treated with immune-modifying drugs while osteoarthritis management centers on joint protection and analgesia.

items.stem: A client with recurrent gout takes daily allopurinol and has colchicine prescribed as needed. Which statement indicates the client understands the treatment plan?
options: "I take allopurinol every day to keep my uric acid down and use colchicine only when a flare starts."
"Allopurinol will relieve the pain of an attack within a few hours of taking it."
"Beer is fine as long as I never miss my daily allopurinol dose."
"I should stop the allopurinol whenever my joints feel completely normal."
items.rationale: Allopurinol lowers uric acid production over time to prevent future attacks but does nothing for acute pain, while colchicine treats the inflammation of a flare and works best when started at the first twinge. Alcohol, organ meats, and shellfish raise uric acid and can trigger attacks even when medication is taken faithfully. Daily urate-lowering therapy continues long term, because stopping it lets crystals re-form; the client should also report diarrhea, an early sign of colchicine toxicity.

items.stem: The nurse teaches a community group of perimenopausal women about preventing osteoporosis. Which points should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Perform weight-bearing exercise such as brisk walking most days of the week
Take in adequate calcium and vitamin D through diet or supplements
Avoid smoking and limit alcohol intake
Choose swimming as the most effective exercise for building bone density
Understand that bone loss cannot be slowed once menopause begins
Obtain bone density screening at the intervals recommended by the provider
items.rationale: Bones respond to the mechanical stress of weight-bearing and resistance exercise by maintaining density, and calcium with vitamin D supplies the raw material for bone remodeling. Smoking and excess alcohol both accelerate bone loss, and screening identifies declining density while treatment such as bisphosphonates can still prevent fractures. Swimming is excellent cardiovascular exercise but is not weight-bearing, and bone loss can absolutely be slowed after menopause with lifestyle measures and medication.

items.stem: A client with fibromyalgia reports widespread muscle pain, poor sleep, and exhaustion. Which recommendation should the nurse make?
options: Rest in bed until the pain resolves completely
Begin a regular program of low-impact exercise such as walking or water aerobics
Request long-term opioid therapy for the muscle pain
Avoid all physical activity on days when pain is present
items.rationale: Regular low-impact aerobic exercise is one of the most effective treatments for fibromyalgia, gradually reducing pain and improving sleep and function, whereas inactivity and bed rest worsen deconditioning and symptoms. Opioids are not effective for the amplified central pain processing of fibromyalgia; medications such as duloxetine or pregabalin, sleep hygiene, and stress management are used instead. The nurse should also affirm that the pain is real, because many clients have felt dismissed.

items.stem: The nurse teaches a client newly diagnosed with systemic lupus erythematosus. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Apply sunscreen and wear protective clothing whenever you are outdoors
Report fever promptly because it may signal a flare or an infection
Stop the prescribed corticosteroid as soon as the facial rash fades
Balance activity with rest periods, especially during flares
Expect that a butterfly-shaped facial rash may appear or worsen after sun exposure
Use a tanning bed as a safe alternative to outdoor sunshine
items.rationale: Ultraviolet light from the sun or tanning beds can trigger both the characteristic butterfly rash across the cheeks and systemic disease flares, so photoprotection is a cornerstone of self-care. Fever is never dismissed because it may herald a flare or an infection in a client whose disease and medications both suppress immunity. Corticosteroids must be tapered rather than stopped abruptly, and pacing activity with rest helps manage the profound fatigue of lupus.

items.stem: A client with human immunodeficiency virus infection has a CD4 count of 180 cells/mm3. Which change in the plan of care should the nurse anticipate?
options: Discontinuing antiretroviral therapy because it is no longer effective
Starting prophylactic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole to prevent Pneumocystis pneumonia
No change, because this CD4 count is within the normal range
Transfer to a protective environment room for the remainder of the illness
items.rationale: A CD4 count below 200 cells/mm3 defines progression to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome and marks the threshold at which Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia becomes likely, so prophylactic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is standard. As counts fall further, other opportunistic infections such as toxoplasmosis and Mycobacterium avium complex become risks with their own prophylaxis thresholds. Antiretroviral therapy is continued and intensified, not stopped, and routine hospitalization in a protective environment is unnecessary.

items.stem: A nursing assistant sustains a needlestick from a client with known human immunodeficiency virus infection. Which teaching about post-exposure prophylaxis is accurate?
options: Begin the antiretroviral regimen as soon as possible, no later than 72 hours after the exposure
Wait for the results of your own antibody test before any medication is considered
Prophylaxis is effective if started any time within two weeks of the exposure
A single dose of antiretroviral medication on the day of exposure is sufficient
items.rationale: Post-exposure prophylaxis works by suppressing the virus before it establishes permanent infection, so the regimen is started as quickly as possible, ideally within hours, and is not effective if begun more than 72 hours after exposure. The full course is taken for 28 days, and baseline and follow-up testing occur alongside, not before, treatment. Pre-exposure prophylaxis is different: it is daily medication taken by uninfected people at ongoing risk before any exposure occurs.

items.stem: Four clients report symptoms after allergen exposures. Which client requires immediate intramuscular epinephrine?
options: A client with itchy hives on one forearm after touching a cat
A client with sneezing and watery eyes during pollen season
A client with throat tightness, audible wheezing, and a blood pressure of 84/50 mm Hg after a bee sting
A client with redness and swelling at an immunization site
items.rationale: Anaphylaxis is a systemic reaction involving the airway, breathing, or circulation, and throat tightness with wheezing and hypotension after a sting demands intramuscular epinephrine without delay because airway swelling and vascular collapse can kill within minutes. Localized hives, seasonal rhinitis symptoms, and injection-site inflammation are limited allergic responses managed with antihistamines, avoidance, or observation. Distinguishing a local reaction from systemic anaphylaxis is the key assessment that drives the treatment.

items.stem: A client has a documented latex allergy. The nurse teaches that which foods may cause a cross-reaction? Select all that apply.
options: Banana
Avocado
Kiwi
White rice
Chestnuts
Baked chicken
items.rationale: Proteins in banana, avocado, kiwi, and chestnut resemble the proteins in natural rubber latex closely enough that the immune system can react to both, a pattern called latex-food syndrome. Clients with latex allergy should be taught to watch for oral itching, hives, or swelling after eating these foods and to report reactions. Rice and poultry contain no cross-reactive latex proteins.

items.stem: The nurse teaches a client with iron-deficiency anemia about taking oral ferrous sulfate. Which instruction is correct?
options: Take the tablet with a full glass of milk to protect the stomach
Take the iron with orange juice on an empty stomach when tolerated
Take an antacid with each dose to prevent heartburn
Stop the medication if the stools turn dark in color
items.rationale: Iron is absorbed best on an empty stomach, and the vitamin C in orange juice enhances absorption, while milk and antacids bind or buffer iron and sharply reduce the amount absorbed. Dark or black stools are an expected, harmless effect of oral iron and are not a reason to stop therapy. If liquid iron is prescribed, it should be diluted and sipped through a straw to prevent staining the teeth.

items.stem: A client has macrocytic anemia and the provider is differentiating vitamin B12 deficiency from folate deficiency. Which finding points specifically to vitamin B12 deficiency?
options: Persistent fatigue with everyday activities
Pallor of the skin and mucous membranes
Numbness and tingling of the hands and feet with unsteady balance
A smooth, sore, reddened tongue
items.rationale: Both deficiencies produce large red cells, fatigue, pallor, and glossitis, but only vitamin B12 deficiency damages the nervous system, causing paresthesias, proprioceptive loss, and gait instability that can become permanent if treatment is delayed. In pernicious anemia the gastric parietal cells fail to make intrinsic factor, so dietary B12 cannot be absorbed and the client needs lifelong parenteral or intranasal replacement. Folate deficiency is corrected with oral folic acid and dietary sources such as green leafy vegetables.

items.stem: The nurse reviews laboratory results for a client with suspected aplastic anemia. Which pattern is consistent with this diagnosis?
options: Decreased red cells, white cells, and platelets
Elevated white cell count with circulating blast cells
Small, pale red cells with normal white cells and platelets
An isolated low platelet count with all other cell lines normal
items.rationale: In aplastic anemia the bone marrow fails, so production of all three cell lines falls and the client shows pancytopenia: anemia causing fatigue, leukopenia causing infection risk, and thrombocytopenia causing bleeding. Elevated white cells with blasts suggest leukemia, microcytic hypochromic cells suggest iron deficiency, and an isolated platelet drop suggests immune thrombocytopenia. Nursing care centers on protecting the client from both infection and bleeding while the marrow is supported or transplanted.

items.stem: A client with sickle cell disease is admitted in vaso-occlusive crisis with severe leg and back pain. Which interventions should the nurse implement first?
options: Apply cold packs to the most painful joints
Begin intravenous hydration, apply oxygen, and give the prescribed opioid analgesic
Restrict oral fluids to prevent circulatory overload
Withhold analgesics until the cause of the pain is confirmed
items.rationale: Vaso-occlusive crisis occurs when sickled cells obstruct small vessels, so the immediate priorities are hydration to dilute the blood and reduce sickling, oxygen to correct the hypoxia that drives further sickling, and aggressive opioid analgesia for pain that is typically severe. Cold promotes vasoconstriction and worsens occlusion, so warmth is used instead. Delaying analgesia is unjustified; the pain of crisis is real and undertreatment is a well-documented problem for these clients.

items.stem: A client with sepsis begins oozing blood from intravenous sites and develops petechiae, and laboratory results show low platelets, low fibrinogen, and an elevated D-dimer. Which explanation describes what is happening?
options: The client has received an accidental overdose of heparin
Widespread clotting throughout small vessels has consumed the platelets and clotting factors, leaving the blood unable to clot
The bone marrow has abruptly stopped producing platelets
The client is having an allergic reaction to the antibiotics
items.rationale: This picture describes disseminated intravascular coagulation, in which sepsis or another trigger activates clotting diffusely, forming microthrombi that damage organs while consuming platelets, fibrinogen, and clotting factors faster than they can be replaced. The paradoxical result is simultaneous clotting and bleeding, reflected in low platelets and fibrinogen with elevated D-dimer from clot breakdown. Treatment targets the underlying cause while blood products replace what has been consumed.

items.stem: The nurse prepares to transfuse a unit of packed red blood cells. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Obtain a full set of baseline vital signs.
Verify the prescription and confirm that consent has been signed.
Begin the transfusion slowly and remain with the client for the first 15 minutes.
Prime the blood administration tubing with 0.9% sodium chloride.
Complete the two-nurse identification check of the client and the unit of blood at the bedside.
items.rationale: The prescription and consent are confirmed before any blood is obtained, and the tubing is primed with normal saline because it is the only compatible solution. The two-nurse bedside verification of the client's identity and the unit's labeling is the single most important safeguard against a fatal hemolytic reaction from mismatched blood. Baseline vital signs taken immediately before starting provide the comparison for detecting a reaction, and the nurse begins slowly and stays for the first 15 minutes because most severe reactions declare themselves early.

items.stem: During a red blood cell transfusion, which finding most clearly indicates an acute hemolytic reaction rather than a febrile nonhemolytic reaction?
options: A temperature increase of 1 degree Celsius with chills and no other symptoms
Scattered hives with itching and no vital sign changes
Flank pain with red-tinged urine and falling blood pressure
Crackles in the lungs with distended neck veins and dyspnea
items.rationale: Acute hemolysis from incompatible blood destroys red cells in the circulation, producing flank pain, hemoglobin in the urine, hypotension, and impending shock and renal injury, and the transfusion must be stopped immediately. Fever and chills alone suggest a febrile nonhemolytic reaction to donor white cell fragments, hives alone suggest a mild allergic reaction, and crackles with venous distention indicate circulatory overload from too-rapid infusion. Differentiating the reaction type determines whether the response is emergency resuscitation, an antipyretic, an antihistamine, or slowing the rate and giving a diuretic.

items.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy has a platelet count of 18,000/mm3. Which bleeding precautions should the nurse implement? Select all that apply.
options: Use the smallest gauge needle possible and hold prolonged pressure after any puncture
Provide a soft-bristled toothbrush for mouth care
Take temperatures rectally to ensure accuracy
Teach the client to use an electric razor instead of a blade
Administer the prescribed aspirin for a mild headache
Instruct the client to avoid straining during bowel movements
items.rationale: With a platelet count this low, spontaneous bleeding is a real danger, so punctures are minimized and compressed, oral care and shaving are done with the gentlest possible tools, and straining is avoided because it can rupture fragile vessels in the rectum or brain. Rectal temperatures and suppositories are prohibited because they can tear the rectal mucosa. Aspirin further impairs the few platelets the client has and should be questioned, with headache also evaluated as possible intracranial bleeding.

items.stem: A client with acute leukemia and an absolute neutrophil count of 300/mm3 develops a temperature of 38.4 degrees Celsius. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.
options: Draw blood cultures from the central line and from a peripheral site.
Administer the prescribed broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotic.
Complete a rapid assessment of vital signs, perfusion, and oxygenation.
Continue frequent monitoring for signs of septic shock.
Notify the oncology provider of the fever and the neutrophil count.
items.rationale: Fever may be the only sign of infection in a client with almost no neutrophils, and it is treated as a medical emergency because sepsis can progress to shock within hours. The nurse rapidly assesses stability first, notifies the provider, and obtains cultures before antibiotics so the organism can be identified, but the broad-spectrum antibiotic must be infused promptly, ideally within an hour of the fever. Ongoing monitoring detects the hypotension and tachycardia of evolving septic shock.

items.stem: A clinic client mentions several recent symptoms. Which combination should the nurse recognize as warranting evaluation for lymphoma?
options: A painless, enlarging lump in the neck with drenching night sweats and unintended weight loss
A tender, warm neck lump that appeared during a sore throat
Symmetric pain and stiffness in the small joints of both hands
A facial rash across the cheeks that worsens in the sun
items.rationale: Painless lymph node enlargement accompanied by drenching night sweats, unexplained fever, and unintended weight loss, together called B symptoms, is the classic presentation of lymphoma and requires prompt evaluation with biopsy. A tender node during a throat infection is a normal reactive response that resolves with the infection. Symmetric hand arthritis suggests rheumatoid disease, and a photosensitive facial rash suggests lupus.

items.stem: The nurse plans care for a client with multiple myeloma. Which interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Encourage a fluid intake of about 3 liters per day unless contraindicated
Use a lift sheet and handle the client gently during repositioning
Maintain strict bed rest to protect the fragile bones
Monitor renal function studies and the serum calcium level
Restrict fluids to reduce the workload on the kidneys
Encourage regular gentle ambulation as tolerated
items.rationale: Myeloma cells erode bone, releasing calcium and creating lytic lesions that fracture with minimal force, so the client is moved gently with a lift sheet while still being walked regularly, because immobility accelerates both bone loss and hypercalcemia. Generous hydration helps the kidneys excrete calcium and the protein light chains that can clog and destroy the tubules, which is also why renal function and calcium are monitored closely. Fluid restriction and strict bed rest would worsen the two greatest threats of the disease.

items.stem: A client with high-burden lymphoma begins induction chemotherapy. Which laboratory pattern should the nurse recognize as tumor lysis syndrome?
options: Elevated potassium, phosphorus, and uric acid with decreased calcium
Elevated calcium and sodium with decreased potassium
Decreased potassium, phosphorus, and uric acid with elevated calcium
Elevated glucose and sodium with normal potassium
items.rationale: When chemotherapy destroys large numbers of tumor cells rapidly, their contents spill into the blood, raising potassium, phosphorus, and uric acid, while the phosphorus binds calcium and drives it down. The hyperkalemia can cause fatal dysrhythmias and the uric acid can crystallize in renal tubules and cause kidney failure. Prevention with aggressive intravenous hydration and agents such as allopurinol or rasburicase begins before chemotherapy, and the nurse monitors these values and the cardiac rhythm closely during treatment.

items.stem: A client with lung cancer reports that the face and neck look swollen every morning, and the nurse observes distended veins across the neck and upper chest with new dyspnea. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Position the client flat with the legs elevated to improve venous return
Elevate the head of the bed and notify the provider immediately
Reassure the client that morning facial puffiness is a common medication effect
Apply warm compresses to the neck and reassess in four hours
items.rationale: Facial and neck swelling with distended chest wall veins and dyspnea indicates superior vena cava syndrome, in which the tumor compresses the great vein returning blood from the head and arms, and it is an oncologic emergency treated urgently with radiation, stenting, or chemotherapy. Elevating the head of the bed uses gravity to reduce venous congestion and ease breathing while the provider is notified. Lying flat worsens the congestion, and dismissing or delaying evaluation risks airway edema and cerebral swelling.

items.stem: A client with metastatic prostate cancer calls the oncology clinic reporting new back pain that is worse when lying down, numbness in both legs, and difficulty starting the urine stream. Which response by the nurse is correct?
options: Advise taking the prescribed analgesic and calling back if the pain persists tomorrow
Recommend gentle back-strengthening exercises and a heating pad
Instruct the client to come in immediately for emergency evaluation
Schedule a routine follow-up appointment for the next available opening
items.rationale: New back pain that worsens when supine, with leg numbness or weakness and new urinary difficulty in a client whose cancer spreads to bone, signals metastatic spinal cord compression, an emergency in which hours matter. Immediate imaging and treatment with corticosteroids, radiation, or surgery can preserve the ability to walk and control the bladder, but function lost before treatment is rarely regained. Any delay through home management or routine scheduling risks permanent paralysis.

items.stem: A client receiving external beam radiation to the chest asks how to care for the skin in the treatment area. Which instruction should the nurse give?
options: Scrub the treatment area daily to remove the marking ink
Wash the area gently with mild soap and lukewarm water, then pat it dry
Apply a heating pad to the area to soothe irritation
Cover the area with adhesive tape to protect it from clothing
items.rationale: Irradiated skin is fragile, so it is cleansed gently with mild soap and lukewarm water and patted rather than rubbed dry, and the ink markings that guide treatment alignment must never be washed off. Heat, cold, sun exposure, adhesive tape, and unapproved lotions or powders all further injure the treatment field. Soft, loose clothing over the area minimizes friction while the skin is vulnerable.

items.stem: A client has a sealed cervical radiation implant in place. Which visitor guideline should the nurse enforce?
options: Visitors may stay as long as they wish because the radiation source is sealed
Limit each visitor to 30 minutes per day and have them sit at least 6 feet from the client
Pregnant visitors may enter if they stay near the doorway
Visitors are safe at the bedside as long as they wear gloves
items.rationale: A sealed internal implant makes the client a temporary radiation source, so exposure to others is controlled through the principles of time, distance, and shielding: visits are limited to about 30 minutes per day at a distance of at least 6 feet. Pregnant women and children under 18 are not permitted to visit at all because developing tissue is most vulnerable to radiation. Gloves protect against contamination, not against the penetrating rays of a sealed source, and staff similarly organize care to minimize their own time in the room.

items.stem: The nurse teaches a client after a right modified radical mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Do not allow blood pressures, injections, or blood draws on the right arm
Wear gloves while gardening and protect the right hand from cuts and burns
Carry heavy grocery bags with the right arm to rebuild its strength
Report swelling, redness, or a feeling of tightness in the right arm
Perform the prescribed arm exercises to restore range of motion
Shave the right underarm with a razor blade once the incision heals
items.rationale: Removing axillary nodes impairs lymph drainage from the arm for life, so anything that constricts, punctures, or injures the arm, including blood pressure cuffs, needlesticks, cuts, and burns, can precipitate lymphedema or infection. New swelling, tightness, or redness is reported promptly because early treatment of lymphedema is far more effective. Prescribed exercises such as hand wall climbing restore shoulder motion, but heavy lifting with the affected arm and blade razors in the numb axilla are avoided, with an electric razor used instead.

items.stem: In which situation must the nurse wash the hands with soap and water rather than use an alcohol-based hand rub?
options: After caring for a client with Clostridioides difficile infection
Before performing a routine head-to-toe assessment
Between caring for two clients when the hands look clean
After removing gloves following an uncomplicated dressing change
items.rationale: Alcohol-based rubs do not kill Clostridioides difficile spores, so soap and water with friction is required to physically remove them from the hands; washing is also required whenever the hands are visibly soiled. In the other situations the hands are not visibly soiled and no spore-forming organism is involved, so an alcohol-based rub is an acceptable and effective choice.

items.stem: The nurse reviews vital signs for four resting adult clients. Which finding is within normal limits?
options: Respiratory rate of 26 breaths/min
Heart rate of 76 beats/min
Oral temperature of 38.6 C (101.5 F)
Blood pressure of 86/48 mm Hg
items.rationale: A resting adult heart rate of 60 to 100 beats/min makes 76 a normal finding. A respiratory rate above the normal 12 to 20 breaths/min indicates tachypnea, an oral temperature of 38.6 C is a fever, and a blood pressure of 86/48 mm Hg is hypotensive; each of those findings warrants further assessment.

items.stem: The nurse is assessing a postoperative client's pain. Which source of information is the most reliable indicator of the pain's presence and intensity?
options: The client's vital sign changes
The client's own report of the pain
The client's facial expression and body language
The nurse's estimate based on the type of surgery
items.rationale: Pain is a subjective experience, so the client's self-report is the single most reliable indicator and should be believed and acted on. Vital signs and nonverbal behavior can be blunted by adaptation or medications and vary widely between individuals, and estimating pain from the procedure substitutes the nurse's judgment for the client's experience.

items.stem: The nurse is reviewing positioning orders on a medical unit. Which client is positioned correctly?
options: A client lying flat in bed for several hours after a lumbar puncture
A client placed in Trendelenburg position to relieve shortness of breath
A client positioned on the left side after a liver biopsy
A client placed in high-Fowler's position to receive a cleansing enema
items.rationale: Lying flat after a lumbar puncture reduces cerebrospinal fluid leakage from the puncture site and helps prevent a spinal headache. A client with dyspnea belongs in high-Fowler's position, not head-down Trendelenburg; after a liver biopsy the client lies on the right side to splint the puncture site against the chest wall; and an enema is given in the left Sims position so the solution follows the natural curve of the sigmoid colon.

items.stem: A provider prescribes oxygen at a precise concentration of 28% for a client with chronic lung disease. Which delivery device should the nurse obtain?
options: Nasal cannula
Venturi mask
Simple face mask
Non-rebreather mask
items.rationale: The Venturi mask mixes oxygen with room air through calibrated adapters, delivering the most precise oxygen concentration of any low- or high-flow device, which is why it is preferred when an exact percentage is prescribed. A nasal cannula runs at 1 to 6 L/min and delivers a variable concentration that changes with the client's breathing pattern, and simple and non-rebreather masks also deliver imprecise, higher concentrations.

items.stem: The nurse prepares to suction a client's tracheostomy. Which technique is correct?
options: Apply suction while gently inserting the catheter
Apply suction only while withdrawing the catheter, limiting each pass to about 10 seconds
Suction the airway on a fixed schedule every hour
Instill normal saline into the tube before each suction pass
items.rationale: Suction is applied only during withdrawal, with each pass limited to roughly 10 seconds, because suctioning removes oxygen along with secretions and can injure the mucosa. Applying suction during insertion traumatizes the airway and depletes more oxygen, suctioning is performed only when assessment shows it is needed rather than on a schedule, and routinely instilling saline can drive secretions deeper and lower oxygen saturation.

items.stem: On the second day after creation of a colostomy, the nurse assesses the stoma. Which finding should be reported to the provider immediately?
options: The stoma appears dark purple to black
The stoma is moist and rosy red
There is mild swelling of the stoma
Flatus is collecting in the pouch
items.rationale: A healthy stoma is moist and red to pink, so a dusky purple or black color signals compromised blood flow and possible necrosis, which is a surgical emergency. Mild edema of a new stoma and the passage of flatus are expected findings in the early postoperative period and simply require continued monitoring.

items.stem: A client who is not permitted to bear weight on the left leg is learning to use crutches. Which technique for going down stairs is correct?
options: Lead with the unaffected right leg, then bring the crutches down
Move the crutches and the affected left leg down first, then bring the unaffected leg down
Hop down each step on the unaffected leg while holding both crutches in one hand
Advance the unaffected leg and both crutches down together in a single motion
items.rationale: Descending stairs, the crutches and the affected leg go down first so the strong leg can control the lowering of the body, remembered as "up with the good, down with the bad." Leading down with the unaffected leg leaves the weak leg and crutches behind and invites a fall, and hopping or moving everything at once sacrifices the stable base of support.

items.stem: The nurse is teaching a client with right-sided leg weakness to walk with a cane. Which instruction is correct?
options: Hold the cane on the right side and step forward with the left leg first
Hold the cane in the left hand and move the cane forward together with the right leg
Hold the cane in the left hand and move the cane forward together with the left leg
Use the cane only when climbing stairs
items.rationale: A cane is held on the strong side, so with right-leg weakness it belongs in the left hand, and it advances together with the weak right leg so the cane and strong leg share the weight-bearing. Holding the cane on the weak side or moving it with the strong leg removes that support, and a cane is used for all ambulation, not just stairs.

items.stem: The nurse observes a client using a standard walker. Which observation indicates correct use?
options: The client moves the walker forward, then steps toward it, keeping the body within the frame
The client carries the walker while going up the stairs
The client pulls on the walker to rise from the chair
The client leans forward over the front bar while stepping
items.rationale: The walker is advanced first and the client then steps into it, staying upright and centered within the frame for a stable base of support. Walkers are never used on stairs, pulling on a walker to stand can tip it over so the client should push up from the chair arms instead, and leaning over the front bar shifts the center of gravity forward and risks a fall.

items.stem: A client's peripheral IV site is cool, pale, and swollen, and the infusion has slowed. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Slow the infusion rate and elevate the arm
Stop the infusion and remove the catheter
Apply pressure over the site while the infusion continues
Flush the catheter briskly to restore the flow
items.rationale: Coolness, pallor, and edema with a sluggish infusion indicate infiltration, meaning fluid is leaking into the surrounding tissue, so the infusion is stopped and the catheter removed before more fluid accumulates; a new line is started at another site. Slowing the rate or applying pressure allows the leak to continue, and flushing forces additional fluid into the tissue. Phlebitis, by contrast, presents with warmth, redness, and a tender cord-like vein.

items.stem: The nurse observes a nursing student administer medications. Which technique is correct?
options: Pulling the pinna down and back to give ear drops to an adult
Using the Z-track method to give an intramuscular injection of iron dextran
Dropping eye medication directly onto the center of the cornea
Massaging the injection site vigorously after a Z-track injection
items.rationale: The Z-track method displaces the skin before injection so the tissue seals over the track afterward, preventing irritating drugs such as iron from leaking into and staining subcutaneous tissue, and the site is not massaged afterward for the same reason. For an adult, the pinna is pulled up and back to straighten the ear canal, while down and back is used for a young child. Eye drops are instilled into the lower conjunctival sac, not onto the sensitive cornea.

items.stem: The nurse watches a nursing student prepare regular and NPH insulin in one syringe. Which action by the student requires the nurse to intervene?
options: Shaking the NPH vial vigorously to mix the suspension
Injecting air into the NPH vial first without withdrawing any insulin
Drawing up the regular insulin before the NPH insulin
Verifying the prepared doses with another nurse
items.rationale: NPH is a suspension that is mixed by gently rolling the vial between the palms; vigorous shaking creates froth and makes the dose inaccurate, so the nurse must intervene. The other actions are correct technique: air is injected into the NPH vial first without drawing medication, the clear regular insulin is drawn up before the cloudy NPH to avoid contaminating the rapid-acting vial, and insulin doses are verified with a second nurse.

items.stem: The nurse is teaching a client how to care for a new hearing aid. Which instruction is correct?
options: Soak the hearing aid in warm, soapy water once a week
Wipe the device with a dry, soft cloth and remove it before showering
Store the hearing aid turned on so it is always ready to use
Clean the ear mold opening with a cotton swab dipped in alcohol each day
items.rationale: Hearing aids are cleaned with a dry, soft cloth and kept away from water, so they are removed before showering, swimming, or using hair spray. Soaking the device or applying alcohol damages the electronic components, and the aid is turned off with the battery compartment opened during storage to preserve the battery.

items.stem: The nurse instructs a client to collect a clean-catch midstream urine specimen. Which instruction is correct?
options: Collect the very first urine that is passed into the container
Cleanse the urinary meatus, begin voiding into the toilet, then collect the middle portion of the stream
Void into a bedpan and pour the urine into the specimen container
Collect the specimen at any time and store it at the bedside until the end of the shift
items.rationale: Cleansing the meatus and discarding the first portion of the stream flushes surface bacteria away so the midstream sample reflects the urine in the bladder, which keeps a culture from being contaminated. The initial stream and urine poured from a bedpan carry skin and container organisms, and specimens must be delivered to the laboratory promptly or refrigerated because bacteria multiply in standing urine.

items.stem: The nurse is totaling a client's fluid intake for the shift. Which practice is correct?
options: Record ice chips at approximately half of their frozen volume
Record ice chips at their full frozen volume
Exclude gelatin desserts because they are solid at serving temperature
Exclude IV piggyback medications from the intake total
items.rationale: Ice occupies more space than the water it melts into, so ice chips are recorded at about half of their volume. Anything that is liquid at room temperature counts as intake, which includes gelatin and ice cream, and all IV fluids, including piggyback medications, are part of the intake total because accurate intake and output records are essential to evaluating fluid balance.

items.stem: A nurse charting in a paper record realizes an entry was written on the wrong client's chart. Which action is correct?
options: Draw a single line through the entry, write "error" with the date and initials, and chart the note in the correct record
Cover the entry completely with correction fluid and rewrite it
Remove the page from the chart and recopy the remaining notes
Black out the entry with a marker so it can no longer be read
items.rationale: A documentation error is corrected with a single line so the original entry remains legible, followed by the correction notation, date, and initials, which preserves the record's integrity as a legal document. Correction fluid, obliterating the entry, or removing pages destroys evidence of what was originally written and suggests tampering.

items.stem: The nurse cares for a client with an indwelling urinary catheter. Which actions help prevent catheter-associated urinary tract infection? Select all that apply.
options: Keep the drainage bag below the level of the bladder at all times.
Perform routine perineal care with soap and water, including after each bowel movement.
Disconnect the catheter from the drainage tubing to collect urine specimens.
Secure the catheter to the client's thigh to prevent tugging.
Evaluate the continued need for the catheter daily and remove it as soon as possible.
Irrigate the catheter with sterile saline once a day to maintain patency.
items.rationale: Keeping the bag dependent prevents urine from flowing back into the bladder, perineal hygiene reduces the organisms that migrate along the catheter, securing the tubing prevents urethral trauma, and prompt removal is the single most effective prevention measure because infection risk rises with every catheter day. The closed drainage system is never broken, so specimens are drawn from the sampling port, and routine irrigation introduces bacteria rather than preventing infection.

items.stem: An immobile older adult scores in the high-risk range on the Braden scale. Which interventions should the nurse add to the plan of care to prevent pressure injury? Select all that apply.
options: Reposition the client at least every 2 hours.
Massage reddened skin over the bony prominences.
Keep the skin clean and dry, applying a moisture barrier after episodes of incontinence.
Consult the dietitian to ensure adequate protein and calorie intake.
Provide a donut-shaped cushion for sitting in the chair.
Place the client on a pressure-redistribution mattress.
items.rationale: A low Braden score reflects high risk, so care focuses on relieving pressure through scheduled repositioning and a redistribution surface, protecting the skin from moisture, and supplying the protein and calories tissue needs to stay intact. Reddened skin over a bony prominence may already be a stage 1 pressure injury with nonblanchable erythema, and massaging it damages fragile underlying tissue, while donut cushions concentrate pressure in a ring and impair circulation.

items.stem: The nurse identifies a hospitalized older adult as being at high risk for falls. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Keep the bed in the lowest position with the wheels locked.
Place the call light within reach and answer it promptly.
Raise all four side rails whenever the client is in bed.
Ensure the client wears nonskid footwear when out of bed.
Lock the wheelchair brakes before every transfer.
Encourage the client to walk to the bathroom without help to build confidence.
items.rationale: A low, locked bed limits injury from a fall, a reachable and promptly answered call light discourages unassisted rising, nonskid footwear improves traction, and locked wheelchair brakes stabilize the chair during transfers. Raising all four side rails is considered a restraint and tempts confused clients to climb over them from a greater height, and a high-fall-risk client should be assisted, not sent to the bathroom alone.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the safe use of physical restraints with a newly licensed nurse. Which statements about restraints are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A provider's order is required and must be renewed within the time limits set by policy and regulation.
Restraints may be ordered on an as-needed (PRN) basis for recurring agitation.
Tie the restraint with a quick-release knot to a part of the bed frame that moves with the client.
Remove the restraint at regular intervals to assess skin, circulation, and range of motion.
Less restrictive alternatives must be attempted before a restraint is applied.
Secure the ties to the side rail so staff can release them quickly.
items.rationale: Restraints are a last resort used only after less restrictive measures fail, under a time-limited provider order that must be renewed, with the limb released at regular intervals to check skin, circulation, and mobility. A quick-release knot on the movable bed frame allows fast removal and keeps the restraint from tightening when the bed position changes. PRN restraint orders are prohibited, and tying to a side rail can injure the client when the rail is lowered.

items.stem: The nurse sets up a sterile field for a dressing change. Which principles of surgical asepsis apply? Select all that apply.
options: The outer 1-inch (2.5-cm) border of the sterile field is considered contaminated.
A sterile object held below waist level is considered contaminated.
Reaching across the sterile field is acceptable as long as the sleeves do not touch it.
The sterile field must be kept within view at all times.
A sterile field that becomes wet is considered contaminated.
A field prepared early may be covered with a clean towel until the procedure begins.
items.rationale: The edges of a sterile field contact the unsterile surface beneath, objects out of sight or below the waist cannot be guaranteed sterile, and moisture wicks organisms up from the surface below, so a wet field is contaminated. Reaching over the field allows microorganisms and debris to fall onto it regardless of whether the sleeves touch, and a field is prepared as close to the procedure time as possible and never covered, because removing the cover drags contaminants across it.

items.stem: The evening before surgery, a client tells the nurse, "I keep thinking something will go wrong tomorrow." Which responses by the nurse are therapeutic? Select all that apply.
options: "Tell me more about what is worrying you."
"Don't worry, you have an excellent surgical team."
"It sounds as though you are feeling frightened about the surgery."
"Why are you scared? This procedure is done all the time."
Sitting quietly with the client and allowing time to talk.
items.rationale: Open-ended exploration, reflecting the client's feelings, and attentive silence all invite the client to express the fear and show that the nurse is willing to listen. Telling the client not to worry is false reassurance that dismisses the concern, and demanding "why" while minimizing the fear puts the client on the defensive and closes off communication.

items.stem: The nurse prepares to irrigate a client's wound and apply a new sterile dressing. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Don sterile gloves.
Remove and discard the soiled dressing while wearing clean gloves.
Apply the new sterile dressing and secure it.
Perform hand hygiene and gather all needed supplies.
Irrigate the wound with the prescribed solution.
Set up the sterile field and open sterile supplies onto it.
items.rationale: Hand hygiene and organized supplies come first so the procedure is not interrupted, and the old dressing is removed with clean gloves because it is a dirty task. After hand hygiene is repeated, the sterile field is prepared, sterile gloves are donned before any sterile item or the wound is touched, the wound is irrigated so debris flows from the cleanest to the most contaminated area, and the sterile dressing is applied last.

items.stem: The nurse is inserting a nasogastric tube that will be used for enteral feeding. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Confirm tube placement with an X-ray before anything is given through the tube.
Measure from the tip of the nose to the earlobe to the xiphoid process, and mark the tube.
Assist the client into high-Fowler's position.
Ask the client to flex the head forward and swallow sips of water while the tube is advanced.
Lubricate the tip of the tube with water-soluble lubricant.
Secure the tube to the client's nose.
items.rationale: High-Fowler's positioning reduces aspiration risk during insertion, and the nose-earlobe-xiphoid measurement estimates the length needed to reach the stomach. A water-soluble lubricant eases passage without the pneumonia risk of oil-based products, flexing the head and swallowing closes the airway and guides the tube into the esophagus, and the tube is secured once it reaches the mark. X-ray confirmation is the gold standard for verifying placement and must occur before any feeding or medication is administered.

items.stem: Fifteen minutes after a unit of packed red blood cells is started, the client reports chills and low back pain. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.
options: Notify the health care provider and the blood bank.
Stop the transfusion immediately.
Return the blood bag and tubing to the blood bank and complete the required documentation.
Infuse 0.9% sodium chloride through new IV tubing to keep the vein open.
Assess the client's vital signs and symptoms.
items.rationale: Chills and back pain during a transfusion suggest a hemolytic reaction, so the transfusion is stopped at once to limit the amount of incompatible blood infused. Normal saline is run through completely new tubing because the original line would flush the remaining blood into the client, vital signs quantify the severity, and the provider and blood bank are then notified. The bag and tubing are returned so the blood bank can investigate, and the two-nurse identity verification and the practice of remaining with the client for the first 15 minutes exist to catch exactly this situation early.

items.stem: A postoperative client's diet order is advanced from clear liquids to full liquids. Which menu item may the nurse now offer that was not permitted on the previous diet?
options: Apple juice
Flavored gelatin
Strained cream of chicken soup
A frozen fruit ice pop
items.rationale: A full liquid diet adds milk-based and opaque liquids such as strained cream soups, pudding, ice cream, and milk to what the client could already have. Apple juice, gelatin, and ice pops are transparent liquids that were already allowed on the clear liquid diet, so they represent no advancement.

items.stem: The nurse checks the meal tray of a client who is prescribed a pureed diet after a stroke. Which item should the nurse remove from the tray?
options: Mashed potatoes with gravy
A soft white dinner roll
Smooth applesauce
Blended cream of wheat cereal
items.rationale: Everything on a pureed diet must have a smooth, pudding-like consistency that requires no chewing, so a dinner roll does not belong on the tray even though it is soft. Bread must be chewed and formed into a bolus and can be pocketed in the cheek and aspirated; foods like that belong on a mechanical soft diet only after swallowing improves.

items.stem: A client newly diagnosed with celiac disease asks which foods are safe on a gluten-free diet. Which foods should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Corn tortillas.
Cream of wheat cereal.
Steamed white rice.
Barley vegetable soup.
A plain baked potato.
Whole wheat toast.
items.rationale: Gluten is a protein found in wheat, barley, and rye, so cream of wheat, barley soup, and wheat toast must all be eliminated. Corn, rice, and potatoes are naturally gluten-free grains and starches and form the foundation of safe substitutions for this client.
