items.stem: A client with chronic kidney disease follows a renal diet with a potassium restriction. Which food selection by the client indicates the need for further teaching?
options: White rice with butter
Green beans
Cranberry juice
A baked potato with the skin
items.rationale: Potatoes, especially with the skin, are among the highest-potassium foods, along with bananas, oranges, tomatoes, and dried fruit, so choosing one shows the teaching has not been understood. White rice, green beans, and cranberry juice are low-potassium choices that fit a renal diet, which also typically limits sodium, phosphorus, and sometimes fluid.

items.stem: A client with heart failure is prescribed a 2-gram sodium diet. Which lunch selection indicates the client understands the diet?
options: Canned tomato soup with saltine crackers
A ham and cheese sandwich with pickles
Baked chicken with fresh steamed vegetables
A hot dog with mustard on a bun
items.rationale: Fresh, unprocessed foods such as baked poultry and steamed vegetables are naturally low in sodium and fit a 2-gram restriction. Canned soups, crackers, cured meats like ham and hot dogs, cheese, and pickles are all heavily salted during processing and would quickly exceed the daily limit.

items.stem: An underweight client with a stage 3 pressure injury is placed on a high-protein, high-calorie diet. Which between-meal snack is the best choice for the nurse to offer?
options: Black coffee and rice cakes
A milkshake made with whole milk and peanut butter
Flavored gelatin and herbal tea
Celery sticks and ice water
items.rationale: A whole-milk and peanut butter milkshake supplies concentrated calories along with the protein needed to build the new tissue required for wound healing. Coffee, rice cakes, gelatin, celery, and water contribute almost no protein or calories, so they do nothing to close this client's nutritional gap.

items.stem: A client recovering from an acute episode of diverticulitis is prescribed a low-residue diet. Which meal selection is appropriate?
options: Bran flakes with fresh strawberries
A raw vegetable salad topped with sunflower seeds
Baked white fish with white rice
Whole grain pasta with steamed broccoli
items.rationale: A low-residue diet rests the inflamed bowel by limiting fiber, so refined grains such as white rice and tender proteins such as baked fish are appropriate. Bran, whole grains, raw fruits and vegetables, seeds, and cruciferous vegetables like broccoli all increase stool bulk and bowel stimulation and are avoided until the inflammation resolves.

items.stem: A speech-language pathologist confirms that a client who had a stroke has dysphagia. Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Thicken liquids to the prescribed consistency.
Instruct the client to tuck the chin toward the chest when swallowing.
Keep the client upright for 30 to 60 minutes after each meal.
Offer thin liquids through a straw to make swallowing easier.
Ask the client to tilt the head back to help food slide down.
Minimize mealtime distractions and offer small bites, checking for pocketed food.
items.rationale: Thickened liquids move slowly enough for a weakened swallow to control, the chin-tuck position narrows the airway entrance during the swallow, and remaining upright for 30 to 60 minutes after eating prevents regurgitated food from being aspirated. Small, unhurried bites with cheek checks catch pocketed food before it is inhaled. Straws propel thin liquid to the back of the throat too quickly, and tilting the head back opens the airway to the bolus; both increase aspiration risk.

items.stem: The nurse observes a client with dysphagia during lunch. Which finding requires the nurse to stop the meal and reassess the client's swallowing?
options: A wet, gurgling voice after swallowing
Adding gravy to moisten dry foods
Taking 40 minutes to finish the meal
Pausing to rest between bites
items.rationale: A wet or gurgling voice quality after swallowing indicates that liquid or food is pooling near or entering the airway, so the meal must be stopped and the swallow reassessed before feeding continues. Moistening foods, eating slowly, and resting between bites are all safe behaviors that are actually encouraged as part of aspiration precautions.

items.stem: The nurse prepares to administer an intermittent enteral feeding through a client's gastrostomy tube. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Verify tube placement and measure the gastric residual volume according to agency policy.
Administer the prescribed feeding slowly.
Perform hand hygiene and raise the head of the bed to at least 30 degrees.
Flush the tube with water again and keep the head of the bed elevated for at least 30 minutes.
Flush the tube with about 30 mL of water.
items.rationale: Hand hygiene and elevating the head of the bed come first because the client must never receive formula while lying flat. Placement and residual checks confirm that it is safe to feed, a pre-feeding water flush verifies patency, and the formula is then given slowly to prevent cramping and dumping. A final flush clears formula from the tube so it does not clog, and the head of the bed stays elevated afterward to prevent aspiration.

items.stem: Before an intermittent enteral feeding, the nurse aspirates 70 mL of gastric contents from a client's nasogastric tube. Agency policy directs holding feedings for residual volumes greater than 250 mL. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Discard the aspirate and administer the feeding
Return the aspirate to the stomach and administer the feeding
Hold the feeding and recheck the residual in 4 hours
Notify the provider before giving any feeding
items.rationale: A residual of 70 mL is well below the 250 mL threshold, so the feeding should be given as scheduled. The aspirate is returned to the stomach because it contains gastric acid, electrolytes, and partially digested formula whose repeated discard can cause fluid and electrolyte imbalance. Holding the feeding or calling the provider for a normal finding delays nutrition unnecessarily.

items.stem: A continuous enteral feeding stops infusing, and the nurse determines that the client's small-bore feeding tube is clogged. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Instill carbonated cola into the tube
Attempt to gently flush the tube with warm water
Reinsert the stylet to clear the blockage
Remove the tube and insert a new one
items.rationale: A gentle warm-water flush with a back-and-forth aspiration motion is the safest and most effective first measure for a clogged feeding tube. Cola and juices are acidic and can curdle formula, making the clog worse, and reinserting the stylet can perforate the tube or the gastrointestinal tract. Replacing the tube exposes the client to the risks of reinsertion and is a last resort.

items.stem: A client receiving enteral feedings develops several liquid stools in one day. Which factors should the nurse consider as possible causes of the diarrhea? Select all that apply.
options: An infusion rate that is too rapid.
The head of the bed being kept at 45 degrees.
Liquid medications that contain sorbitol.
Formula left hanging longer than the recommended time.
A hypertonic, concentrated formula.
Formula administered at room temperature.
items.rationale: Rapid infusion and hypertonic formulas pull water into the bowel faster than it can be absorbed, sorbitol in liquid medications acts as an osmotic laxative, and formula hung past its recommended time allows bacterial growth that causes infectious diarrhea. Keeping the head of the bed elevated is an aspiration precaution unrelated to stools, and room temperature is the correct way to give formula, since cold formula causes cramping rather than proper administration.

items.stem: The nurse notes that a client's total parenteral nutrition (TPN) is infusing 2 hours behind schedule after being paused for a procedure. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Increase the infusion rate until the volume catches up
Continue the infusion at the prescribed rate
Stop the TPN and hang 0.9% sodium chloride
Administer the missed volume as an intravenous bolus
items.rationale: TPN is never sped up to catch up, because the concentrated dextrose load would cause hyperglycemia, osmotic diuresis, and fluid overload. The nurse continues at the prescribed rate and documents the interruption. Stopping the solution abruptly risks rebound hypoglycemia, and a bolus of hypertonic dextrose would be dangerous.

items.stem: A client's bag of total parenteral nutrition empties before the next bag has arrived from the pharmacy. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Flush and cap the line until the new bag arrives
Infuse 0.9% sodium chloride at the prescribed TPN rate
Infuse 10% dextrose in water until the new bag is available
Hang a bag of TPN from the unit's stock supply
items.rationale: The pancreas continues secreting insulin in response to the high glucose load of TPN, so stopping the infusion abruptly causes rebound hypoglycemia. Dextrose 10% in water maintains a glucose supply until the new bag arrives. Capping the line or running saline provides no glucose, and TPN is a custom-compounded prescription that is not kept as floor stock.

items.stem: The nurse cares for a client receiving total parenteral nutrition (TPN) through a central line. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Infuse the TPN through a dedicated line or lumen.
Piggyback intravenous antibiotics into the TPN tubing to limit line access.
Monitor capillary blood glucose at regular intervals.
Change the TPN tubing and filter according to agency policy.
Weigh the client once weekly to track fluid status.
Compare the label of each new bag with the provider's prescription.
items.rationale: TPN runs through a dedicated line or lumen, and no other medications or fluids are added to it, because the solution is a prime medium for incompatibilities and bacterial growth; for the same reason the tubing and filter are changed on a strict schedule. Regular glucose monitoring detects hyperglycemia from the dextrose load, and each custom-mixed bag is verified against the prescription before hanging. Clients on TPN are weighed daily, not weekly, to track fluid and nutritional status.

items.stem: The health care team is evaluating whether a malnourished client is responding to the nutrition support started earlier this week. Which laboratory value is the most useful indicator of the client's recent nutritional status?
options: Serum albumin
Prealbumin
Hemoglobin
Total lymphocyte count
items.rationale: Prealbumin has a half-life of only about 2 to 3 days, so it rises or falls quickly and reflects the response to nutrition therapy started within the past week. Albumin has a half-life of about 21 days and lags weeks behind actual intake, while hemoglobin and lymphocyte counts are altered by bleeding, infection, and many other nonnutritional factors.

items.stem: The nurse delegates measurement of a client's intake to assistive personnel. Which consumed items should be recorded as fluid intake? Select all that apply.
options: A cup of chicken broth.
A dish of flavored gelatin.
A bowl of vanilla ice cream.
A slice of buttered toast.
A cup of ice chips.
items.rationale: Anything that is liquid at room temperature counts as fluid intake, which includes broth, gelatin, and ice cream even though gelatin and ice cream are served in semi-solid form. Ice chips are recorded at approximately half their volume because ice occupies more space than the water it melts into. Solid foods such as toast are not part of the fluid record.

items.stem: The nurse assesses a client who has had vomiting and diarrhea for 2 days. Which findings support a diagnosis of fluid volume deficit?
options: Bounding pulses and crackles in the lungs
Weight gain and distended neck veins
Tachycardia and dark, concentrated urine
A slow pulse and pale, dilute urine
items.rationale: With fluid volume deficit the heart rate rises to compensate for reduced circulating volume, and the kidneys conserve water, producing a small amount of dark, concentrated urine. Bounding pulses, crackles, weight gain, and neck vein distention are hallmarks of fluid volume excess, and a slow pulse with dilute urine does not fit hypovolemia.

items.stem: The nurse assesses a client with heart failure who is at risk for fluid volume excess. Which findings indicate that the client is retaining fluid? Select all that apply.
options: Crackles heard at the lung bases.
Skin that tents when pinched.
A bounding radial pulse.
A weight gain of 1.4 kg (3 lb) since yesterday.
Distended neck veins while sitting upright.
Dark amber, concentrated urine.
items.rationale: Excess fluid backs up into the lungs as crackles, expands the vascular volume to produce bounding pulses and visible neck vein distention, and shows up fastest as rapid weight gain, which is the most reliable single indicator. Tenting skin turgor and concentrated urine point in the opposite direction, toward fluid volume deficit.

items.stem: The nurse needs to assess skin turgor in an 88-year-old client suspected of having dehydration. Where should the nurse test the skin?
options: On the back of the hand
Over the sternum or forehead
On the inner forearm
Over the shin
items.rationale: Aging skin loses elastin, so skin on the hands, forearms, and legs tents even when an older adult is well hydrated, producing a false-positive result. The skin over the sternum, forehead, or clavicle retains its elasticity into old age and gives a much more accurate reflection of hydration status.

items.stem: While the nurse performs digital removal of a fecal impaction, the client suddenly becomes pale and diaphoretic, and the pulse falls to 46 beats/min. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Stop the procedure and monitor the client's vital signs
Ask the client to take slow, deep breaths and continue
Reposition the client and complete the removal quickly
Administer the prescribed PRN antiemetic
items.rationale: Stimulation of the rectum can trigger a vagal response, and pallor, diaphoresis, and bradycardia show that it is happening; the stimulus must be removed immediately by stopping the procedure. The nurse then monitors vital signs and notifies the provider if the bradycardia does not resolve. This risk is why the pulse is assessed before and during the procedure and why it is used cautiously in clients with cardiac disease.

items.stem: Midway through administration of a soapsuds cleansing enema, the client reports abdominal cramping. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Remove the tubing and stop the procedure
Lower the height of the solution container
Raise the container to finish the instillation faster
Ask the client to bear down while the solution infuses
items.rationale: Cramping during an enema is usually caused by solution flowing in too quickly, so lowering the container, or briefly clamping the tubing, slows the flow and relieves the cramping while allowing the enema to be completed. Stopping entirely is unnecessary, raising the container would worsen the cramping, and bearing down would expel the solution before it can work.

items.stem: The nurse prepares to administer a cleansing enema to an adult client. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Raise the solution container about 30 to 45 cm (12 to 18 in) above the anus and open the clamp.
Encourage the client to retain the solution as long as possible before defecating.
Assist the client into the left side-lying position with the right knee flexed.
Lubricate the tip of the tubing and insert it 7.5 to 10 cm (3 to 4 in), aiming toward the umbilicus.
Clamp and withdraw the tubing once the solution has been instilled.
items.rationale: The left side-lying position lets the solution flow downhill along the natural curve of the sigmoid colon, and a lubricated tip inserted 7.5 to 10 cm toward the umbilicus follows the direction of the rectum without traumatizing the mucosa. Hanging the container 30 to 45 cm above the anus produces a slow, tolerable flow, since greater height means faster flow and more cramping. After the tubing is clamped and removed, retaining the solution longer softens more stool and produces a more effective result.

items.stem: The nurse teaches a client how to collect stool at home for guaiac fecal occult blood testing. Which client statement indicates that the teaching was effective?
options: 'One sample from a single bowel movement is all the laboratory needs.'
'I should keep taking my ibuprofen for arthritis while I collect the samples.'
'A positive result means that I have colon cancer.'
'I will avoid eating red meat for 3 days before I collect the samples.'
items.rationale: Red meat contains animal hemoglobin that can turn a guaiac test falsely positive, so it is avoided for about 3 days before and during collection, along with high doses of vitamin C, which causes false negatives. Samples are typically taken from three separate bowel movements, NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are held because they can cause gastrointestinal bleeding, and a positive result only indicates hidden blood that requires follow-up testing, not a cancer diagnosis.

items.stem: Halfway through a 24-hour urine collection, the nurse learns that one voided specimen was accidentally discarded. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Continue the collection and note the missed specimen on the requisition
Extend the collection time by 2 hours to make up for the loss
Discard the urine collected so far and restart the 24-hour collection
Send the collected urine to the laboratory for partial analysis
items.rationale: A 24-hour urine test measures the total amount of a substance excreted over exactly 24 hours, so every single voiding must be included; one missed specimen invalidates the entire collection. The only correct response is to discard what has been collected and begin again, starting the clock after a discarded first void and keeping the container chilled if required.

items.stem: The nurse teaches a client to collect a clean-catch midstream urine specimen. Place the client's steps in the correct order.
options: Remove the container from the stream and finish voiding into the toilet.
Begin voiding into the toilet.
Perform hand hygiene and cleanse around the urinary meatus with the antiseptic wipes.
Replace the lid, touching only the outside of the container.
Pass the sterile container into the stream and collect about 30 mL of urine.
items.rationale: Hand hygiene and cleansing the meatus reduce the skin bacteria that could contaminate the culture. The first part of the stream flushes organisms from the distal urethra into the toilet, so the specimen caught midstream best represents the urine actually in the bladder. Removing the container before the stream ends and touching only the outside of the container and lid keep the specimen sterile.

items.stem: A urine culture is prescribed for a client with an indwelling urinary catheter. How should the nurse obtain the specimen?
options: Open the drainage bag spigot and let urine flow into a sterile cup
Disconnect the catheter from the drainage tubing and collect from the catheter
Withdraw urine from the needleless sampling port with a sterile syringe after cleansing the port
Send the entire drainage bag and its contents to the laboratory
items.rationale: Fresh urine for culture is obtained by briefly clamping the tubing below the sampling port, scrubbing the port with antiseptic, and aspirating with a sterile syringe. Urine that has been sitting in the drainage bag is stale and bacteria-laden, so bag urine gives inaccurate results, and disconnecting the catheter from the tubing breaks the closed system and raises the risk of catheter-associated urinary tract infection.

items.stem: A sputum specimen for culture is prescribed for a client with a productive cough. When is the best time for the nurse to collect the specimen?
options: Early in the morning when the client first awakens
Immediately after the client eats breakfast
After the client uses an antiseptic mouthwash
At bedtime, after the day's activity has loosened secretions
items.rationale: Secretions pool in the airways overnight, so a specimen collected on first awakening is the most concentrated and most likely to contain the organisms being sought. The client should rinse the mouth with plain water only, because antiseptic mouthwash kills the very organisms the culture is meant to grow, and collecting before breakfast avoids food particles in the specimen and reduces gagging.

items.stem: The nurse is collecting an aerobic culture from a client's open wound. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Cleanse the wound bed with sterile normal saline to remove old drainage.
Place the swab in the culture tube without touching the outside of the tube and secure the cap.
Apply a new sterile dressing, then label the specimen and send it to the laboratory.
Perform hand hygiene, apply gloves, and remove and discard the soiled dressing.
Rotate the culture swab over viable tissue in the wound bed, avoiding the wound edges and any eschar.
items.rationale: After the soiled dressing is removed, the wound is cleansed with normal saline before culturing, because old exudate and surface debris contain skin flora and dead organisms that would contaminate the result. The swab is rotated over viable granulation tissue, since wound edges and eschar harbor colonizing bacteria rather than the organisms actually infecting the tissue. The swab then goes directly into its transport tube to avoid contamination, and the wound is redressed and the labeled specimen sent promptly.

items.stem: The nurse empties a client's Jackson-Pratt drain and records the output. Which action must the nurse take next so that the drain works properly?
options: Close the port first and then squeeze the bulb firmly
Leave the bulb expanded so drainage can flow in freely
Pin the bulb to the gown above the level of the wound
Compress the bulb fully and close the port while it is still compressed
items.rationale: A Jackson-Pratt drain is a closed active drain that works by negative pressure, so the bulb must be squeezed flat and the port closed while the bulb is still compressed; as the bulb slowly re-expands it pulls drainage out of the wound. Closing the port before squeezing traps air, an expanded bulb exerts no suction at all, and the bulb is secured below the wound to assist drainage by gravity.

items.stem: Assistive personnel ask the nurse why a client's Penrose drain has no collection bulb attached. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: 'It is an open drain that lets fluid seep passively into the absorbent dressing.'
'The bulb was removed because the drainage has stopped.'
'It drains by gravity into the urinary drainage bag at the bedside.'
'A suction machine must be connected to it at the start of each shift.'
items.rationale: A Penrose is a soft, flat, open passive drain that allows fluid to move along its surface by gravity and capillary action into the dressing, so no collection device is ever attached. A sterile safety pin placed through the external portion keeps the drain from slipping into the wound, and the nurse should expect soiled dressings that need frequent changes and surrounding skin protection.

items.stem: The nurse reviews wound documentation for four clients. Which wound is healing by secondary intention?
options: A surgical incision with edges approximated by staples
A laceration closed with sutures in the emergency department
A stage 3 pressure injury left open and filling with granulation tissue
A contaminated abdominal wound left open for 4 days and then sutured closed
items.rationale: Secondary intention healing occurs when wound edges cannot be approximated, so the defect must fill from the bottom up with granulation tissue, then contract and re-epithelialize; open pressure injuries heal this way. It takes longer, scars more, and carries a higher infection risk than the primary intention healing of stapled or sutured incisions, while a wound intentionally left open and closed later heals by tertiary, or delayed primary, intention.

items.stem: On postoperative day 5, an obese client with an abdominal incision tells the nurse, 'It felt like something suddenly let go when I coughed.' Which assessment finding would most support impending wound dehiscence?
options: A ridge of healing tissue palpable beneath the incision
A sudden increase in serosanguineous drainage from the incision
Well-approximated wound edges with mild redness
Scant purulent drainage at one staple site
items.rationale: Dehiscence most often occurs around postoperative days 4 to 5, when the wound is at its weakest, and a sudden gush of serosanguineous fluid combined with a sensation of giving way is its classic warning. A palpable healing ridge and approximated edges are reassuring signs of normal repair, and scant purulent drainage suggests localized infection rather than separation. The nurse should keep the client in bed, have the client splint the incision, and notify the surgeon.

items.stem: A client's abdominal wound eviscerates while the nurse is in the room, and loops of bowel protrude through the incision. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.
options: Place the client in low-Fowler's position with the knees flexed.
Stay with the client and use the call light to summon help.
Keep the client NPO and monitor vital signs for signs of shock.
Cover the protruding organs with sterile dressings moistened with sterile normal saline.
Notify the surgeon and prepare the client to return to the operating room.
items.rationale: The nurse never leaves an eviscerating client, so help is summoned with the call light first, and the exposed bowel is immediately covered with saline-moistened sterile dressings to keep the tissue from drying and becoming necrotic; the organs are never pushed back in. Low-Fowler's position with the knees flexed reduces tension on the abdominal muscles so no further tissue protrudes. The client is kept NPO and observed for shock because evisceration is a surgical emergency that the surgeon must repair in the operating room.

items.stem: After removing a client's surgical staples, the provider applies adhesive wound closure strips. Which discharge instruction should the nurse give about the strips?
options: Peel the strips off after 24 hours
Allow the strips to loosen and fall off on their own
Reinforce the strips with a new layer each morning
Apply antibiotic ointment on top of the strips daily
items.rationale: Adhesive closure strips continue to support the incision after staples are removed, while the new tissue is still weak. They are left in place until they loosen and detach on their own, usually within a week or so, because peeling them off early pulls on the healing edges. Adding layers or applying ointment over them is unnecessary and loosens the adhesive.

items.stem: The nurse applies an elastic roller bandage to a client's sprained ankle and lower leg. Which technique is correct?
options: Begin at the distal end and wrap toward the knee, overlapping each turn
Begin below the knee and wrap downward toward the toes
Stretch the bandage as tightly as possible for maximum support
Cover the toes completely so the bandage will not unravel
items.rationale: Wrapping from the distal end toward the body pushes venous blood back toward the heart instead of trapping it in the foot, which prevents swelling below the bandage. The bandage is applied with even, moderate tension because excessive tightness impairs circulation, and the toes are left exposed so the nurse can check their color, warmth, movement, and capillary refill.

items.stem: A client who twisted an ankle 2 hours ago asks the nurse for a heating pad to ease the pain. Which response by the nurse is best?
options: 'Heat is fine as long as you keep it on the lowest setting.'
'You should alternate heat and cold every 10 minutes today.'
'Cold is used for the first 24 hours to limit swelling; heat could make it worse right now.'
'Neither heat nor cold is helpful for a sprain.'
items.rationale: During the first 24 hours after a soft tissue injury, cold causes vasoconstriction that limits bleeding into the tissue, reduces edema, and numbs pain. Heat produces vasodilation, so applying it this early would increase swelling and bleeding at any setting. After the acute swelling stabilizes, heat becomes useful to promote circulation, healing, and comfort.

items.stem: The nurse applies an ice pack to a client's swollen knee. Which actions ensure that the therapy is safe? Select all that apply.
options: Place a cloth barrier between the ice pack and the skin.
Apply the ice pack directly to the skin for a stronger effect.
Limit each application to about 20 minutes.
Check the skin during the treatment.
Leave the ice pack in place continuously for 2 hours.
Remove the pack immediately if the skin becomes numb or mottled.
items.rationale: A cloth barrier protects the skin from direct thermal injury, applications are limited to roughly 20 to 30 minutes, and the skin is inspected during therapy because tissue damage can develop without the client noticing. Numbness, mottling, or blanching signals impending cold injury and requires immediate removal. Direct or prolonged application does not improve the effect; beyond the time limit, reflex vasodilation occurs and tissue injury becomes likely.

items.stem: A postpartum client is prescribed sitz baths for perineal discomfort. Which nursing action is most important during the treatment?
options: Check on the client frequently for dizziness or weakness
Have the client remain in the bath for at least 45 minutes
Fill the basin with the hottest water the client can tolerate
Lock the bathroom door to ensure the client's privacy
items.rationale: Warm water immersing the perineum causes widespread vasodilation that can make the client lightheaded or faint, so the nurse keeps the call light within reach and checks frequently. A sitz bath lasts about 15 to 20 minutes in comfortably warm, not hot, water, and the door must remain unlocked so staff can reach the client quickly if she feels faint.

items.stem: The nurse reviews safe body mechanics with assistive personnel before they reposition a heavy client. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Keep the load close to your body.
Raise the bed to about waist height before moving the client.
Twist at the waist to reach the far side of the bed.
Bend at the knees and hips with your feet apart.
Hold the client away from you with your arms extended.
Use the large muscles of your legs to do the lifting.
items.rationale: Keeping the load close and using the strong leg muscles instead of the back minimizes strain on the spine, a waist-height bed prevents stooping, and bending at the knees and hips with a wide base of support provides stability and leverage. Twisting the trunk and lifting with the arms extended concentrate force on the lower back and are leading causes of caregiver injury; the whole body should pivot instead.

items.stem: The nurse and two assistants prepare to logroll a client with a spinal injury onto the side. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Place pillows behind the back and under the head to keep the spine aligned.
Cross the client's arms over the chest and place a pillow between the knees.
Raise the bed to working height, with one caregiver holding the client's head and neck in alignment.
On a coordinated count of three, roll the client as a single unit onto the side.
Use the drawsheet to move the client as one unit toward the edge of the bed opposite the direction of the turn.
items.rationale: One caregiver controls the head and neck for the entire procedure so the spine is never twisted. The client is first moved toward the far side of the bed so the turn will leave the body centered rather than at the edge, and crossing the arms and placing a pillow between the knees lets the body move as one rigid unit. The coordinated count ensures everyone turns the client simultaneously, and pillows placed afterward hold the spine in neutral alignment.

items.stem: The nurse performs passive range-of-motion exercises for a client recovering from a stroke. Which technique is correct?
options: Ask the client to push against resistance during each movement
Move each joint slowly just to the point of resistance and then stop
Continue each movement slightly past the point of pain to gain flexibility
Move the extremities quickly through the sequence to save the client's energy
items.rationale: In passive range of motion the nurse supports the extremity above and below the joint and moves it slowly and smoothly, stopping at the first sign of resistance or pain to avoid injuring the joint and soft tissue. Pushing against resistance describes active-resistive exercise done by the client, and forcing past pain or moving quickly can tear tissue or trigger muscle spasm.

items.stem: The nurse teaches assistive personnel about applying knee-high antiembolism stockings to a postoperative client. Which points should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Apply the stockings before the client gets out of bed in the morning.
Measure the client's legs to select the correct stocking size.
Fold the top of the stocking down if it seems too long.
Remove the stockings at least once each shift to inspect the skin.
Smooth out any wrinkles after the stockings are on.
Massage the client's calves before reapplying the stockings.
items.rationale: Stockings are applied before the legs become dependent, ideally before the client rises in the morning, because dependent edema makes them ineffective and hard to apply. The legs are measured so the size compresses correctly, wrinkles are smoothed because they create pressure points, and the stockings are removed regularly for hygiene and skin inspection. Folding the top down creates a constricting band that acts like a tourniquet, and the calves are never massaged because an unrecognized clot could be dislodged.

items.stem: Sequential compression devices are prescribed for a postoperative client. During the evening assessment the nurse finds that the client's left calf is newly swollen, warm, and tender. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Apply the devices to both legs as prescribed
Apply the device to the right leg only and massage the left calf
Apply the devices and recheck the left calf in 2 hours
Withhold the devices and notify the health care provider of the findings
items.rationale: Unilateral calf swelling, warmth, and tenderness suggest a deep vein thrombosis, and compressing a leg that may contain a clot could dislodge it and cause a pulmonary embolism. The devices are withheld and the provider is notified so diagnostic studies, such as venous ultrasound, can be ordered. The calf is never massaged for the same reason.

items.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients. Which client has the highest risk for falling?
options: A 79-year-old taking a diuretic who has orthostatic hypotension and fell at home last month
A 45-year-old on postoperative day 1 who ambulates with a steady gait
A 62-year-old with well-controlled hypertension who walks unassisted
A 30-year-old with a short arm cast who reports mild pain
items.rationale: A history of a recent fall is the single strongest predictor of future falls, and this client adds advanced age, orthostatic hypotension that causes dizziness on standing, and a diuretic that produces urgency and volume shifts. Because these risk factors compound one another, this client needs the most aggressive fall precautions. The other clients each have at most one minor risk factor.

items.stem: The nurse answers a bed alarm and finds a client lying on the floor beside the bed. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.
options: With adequate help or lift equipment, assist the client back into bed.
Document the facts of the fall in the medical record and complete an incident report.
Begin increased monitoring, such as vital signs and neurologic checks, per agency policy.
Assess the client for injuries before moving the client.
Notify the health care provider about the fall.
items.rationale: The client is assessed where found, because moving someone with an undetected hip fracture or spinal injury could make it worse. Once cleared, the client is returned to bed with enough help or equipment to protect both client and staff, and the provider is notified so the client can be examined and orders obtained. Increased monitoring detects delayed signs of injury such as a slow intracranial bleed, and the record documents objective facts while the incident report, which is not referenced in the chart, goes through the facility's quality process.

items.stem: A confused older adult repeatedly tries to climb out of bed unassisted. Which fall-prevention interventions can the nurse use without applying restraints? Select all that apply.
options: Move the client to a room close to the nurses' station.
Activate the bed exit alarm.
Arrange for a sitter or family member to stay with the client.
Raise all four side rails whenever the client is in bed.
Apply a vest restraint at night as a precaution.
Offer toileting assistance on a regular schedule.
items.rationale: Placing the client near the station allows constant observation, a bed exit alarm alerts staff the moment the client begins to rise, a sitter provides one-to-one supervision, and scheduled toileting removes the most common reason confused clients climb out of bed. Raising all four side rails is itself a form of restraint that entices clients to climb over them and fall from a greater height, and restraints are a last resort requiring a provider's order, never a precaution or convenience.

items.stem: A hospitalized 80-year-old client reports being unable to sleep at night. Which interventions should the nurse implement? Select all that apply.
options: Cluster nighttime care to limit the number of awakenings.
Offer a back massage as part of the bedtime routine.
Eliminate caffeinated drinks in the afternoon and evening.
Encourage several long naps during the day.
Request a prescription for diphenhydramine at bedtime.
Reduce hallway noise and dim the room lights at night.
items.rationale: Grouping assessments and care together protects the client's sleep cycles, a back massage and consistent bedtime routine promote relaxation, caffeine is a stimulant whose effects last longer in older adults, and noise and light are the most common hospital sleep disruptors. Long daytime naps reduce nighttime sleep pressure and worsen the problem, and diphenhydramine is inappropriate for older adults because its anticholinergic effects cause confusion, urinary retention, and falls.

items.stem: The nurse enters the room of a client using patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) and sees the client's spouse press the button while the client sleeps. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Thank the spouse for helping to keep the client comfortable
Ask the spouse to press the button only when the client grimaces
Explain that only the client may press the button, and assess the client's sedation and breathing
Remove the PCA pump and request an oral analgesic instead
items.rationale: The built-in safety of PCA is that a client who becomes too sedated cannot press the button, so drug delivery stops before dangerous respiratory depression develops. When someone else presses the button, called PCA by proxy, that safeguard is bypassed, so the nurse must stop the practice, reinforce the teaching, and immediately assess the client's sedation level and respiratory status. Removing the pump punishes the client for someone else's action and leaves the pain untreated.

items.stem: A client with chronic low back pain wants to rely less on medication. Which nonpharmacologic comfort measures can the nurse offer? Select all that apply.
options: Guided imagery.
Listening to preferred music.
Repositioning with pillow support.
An additional dose of the PRN opioid.
Progressive muscle relaxation.
Encouraging the client to ignore the pain.
items.rationale: Guided imagery, music, and progressive muscle relaxation are cognitive-behavioral techniques that reduce the perception of pain, and careful positioning with pillow support relieves mechanical strain on the back; all of these complement, and can reduce reliance on, medication. An opioid dose is a pharmacologic measure, and telling a client to ignore pain dismisses a subjective experience the nurse is obligated to believe and address.

items.stem: The nurse reviews hearing aid care with an older adult. Which client statement indicates a need for further teaching?
options: 'I will wipe the hearing aid with a soft, dry cloth.'
'I will soak the hearing aid in warm, soapy water once a week.'
'I will open the battery door at night when I take it out.'
'I will put the hearing aid in after I finish using my hairspray.'
items.rationale: A hearing aid is an electronic device that moisture destroys, so it must never be soaked or worn while bathing or swimming; cleaning is done with a soft, dry cloth. Opening the battery door at night conserves the battery and lets moisture evaporate, and applying hairspray or lotions before insertion prevents residue from clogging the microphone and receiver.

items.stem: The nurse prepares to remove and clean a client's prosthetic eye. Which action is correct?
options: Depress the lower eyelid so the prosthesis slides out
Grasp the prosthesis with dry gauze and pull it out firmly
Clean the prosthesis with an alcohol wipe before reinserting it
Store the prosthesis dry in an unlabeled open container
items.rationale: Gently pressing down on the lower eyelid breaks the suction holding the prosthesis so it slides out into the nurse's hand without force. The prosthesis is cleaned with normal saline or mild soap and water, because alcohol and other solvents damage the acrylic surface, and when not being worn it is stored in a labeled container with water or saline to protect it.

items.stem: The nurse admits an older adult with presbycusis who reads lips. Which communication technique is most effective?
options: Raise the voice and exaggerate each word
Face the client at eye level and speak clearly in a lower-pitched voice
Speak from the doorway so the voice carries across the room
Direct most questions to the client's family members
items.rationale: Presbycusis affects high-frequency hearing first, so a lower-pitched voice is heard more easily, and facing the client in good light supports lip reading. Shouting and exaggerating distort both the sound of speech and the lip movements the client depends on, distance and background noise degrade what hearing remains, and speaking through family members excludes the client from his or her own care.

items.stem: A client who has been in protective isolation for 3 weeks is increasingly withdrawn, naps most of the day, and tells the nurse the wall clock 'sometimes melts.' Which nursing action is most appropriate?
options: Provide meaningful stimulation, such as opening the blinds, music, and scheduled conversations
Limit staff visits to reduce the client's confusion
Keep the room dim and quiet so the client can rest
Ask the provider to prescribe an antipsychotic medication
items.rationale: Weeks of isolation with monotonous surroundings produce sensory deprivation, which manifests as withdrawal, excessive sleep, and perceptual distortions like the melting clock. The treatment is to enrich the environment with meaningful input, including natural light, music, conversation, orientation cues, and scheduled human contact. Further reducing stimulation would worsen the symptoms, and the distortions are environmental in origin, not a psychotic illness requiring medication.

items.stem: The nurse applies a prescribed warm compress to an 86-year-old client's leg. Which precaution is most important?
options: Use a lower temperature and check the skin more often than for a younger adult
Apply the compress at a higher temperature so it penetrates the thinner skin
Rely on the client to report burning before checking the site
Leave the compress in place until it has cooled completely
items.rationale: Aging skin is thin and fragile, and older adults have diminished temperature sensation and slower protective vascular responses, so they can sustain a burn without ever feeling excessive heat. The nurse therefore uses a lower temperature and inspects the skin directly and frequently rather than waiting for the client to report discomfort. Higher temperatures and unattended applications are exactly how thermal injuries occur in this age group.

items.stem: A client dies on the unit, and no autopsy is planned. Which actions should the nurse take when providing postmortem care? Select all that apply.
options: Ask the family whether cultural or religious practices should be part of the care.
Send the client's dentures home with the family in a labeled cup.
Remove tubes and lines according to agency policy.
Place the client supine with a small pillow under the head.
Delay the family's viewing until the body has been transported to the morgue.
Gently close the client's eyes and place the dentures in the mouth.
items.rationale: Many cultures and religions have specific rituals surrounding death, so the family is asked before care begins and their practices are honored whenever possible. Because no autopsy is planned, tubes and lines are removed per policy, and positioning the body supine with a pillow under the head prevents blood from pooling and discoloring the face. Closing the eyes and inserting the dentures preserve a natural appearance for the viewing, which should occur in the room after the body is prepared, not after transport to the morgue.

items.stem: The nurse admits a client to a medical unit. Which part of the room orientation is most important to complete first?
options: Demonstrating the call light and confirming the client can reach and use it
Reviewing the cafeteria menu and meal delivery times
Explaining how to operate the television and telephone
Introducing the client to the roommate
items.rationale: The call light is the client's only way to summon help in an emergency, so demonstrating it, watching the client use it, and keeping it within reach is the safety priority of any admission orientation. Meals, entertainment, and introductions matter for comfort but can wait until the client can reliably call for assistance.

items.stem: A client visits the clinic believing she is pregnant. Which finding would the nurse recognize as a positive sign of pregnancy?
options: Amenorrhea with nausea in the morning
A positive serum hCG level
Fetal heart sounds auscultated by the examiner
Bluish discoloration of the cervix and vagina
items.rationale: Positive signs of pregnancy are those that can only be caused by a fetus, such as fetal heart tones heard by an examiner, fetal movement palpated by an examiner, or visualization on ultrasound. Amenorrhea and nausea are presumptive (subjective) signs, while a positive hCG and cervical color changes are probable signs because conditions other than pregnancy can also produce them.

items.stem: A client is currently 16 weeks pregnant. Her history includes a daughter born at 39 weeks, twin sons born at 34 weeks, and a miscarriage at 10 weeks. All three children are living. Using the GTPAL system, how should the nurse document her obstetric history?
options: G3 T1 P1 A1 L3
G4 T1 P1 A1 L3
G4 T1 P2 A1 L3
G4 T2 P1 A0 L2
items.rationale: She has been pregnant 4 times counting the current pregnancy (G4), had 1 term birth at 39 weeks (T1), 1 preterm birth (P1, because the twin gestation counts as a single birth event), 1 abortion or miscarriage (A1), and 3 living children (L3). Counting the twins as two preterm births or omitting the current pregnancy from gravidity are the most common calculation errors.

items.stem: A client reports that the first day of her last menstrual period was September 8. Using Naegele's rule, which estimated date of delivery should the nurse calculate?
options: June 1
June 8
December 15
June 15
items.rationale: Naegele's rule adds 7 days to the first day of the last menstrual period and then subtracts 3 months: September 8 plus 7 days is September 15, and 3 months earlier is June 15. December 15 results from adding rather than subtracting 3 months, and June 8 omits the 7-day addition.

items.stem: A nurse teaches a client who is planning to become pregnant about taking a daily folic acid supplement. What is the primary purpose of this supplement?
options: Reducing the risk of neural tube defects
Preventing iron-deficiency anemia
Lowering the risk of gestational diabetes
Promoting fetal lung maturity
items.rationale: Adequate folic acid before conception and during early pregnancy supports neural tube closure, which is complete within the first weeks of gestation, so supplementation lowers the risk of defects such as spina bifida. Iron, not folic acid, prevents iron-deficiency anemia, and folic acid has no direct role in glucose control or fetal lung maturation.

items.stem: A pregnant client is prescribed an oral iron supplement. Which instructions should the nurse include in the teaching? Select all that apply.
options: Take the supplement with a glass of orange juice.
Take the supplement with a glass of milk.
Expect your stools to appear dark or black.
Increase fluids and fiber in your diet.
Stop the supplement once your energy improves.
Take the supplement between meals if your stomach tolerates it.
items.rationale: Vitamin C from orange juice enhances iron absorption, dark stools are a harmless expected effect, extra fluids and fiber counteract the constipation iron commonly causes, and absorption is best on an empty stomach when tolerated. Milk and other calcium sources interfere with absorption, and the supplement should be continued as prescribed rather than stopped when symptoms improve.

items.stem: A nurse teaches a client at 30 weeks gestation about warning signs that must be reported to the provider right away. Which findings should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Leaking of fluid from the vagina
Mild ankle swelling at the end of the day
Blurred vision or spots before the eyes
Burning or pain with urination
A noticeable decrease in fetal movement
Occasional irregular tightening of the abdomen
items.rationale: Leaking fluid may indicate ruptured membranes, visual changes can signal preeclampsia, painful urination suggests an infection that can trigger preterm labor, and decreased fetal movement may reflect fetal compromise, so each requires prompt evaluation. Dependent ankle edema and irregular Braxton Hicks contractions are expected findings in late pregnancy.

items.stem: A low-risk pregnant client asks when she will be checked for gestational diabetes. At which point in pregnancy is routine screening with an oral glucose challenge performed?
options: 8 to 12 weeks
16 to 20 weeks
24 to 28 weeks
32 to 36 weeks
items.rationale: Routine screening for gestational diabetes is done between 24 and 28 weeks, when placental hormones that oppose insulin have risen enough to unmask impaired glucose tolerance. Screening earlier is reserved for clients with risk factors such as obesity or a prior history of gestational diabetes, and waiting past 28 weeks delays treatment that protects the fetus.

items.stem: A nurse assesses a client at 34 weeks gestation. Which findings support a diagnosis of preeclampsia with severe features? Select all that apply.
options: Blood pressure of 162/110 mm Hg on two readings
Proteinuria of 3+ on dipstick
A persistent headache unrelieved by acetaminophen
Epigastric pain in the right upper quadrant
Glucose of 2+ in the urine
Fetal heart rate of 140 beats per minute
items.rationale: Severely elevated blood pressure, significant proteinuria, a persistent headache, and epigastric or right upper quadrant pain all reflect the widespread vasospasm and organ involvement of severe preeclampsia; the abdominal pain in particular suggests liver capsule distention. Glucosuria points toward gestational diabetes rather than preeclampsia, and a fetal heart rate of 140 is a normal finding.

items.stem: A client receiving an intravenous magnesium sulfate infusion for severe preeclampsia has a respiratory rate of 10 breaths per minute, absent patellar reflexes, and urine output of 22 mL/hr. After stopping the infusion, which medication should the nurse prepare to administer?
options: Protamine sulfate
Naloxone
Calcium gluconate
Flumazenil
items.rationale: Respirations below 12, absent deep tendon reflexes, and urine output under 30 mL/hr indicate magnesium toxicity, and calcium gluconate is the antidote because calcium directly counteracts the neuromuscular and respiratory depression magnesium causes. Protamine reverses heparin, naloxone reverses opioids, and flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines, so none of them treats magnesium excess.

items.stem: A client at 31 weeks gestation arrives reporting bright red vaginal bleeding without pain. Her uterus is soft and nontender. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
options: Abruptio placentae
Placenta previa
Preterm labor
Threatened abortion
items.rationale: Painless, bright red bleeding in the third trimester with a soft, relaxed uterus is the classic picture of placenta previa, in which the placenta implants over or near the cervical opening; vaginal examinations are avoided because they can tear the placenta. Abruptio placentae typically causes painful, dark bleeding with a rigid, tender uterus, and a threatened abortion occurs in early pregnancy, not at 31 weeks.

items.stem: Immediately after a laboring client's membranes rupture, the fetal heart rate drops sharply and the nurse sees a loop of umbilical cord at the vaginal opening. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Gently push the cord back into the vagina
Position the client with her hips elevated in a knee-chest position
Cover the exposed cord with dry sterile gauze
Prepare the client for an immediate vaginal birth
items.rationale: The priority with a prolapsed cord is to relieve pressure on it so fetal oxygenation continues, which is achieved by placing the client in a knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg position while the presenting part is held off the cord with a sterile gloved hand. The cord is never pushed back inside, it should be covered with saline-moistened rather than dry gauze, and the expected delivery route is an emergency cesarean, not a vaginal birth.

items.stem: A nurse is caring for a client in labor. Which event marks the beginning of the second stage of labor?
options: Onset of regular painful contractions
An overwhelming urge to bear down
Delivery of the placenta
Complete cervical dilation of 10 centimeters
items.rationale: The second stage of labor begins when the cervix is completely dilated at 10 centimeters and ends with the birth of the baby. Regular contractions mark the first stage, an urge to push can occur before full dilation and is not the defining criterion, and placental delivery occurs during the third stage.

items.stem: A fetal monitor tracing shows uniform decelerations that begin after each contraction starts, reach their lowest point after the contraction peaks, and return to baseline after the contraction ends. What is the most likely cause of this pattern?
options: Compression of the fetal head
Compression of the umbilical cord
Insufficient blood flow through the placenta
Normal fetal movement
items.rationale: Decelerations that are offset after the contraction in this way are late decelerations, which reflect uteroplacental insufficiency: the placenta cannot deliver enough oxygen during the stress of a contraction. Head compression produces early decelerations that mirror the contraction, cord compression produces abrupt variable decelerations, and fetal movement produces accelerations, which are a reassuring sign.

items.stem: A laboring client's fetal monitor shows repetitive abrupt, V-shaped drops in the fetal heart rate that vary in their timing relative to contractions. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Administer oxygen at 10 L/min by nonrebreather mask
Perform a vaginal examination to assess for cord prolapse
Document the tracing as a reassuring pattern
Reposition the client onto her other side
items.rationale: Abrupt, variably timed decelerations are variable decelerations caused by umbilical cord compression, and a maternal position change is the first intervention because shifting the fetus often relieves pressure on the cord. Oxygen and a vaginal examination may follow if repositioning does not resolve the pattern, and this tracing is not reassuring, so documentation alone is unsafe.

items.stem: A client receiving an oxytocin infusion develops recurrent late decelerations on the fetal monitor. Place the nursing actions in the order they should be performed.
options: Notify the health care provider
Turn the client onto her left side
Apply oxygen at 10 L/min by nonrebreather mask
Discontinue the oxytocin infusion
Increase the rate of the primary intravenous fluids
items.rationale: Late decelerations signal uteroplacental insufficiency, so the nurse first improves placental perfusion by turning the client to her side, then removes the cause of excessive uterine activity by stopping the oxytocin. Oxygen and an intravenous fluid bolus further increase the oxygen delivered across the placenta, and the provider is notified once these immediate intrauterine resuscitation measures are under way.

items.stem: A client receiving oxytocin to augment labor has contractions every 1.5 minutes lasting 100 seconds, and the fetal monitor shows recurrent late decelerations. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Increase the rate of the primary intravenous line
Discontinue the oxytocin infusion
Document the pattern and continue monitoring
Place the client in a supine position
items.rationale: Contractions closer than every 2 minutes and lasting longer than 90 seconds indicate uterine tachysystole, which limits placental blood flow between contractions; because oxytocin is driving the pattern, stopping the infusion is the first action. Fluids and other resuscitation measures follow, continued monitoring alone ignores fetal compromise, and supine positioning worsens placental perfusion by compressing the vena cava.

items.stem: A nurse reviews home care instructions with the parents of a newborn boy who was circumcised. Which parent statement indicates a need for further teaching?
options: I will place my baby on his back for every sleep.
I will keep the diaper folded down below the umbilical cord.
I will wash off the yellow crust that forms on the circumcision site.
I will give sponge baths until the cord falls off.
items.rationale: The yellowish exudate that forms over a healing circumcision is part of normal granulation and should not be removed, so this statement shows a knowledge gap. Supine sleep positioning reduces the risk of sudden infant death, and keeping the cord dry by folding the diaper down and giving sponge baths until it detaches are both correct cord care practices.

items.stem: On postpartum day 5, a client has a moderate amount of pinkish-brown vaginal discharge. What is the nurse's best action?
options: Document the finding as expected
Notify the health care provider
Massage the fundus vigorously
Prepare to administer a uterotonic medication
items.rationale: Lochia normally progresses from red rubra during the first few days, to pinkish-brown serosa from about day 4 through day 10, and then to whitish alba, so this discharge is an expected finding that only needs documentation. Provider notification, fundal massage, or uterotonics would be indicated for abnormal findings such as a return to bright red bleeding, foul odor, or a boggy uterus.

items.stem: One hour after a vaginal birth, a nurse finds a client's perineal pad saturated with blood and her fundus soft and boggy. Place the nursing actions in the order they should be performed.
options: Administer the prescribed intravenous oxytocin
Massage the fundus until it becomes firm
Reassess fundal tone and quantify the blood loss
Assist the client to empty her bladder
Notify the health care provider
items.rationale: Uterine atony is the most common cause of early postpartum hemorrhage, so the nurse immediately massages the boggy fundus to stimulate contraction, then empties the bladder because a full bladder displaces the uterus and prevents it from clamping down. The provider is notified so uterotonic orders can be carried out, and ongoing reassessment with quantified blood loss evaluates whether the interventions are working. A fundus that is deviated to one side is another clue that the bladder is full.

items.stem: A nurse reviews postpartum charts. Which client should the nurse prepare to receive Rho(D) immune globulin within 72 hours of birth?
options: An Rh-negative mother who delivered an Rh-positive newborn
An Rh-positive mother who delivered an Rh-negative newborn
An Rh-negative mother who delivered an Rh-negative newborn
An Rh-positive mother who delivered an Rh-positive newborn
items.rationale: Rho(D) immune globulin prevents an Rh-negative mother from forming antibodies against Rh-positive fetal blood cells that entered her circulation at birth, protecting future Rh-positive pregnancies from hemolytic disease; it is also given prophylactically at about 28 weeks gestation. An Rh-positive mother cannot be sensitized, and an Rh-negative newborn carries no Rh antigen to provoke antibody formation, so the other pairings do not require the medication.

items.stem: A breastfeeding client 3 weeks postpartum is diagnosed with mastitis of the right breast and started on an oral antibiotic. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Continue to breastfeed or pump frequently on both breasts.
Begin each feeding on the affected breast to promote emptying.
Stop breastfeeding until the antibiotic course is finished.
Apply warm compresses or take a warm shower before feedings.
Finish the entire course of the prescribed antibiotic.
Wear a tight binder to suppress milk production.
items.rationale: Mastitis is treated by keeping the breast well drained, so frequent feeding or pumping continues, feedings can start on the affected side while the infant sucks most vigorously, warmth promotes milk flow before feeds, and the full antibiotic course prevents recurrence and abscess formation. Stopping breastfeeding or binding the breasts causes milk stasis, which worsens the infection rather than treating it.

items.stem: At 1 minute of life, a newborn has a heart rate of 112 beats per minute, a slow and weak cry, some flexion of the extremities, a grimace in response to suctioning, and a pink body with blue hands and feet. Which Apgar score should the nurse assign?
items.rationale: The heart rate above 100 earns 2 points, while the weak cry, partial flexion, grimace, and acrocyanosis each earn 1 point, for a total of 6. Scoring the heart rate as only 1 point or crediting 2 points for the grimace or muscle tone produces the incorrect neighboring totals; a score of 4 to 6 indicates moderate difficulty transitioning, so the newborn needs continued stimulation and observation.

items.stem: A nurse monitors a large-for-gestational-age newborn of a mother with gestational diabetes. Which findings suggest the newborn is hypoglycemic? Select all that apply.
options: Heart rate of 150 beats per minute
Jitteriness and tremors
Poor feeding effort
Respiratory rate of 45 breaths per minute
Lethargy with a weak cry
Temperature instability
items.rationale: The newborn brain depends on glucose, so low levels produce jitteriness, poor feeding, lethargy with a weak cry, and difficulty maintaining temperature; infants of diabetic mothers are at particular risk because fetal insulin levels remain high after birth. A heart rate of 150 and a respiratory rate of 45 are within the normal newborn ranges of roughly 110 to 160 beats and 30 to 60 breaths per minute, so neither indicates hypoglycemia.

items.stem: A newborn with physiologic jaundice is placed under phototherapy lights. Which intervention should the nurse include in the plan of care?
options: Apply a moisturizing lotion before each session under the lights
Cover the newborn's eyes with protective shields while under the lights
Keep the newborn fully swaddled in a lightweight blanket
Limit feedings to reduce the frequency of stooling
items.rationale: Phototherapy light can injure the retina, so opaque eye shields are applied whenever the newborn is under the lights and removed during feedings for bonding and eye assessment. Lotions can cause burns, swaddling blocks the skin exposure the treatment depends on, and feedings are encouraged rather than limited because bilirubin is excreted in stool and hydration must be maintained.

items.stem: A client at 10 weeks gestation with an uncomplicated pregnancy asks how often she will need to come for prenatal visits. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: "Every 2 weeks until 28 weeks, then every week until delivery."
"Every 4 weeks until 28 weeks, every 2 weeks until 36 weeks, then weekly until birth."
"Once each trimester unless a problem develops."
"Every 4 weeks throughout the pregnancy, with extra visits only if you have complaints."
items.rationale: The standard schedule for a low-risk pregnancy is monthly visits through 28 weeks, visits every 2 weeks from 28 to 36 weeks, and weekly visits from 36 weeks until birth, because the risks of hypertensive disorders, growth problems, and preterm labor rise in the third trimester. Visits every 2 weeks from the start or once per trimester do not match the recommended frequency, and monthly visits to term would miss the closer surveillance needed late in pregnancy.

items.stem: A client presents for her first prenatal visit at 9 weeks gestation. Which laboratory tests should the nurse expect to be obtained at this visit? Select all that apply.
options: Blood type and Rh factor with antibody screen
Rubella immunity titer
One-hour glucose challenge test
Hepatitis B surface antigen
Group B streptococcus rectovaginal culture
Syphilis and HIV serology
items.rationale: The initial prenatal panel establishes baseline and risk information: blood type, Rh status, and antibody screen identify isoimmunization risk, the rubella titer determines immunity, and hepatitis B, syphilis, and HIV testing allow treatment that protects the fetus, along with a complete blood count and urinalysis. The glucose challenge is scheduled at 24 to 28 weeks when placental hormones peak insulin resistance, and the group B streptococcus culture is done at 35 to 37 weeks so the result reflects colonization at the time of birth.

items.stem: A client at 26 weeks gestation is scheduled for a 1-hour glucose challenge test. Which instruction should the nurse give?
options: "Fast for 8 hours before the test and bring your morning insulin."
"You do not need to fast; you will drink a 50-gram glucose solution and have blood drawn 1 hour later."
"Collect all of your urine for 24 hours and bring the container to the laboratory."
"Avoid all carbohydrates for 3 days before the test so the results are accurate."
items.rationale: The 1-hour glucose challenge is a screening test done at 24 to 28 weeks that requires no fasting; the client drinks a 50-gram glucose load and a venous sample is drawn 1 hour later, with a value of 130 to 140 mg/dL or higher prompting a diagnostic 3-hour oral glucose tolerance test. Fasting and a 100-gram load apply to the 3-hour diagnostic test, a 24-hour urine collection measures protein for preeclampsia, and carbohydrate restriction before testing would falsely alter the result.

items.stem: A client at 36 weeks gestation asks why the provider is collecting a vaginal and rectal swab today. Which explanation by the nurse is correct?
options: "The swab checks for group B streptococcus so we know whether you need antibiotics during labor."
"The swab confirms that your membranes are still intact."
"The swab measures the length of your cervix to predict preterm labor."
"The swab screens for chlamydia and gonorrhea, which are tested only late in pregnancy."
items.rationale: Late in the third trimester, typically between 35 and 37 weeks, a single rectovaginal swab is obtained to identify colonization with group B streptococcus, a normal vaginal organism that can cause sepsis, pneumonia, or meningitis in the newborn; a positive result means the client will receive intravenous antibiotics during labor. Intact membranes are assessed by nitrazine or fern testing, cervical length is measured by ultrasound, and sexually transmitted infection screening is done at the first prenatal visit.

items.stem: A client at 17 weeks gestation is told that her quad screen shows an elevated maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein level. She asks the nurse what this means. Which response is most appropriate?
options: "This result confirms that your baby has a neural tube defect."
"This is a screening result; a targeted ultrasound and possibly an amniocentesis will be offered to look further."
"This means the baby most likely has Down syndrome."
"An elevated level is normal at 17 weeks and needs no follow-up."
items.rationale: The quad screen, drawn between 15 and 20 weeks, is a screening test rather than a diagnostic one, so an elevated alpha-fetoprotein raises the possibility of an open neural tube defect, abdominal wall defect, multiple gestation, or simply inaccurate dating and must be followed with ultrasound and an offer of amniocentesis. Telling the client the defect is confirmed is inaccurate and frightening, a low rather than high alpha-fetoprotein is associated with trisomy 21, and dismissing the result would forfeit the chance for diagnosis and planning.

items.stem: A nurse cares for a client at 16 weeks gestation who is having a genetic amniocentesis. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Confirm that informed consent has been signed before the procedure
Instruct the client to remain on strict bed rest for 1 week afterward
Assess the fetal heart rate before and after the procedure
Administer Rh immune globulin afterward if the client is Rh negative
Teach the client to report fever, fluid leaking from the vagina, or persistent cramping
Tell the client that complete chromosome results will be available the same day
items.rationale: Amniocentesis is an invasive procedure that requires informed consent, fetal heart rate assessment before and after to detect distress, and Rh immune globulin for Rh-negative clients because fetal blood can enter the maternal circulation during the needle pass; the client is taught to report signs of infection, membrane rupture, or labor. Only brief rest and avoidance of strenuous activity for a day or two are needed rather than prolonged bed rest, and cultured chromosome results usually take 1 to 2 weeks.

items.stem: A 38-year-old client at 11 weeks gestation is deciding between chorionic villus sampling and amniocentesis for genetic testing. Which statement about chorionic villus sampling should the nurse include?
options: "It is performed between 15 and 20 weeks and also screens for neural tube defects."
"It can be done now, between 10 and 13 weeks, but it cannot detect neural tube defects."
"It carries no risk of pregnancy loss because no needle enters the uterus."
"It analyzes fetal cells from the amniotic fluid to identify chromosomal abnormalities."
items.rationale: Chorionic villus sampling obtains placental tissue between 10 and 13 weeks, giving earlier chromosomal results than amniocentesis, but because no amniotic fluid is sampled it cannot measure alpha-fetoprotein and therefore cannot detect neural tube defects. Sampling is done through the cervix or abdomen and carries a small risk of pregnancy loss and limb defects, and analysis of fetal cells in amniotic fluid describes amniocentesis, which is done after 15 weeks.

items.stem: A nurse performs a nonstress test on a client at 36 weeks gestation. Which tracing should the nurse interpret as reactive?
options: Two fetal heart rate accelerations of at least 15 beats per minute lasting at least 15 seconds within a 20-minute period
A baseline fetal heart rate of 140 beats per minute with no accelerations over 40 minutes
Three uterine contractions in 10 minutes with no late decelerations
A fetal heart rate that drops 15 beats per minute with each fetal movement
items.rationale: A reactive nonstress test shows at least two accelerations peaking 15 beats above baseline and lasting 15 seconds within 20 minutes, which indicates an intact, well-oxygenated fetal autonomic nervous system. A tracing with no accelerations over 40 minutes is nonreactive and requires further evaluation, three contractions without late decelerations describes a negative contraction stress test, and decelerations with movement are not a reassuring finding.

items.stem: A nurse prepares to perform a nonstress test on a client at 35 weeks gestation. Place the steps in the order they should be performed.
options: Interpret the tracing for accelerations after 20 minutes and extend to 40 minutes if the criteria are not met
Apply the ultrasound transducer over the fetal back and the tocotransducer over the fundus
Position the client in a semi-Fowler or lateral tilt position and obtain baseline vital signs
Give the client an event marker and instruct her to press it whenever she feels the fetus move
Explain the purpose of the test and verify the client's identity and the provider's order
items.rationale: The nurse first explains the test and verifies the order, positions the client in a semi-Fowler or side-lying position to avoid supine hypotension, applies the ultrasound transducer over the fetal heart and the tocotransducer on the fundus, and gives the client the event marker so fetal movements can be correlated with accelerations. The tracing is evaluated after 20 minutes and, if fewer than two qualifying accelerations are seen, the test is extended to 40 minutes because the fetus may be in a sleep cycle before it is called nonreactive.

items.stem: After a nonreactive nonstress test, a client at 34 weeks gestation is scheduled for a biophysical profile. She asks the nurse what the test involves. Which explanation is accurate?
options: "A contraction stress test will be done to see how the baby tolerates labor."
"An ultrasound will assess the baby's breathing movements, body movements, muscle tone, and amniotic fluid volume, combined with the nonstress test result."
"A sample of amniotic fluid will be tested to determine whether the baby's lungs are mature."
"Doppler flow through the umbilical artery will be measured to detect placental insufficiency."
items.rationale: The biophysical profile combines a nonstress test with four ultrasound observations of fetal breathing movements, gross body movements, tone, and amniotic fluid volume; each component earns 0 or 2 points, so a score of 8 to 10 is reassuring, 6 is equivocal and calls for repeat testing, and 4 or less suggests fetal compromise. A contraction stress test, an amniocentesis for lung maturity, and umbilical artery Doppler studies are separate forms of fetal assessment that are not part of the profile.

items.stem: A client at 38 weeks gestation with gestational diabetes undergoes a contraction stress test. The tracing shows three contractions in 10 minutes with late decelerations following more than half of the contractions. How should the nurse interpret this result?
options: Negative, which is reassuring and indicates the fetus can tolerate labor
Positive, which suggests uteroplacental insufficiency and requires provider notification
Equivocal, which requires the test to be repeated in 24 hours
Unsatisfactory, because fewer than four contractions occurred in 10 minutes
items.rationale: A contraction stress test is positive when late decelerations accompany 50% or more of adequate contractions, even if fewer than three contractions occur, and it indicates the fetus may not tolerate the reduced placental blood flow of labor, so the provider must be notified and delivery may be expedited. A negative test shows three adequate contractions in 10 minutes with no late decelerations, equivocal results have intermittent late or significant variable decelerations, and unsatisfactory refers to inability to achieve three contractions in 10 minutes or an uninterpretable tracing.

items.stem: A client at 7 weeks gestation who was diagnosed yesterday with an unruptured tubal pregnancy calls the clinic reporting sudden severe lower abdominal pain, dizziness, and new aching in her right shoulder. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Instruct her to take acetaminophen and rest with a heating pad on her abdomen
Schedule her for repeat quantitative hCG testing in 48 hours
Direct her to call emergency services for immediate transport to the hospital
Reassure her that shoulder discomfort is a common complaint of early pregnancy
items.rationale: Sudden severe pain with dizziness and referred shoulder pain indicates tubal rupture with intra-abdominal bleeding that irritates the diaphragm, a life-threatening hemorrhage that requires emergency transport, intravenous access, and surgical management. Analgesics and heat would mask a surgical emergency, delaying evaluation for 48 hours is unsafe once signs of rupture appear, and shoulder pain in this context is a sign of peritoneal blood rather than a normal pregnancy complaint.

items.stem: A client with an unruptured ectopic pregnancy is discharged after a single intramuscular dose of methotrexate. Which statement indicates she understood the nurse's teaching?
options: "I will keep taking my prenatal vitamin with folic acid so the medication works better."
"I will avoid alcohol and use sunscreen, and I will return for my hCG levels on days 4 and 7."
"I can take ibuprofen for the cramping until my follow-up appointment."
"Once the pain goes away I can stop coming for blood tests."
items.rationale: Methotrexate is a folic acid antagonist that stops trophoblastic cell division, so the client must avoid folic acid supplements and alcohol, which increase toxicity, use sun protection because of photosensitivity, and return for serial hCG levels on days 4 and 7 to confirm the level is falling. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs interact with methotrexate and can mask the pain of rupture, and hCG monitoring continues until the level is undetectable regardless of symptoms.

items.stem: A client at 12 weeks gestation is being evaluated for a suspected hydatidiform mole. Which findings support this diagnosis? Select all that apply.
options: Uterine size larger than expected for gestational age
Serum hCG level far higher than expected for the gestational age
Dark brown vaginal discharge resembling prune juice
Fetal heart tones heard with a Doppler device
Blood pressure of 148/94 mm Hg with proteinuria
Serum hCG level lower than expected for the gestational age
