Once the infant is positioned at the prescribed distance and the lights are on, the start time is documented and ongoing monitoring begins.

items.stem: A parent asks why the newborn needs a vitamin K injection shortly after birth. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: Newborns lack the intestinal bacteria that make vitamin K, so the injection prevents serious bleeding
The injection boosts the newborn's immune system against common infections
Vitamin K helps the newborn digest milk during the first week of life
The injection prevents low blood sugar during the transition after birth
items.rationale: Vitamin K is synthesized by intestinal bacteria, but the newborn gut is sterile at birth and breast milk contains little vitamin K, leaving the infant unable to produce several clotting factors. A single intramuscular dose, given in the vastus lateralis, prevents vitamin K deficiency bleeding of the newborn. It has no role in immunity, digestion, or glucose regulation.

items.stem: A parent asks why erythromycin ointment is placed in the newborn's eyes after birth. Which response by the nurse is correct?
options: It prevents serious eye infections that can be acquired from the birth canal
It keeps the eyes moist because newborns cannot yet produce tears
It treats the puffiness of the eyelids caused by the birth process
It improves the newborn's ability to focus during bonding
items.rationale: Prophylactic erythromycin ointment protects against ophthalmia neonatorum, a sight-threatening conjunctivitis caused by gonococcal and, to a lesser degree, chlamydial organisms encountered during passage through the birth canal. It is administered to all newborns regardless of the mother's known history and may transiently blur the infant's vision. It does not lubricate the eyes, treat edema, or affect visual focus.

items.stem: The nurse teaches parents about care of the umbilical cord stump. Which statement indicates correct understanding?
options: "We will fold the diaper below the cord and let it air-dry until it falls off."
"We will pull the cord off gently once it becomes loose."
"A full tub bath tomorrow will help keep the cord clean."
"A little foul-smelling drainage around the base is expected."
items.rationale: Keeping the stump clean and dry with the diaper folded below it promotes natural separation, which usually occurs in one to two weeks. Sponge baths are used until the cord detaches, and the stump must never be pulled off even when partially loose. Foul odor, purulent drainage, or spreading redness at the base are signs of omphalitis and must be reported to the provider.

items.stem: A newborn was circumcised using the Plastibell technique. Which statement by the mother indicates a need for further teaching?
options: "I will wrap the tip in petroleum jelly gauze at every diaper change."
"The plastic ring should fall off on its own in about a week."
"A yellow crust on the site in a day or two is normal, and I will not wipe it away."
"I will call the provider if there is active bleeding or no wet diaper for several hours."
items.rationale: Petroleum gauze is applied after clamp circumcisions such as the Gomco to keep the site from adhering to the diaper, but it is not used with the Plastibell because the ring itself protects the glans and the ointment can cause the ring to slip off prematurely. The ring detaches naturally in about five to eight days. Yellowish exudate on day two is normal granulation tissue, while bleeding or failure to void requires provider notification.

items.stem: A parent notices the newborn throwing out both arms with fingers fanned when startled by a loud noise, and asks when this response will go away. Which reply by the nurse is accurate?
options: "That startle response usually disappears by around six months of age."
"It should be gone within the first two weeks of life."
"Most babies keep this reflex until their second birthday."
"This reflex remains present throughout life."
items.rationale: The parent is describing the Moro reflex, a normal newborn response of symmetric arm extension and abduction followed by flexion, which typically fades by about six months as the nervous system matures. Persistence well beyond that age, or an asymmetric response, suggests neurologic dysfunction or injury such as a fractured clavicle. Other timelines differ: rooting fades around four months, while the Babinski response of fanning toes can normally persist toward one year or more.

items.stem: While assessing a quietly resting 1-day-old newborn held in an upright position, the nurse palpates the anterior fontanelle. Which finding requires immediate provider notification?
options: A fontanelle that is soft and flat
Slight pulsation felt over the fontanelle
A tense, bulging fontanelle while the newborn is calm
Brief firmness of the fontanelle during vigorous crying
items.rationale: A fontanelle that bulges while the infant is calm and upright suggests increased intracranial pressure from conditions such as hemorrhage, hydrocephalus, or meningitis and must be reported at once. A soft, flat fontanelle with slight pulsation is the normal finding, and transient fullness during crying resolves when the infant quiets. A markedly sunken fontanelle would instead point to dehydration.

items.stem: At birth, a newborn has soft swelling over the top of the scalp that crosses the suture lines. How should the nurse explain this finding to the parents?
options: It is caput succedaneum, scalp edema from pressure during birth that resolves within a few days
It is a cephalohematoma, bleeding under the scalp bone covering that may take weeks to resolve
It is molding of the skull bones that indicates possible birth trauma
It is early hydrocephalus that requires an urgent head ultrasound
items.rationale: Caput succedaneum is diffuse edema of the presenting scalp caused by pressure against the cervix; because it lies above the periosteum it crosses suture lines, is present at birth, and resolves in days. A cephalohematoma is blood beneath the periosteum, so it never crosses sutures, often appears hours after birth, resolves over weeks, and increases the risk of jaundice as the collected blood breaks down. Neither finding signals hydrocephalus.

items.stem: A mother being discharged 20 hours after birth asks why the newborn's metabolic screening blood test must be repeated at the follow-up visit. Which explanation by the nurse is correct?
options: The screen is most accurate after the newborn has taken milk feedings for at least 24 hours
The first sample is usually lost during laboratory processing
State law requires two identical tests for every newborn
A repeat is needed only when the first result is abnormal
items.rationale: Screening for disorders such as phenylketonuria depends on the newborn having metabolized protein from milk feedings, so a sample drawn before 24 hours of age can miss an affected infant and must be repeated. Early-discharge newborns therefore have the screen redrawn at the outpatient follow-up visit. Hearing screening, by contrast, is completed for all newborns before discharge and does not depend on feeding.

items.stem: A newborn born at 31 weeks develops grunting and retractions, and the team prepares to administer surfactant through an endotracheal tube. The parents ask what the medication does. Which explanation by the nurse is best?
options: It lowers surface tension in the air sacs so they stay open between breaths
It dissolves mucus that is blocking the baby's large airways
It fights the lung infection that is causing the fast breathing
It stimulates the brain's breathing center to prevent apnea
items.rationale: Respiratory distress syndrome in preterm infants results from a deficiency of surfactant, the substance that lowers alveolar surface tension; without it the alveoli collapse at the end of each breath, and the work of reinflating them exhausts the infant. Exogenous surfactant instilled into the trachea coats the alveoli so they remain open, improving oxygenation. It is not a mucolytic, an antibiotic, or a respiratory stimulant such as caffeine.

items.stem: Before a gavage feeding, the nurse notes that a preterm newborn has a distended, taut abdomen, a large residual of undigested formula, and a small streak of blood in the stool. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Withhold the feeding and notify the provider immediately
Give the feeding slowly over 60 minutes and recheck the residual
Massage the abdomen to stimulate peristalsis before feeding
Document the findings and continue the prescribed feeding schedule
items.rationale: Abdominal distension, increasing gastric residuals, and bloody stools are cardinal early signs of necrotizing enterocolitis, an inflammatory bowel injury of preterm infants that can rapidly progress to perforation and sepsis. Enteral feedings must be stopped and the provider notified so the infant can be made NPO with gastric decompression, abdominal imaging, and antibiotics. Continuing feedings or massaging the fragile bowel could worsen the injury.

items.stem: The nurse encourages the parents of a stable preterm newborn to provide kangaroo care. Which outcomes are associated with this practice? Select all that apply.
options: More stable temperature, heart rate, and breathing patterns
Stronger parent-infant attachment
Improved maternal milk production and breastfeeding success
Elimination of the need for temperature monitoring
Improved infant weight gain over time
items.rationale: Kangaroo care, holding the diaper-clad infant upright against a parent's bare chest, uses the parent's body heat to stabilize the infant's temperature and is associated with steadier heart rate and respirations, better weight gain, longer sleep, enhanced bonding, and increased milk supply. The infant still requires routine monitoring during and after sessions, so kangaroo care supplements rather than replaces standard thermoregulation surveillance.

items.stem: A newborn with neonatal abstinence syndrome is irritable, tremulous, and feeding poorly. Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Swaddle the newborn snugly with the extremities flexed
Position the crib in a dimly lit, quiet area
Offer small, frequent feedings of high-calorie milk as prescribed
Invite visitors to talk and play with the newborn to distract from withdrawal
Cluster nursing care to minimize handling
Place the newborn prone after feedings to reduce spitting up
items.rationale: Newborns withdrawing from intrauterine substance exposure have hyperactive, disorganized nervous systems, so care centers on reducing stimulation: snug flexed swaddling, dim quiet surroundings, gentle vertical rocking, and clustered care. Small frequent high-calorie feedings offset the energy burned by constant movement and poor coordination. Extra social stimulation worsens symptoms, and every newborn is placed supine for sleep regardless of spitting up.

items.stem: The parents of a newborn born at 35 weeks are preparing for discharge. Which statement about car safety indicates the teaching was effective?
options: "The nurses will watch our baby in the car seat before discharge to be sure the breathing and heart rate stay stable."
"We can lay the car seat flat in the back seat so the baby sleeps better on the ride home."
"The front passenger seat is fine as long as the car seat faces the rear."
"Once the baby is home, riding in the car seat for long trips without breaks is safe."
items.rationale: Late preterm and preterm infants have immature airway tone, so a car seat tolerance screen is performed before discharge: the infant sits in the family's own semi-reclined car seat for about 90 to 120 minutes while oxygen saturation, heart rate, and breathing are monitored for apnea, bradycardia, or desaturation. The seat is installed rear-facing in the back seat at the angle the manufacturer specifies, never flat and never in front of an airbag, and long trips require breaks out of the seat.

items.stem: The nurse reviews reduction of sudden infant death syndrome risk with new parents. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Place the infant on the back for every sleep, including naps
Bring the infant into the parents' bed at night for closeness
Offer a pacifier at nap time and bedtime once breastfeeding is established
Keep pillows, bumper pads, and stuffed toys out of the crib
Dress the infant in several heavy blanket layers for warm sleep
Room-share with the infant on a separate sleep surface for at least the first six months
items.rationale: Supine positioning for every sleep, a bare crib with a firm mattress, pacifier use at sleep times, and room-sharing without bed-sharing are the core evidence-based measures that reduce sudden infant death syndrome. Bed-sharing and soft objects create suffocation and entrapment hazards. Overheating from heavy layering also raises risk, so the infant should wear only one layer more than an adult would find comfortable, with the head kept uncovered.

items.stem: A nurse performs a well-child assessment on a 6-month-old infant. Which developmental finding is expected at this age?
options: Picks up small objects with a neat pincer grasp
Rolls from the back to the abdomen
Sits steadily without any support
Pulls to a standing position at furniture
items.rationale: By about 6 months an infant can roll in both directions, having first rolled front to back around 4 to 5 months. Sitting steadily without support is expected closer to 8 months, the refined pincer grasp develops around 9 to 11 months, and pulling to stand typically appears near 9 to 10 months, so those findings would be advanced for this age.

items.stem: A nurse selects a toy for a hospitalized 2-year-old. Which choice is most appropriate for this child's developmental stage?
options: A board game played with rules
A musical mobile hung over the bed
A push-pull toy on wheels
A necklace kit with small beads
items.rationale: Toddlers are refining gross motor skills and enjoy push-pull toys, and at this age they engage in parallel play, playing alongside rather than cooperatively with other children. Board games with rules suit school-age children, a mobile is an infant toy, and small beads are a choking hazard for any child under about 3 years.

items.stem: Four children are scheduled to receive the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine today. For which child should the nurse withhold the vaccine and notify the provider?
options: A child with a runny nose and a temperature of 99.1 F
A child taking amoxicillin for an ear infection
A child whose sibling has a history of febrile seizures
A child who is severely immunosuppressed from chemotherapy
items.rationale: MMR is a live attenuated vaccine, so it is contraindicated in children with severe immunosuppression, such as those receiving chemotherapy, because the weakened virus could cause disease. A mild illness with low-grade fever, current antibiotic therapy, and a family history of febrile seizures are not contraindications to vaccination.

items.stem: A nurse teaches new parents about transporting their newborn home from the hospital. Which instruction is correct?
options: Secure the car seat rear-facing in the back seat
Secure the car seat forward-facing in the back seat
Secure the car seat rear-facing in the front passenger seat
Hold the newborn in a caregiver's lap in the back seat
items.rationale: Infants ride rear-facing in the back seat, and children should remain rear-facing as long as possible until they outgrow the seat's height or weight limit, because this position best protects the head and spine in a crash. The front seat is unsafe due to the passenger airbag, forward-facing is for older children, and a caregiver's arms cannot restrain an infant during a collision.

items.stem: A 4-year-old arrives with a sudden high fever, drooling, a muffled voice, and sitting upright leaning forward on outstretched arms. Which action should the nurse avoid?
options: Allowing the child to remain upright on the parent's lap
Inspecting the throat with a tongue depressor
Keeping emergency airway equipment at the bedside
Maintaining a calm, quiet environment
items.rationale: Sudden high fever, drooling, dysphonia, and tripod positioning suggest epiglottitis, a bacterial infection classically caused by Haemophilus influenzae type b; inserting anything into the throat can trigger laryngospasm and complete airway obstruction. Keeping the child calm and upright and having airway equipment ready are appropriate. In contrast, croup is viral, develops gradually, and produces a barky cough treated with cool humidified air.

items.stem: A nurse needs to assess pain in a 3-month-old infant after surgery. Which pain assessment tool is most appropriate?
options: The FACES picture scale
A 0-to-10 numeric rating scale
The FLACC behavioral scale
A visual analog line scale
items.rationale: The FLACC scale scores observable behaviors, face, legs, activity, cry, and consolability, making it suited to preverbal infants and young children who cannot report pain. The FACES scale requires a child of about 3 years or older to point to a face, and numeric or visual analog scales require the abstract self-report abilities of school-age children and adolescents.

items.stem: A 4-month-old infant is admitted with bronchiolitis caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Suction the nares with a bulb syringe before feedings
Place the infant on contact precautions
Offer small, frequent feedings and monitor hydration
Administer the prescribed intravenous antibiotics
Monitor oxygen saturation continuously
Perform scheduled chest physiotherapy every 2 hours
items.rationale: Care for bronchiolitis is supportive: clearing nasal secretions before feeds helps the obligate nose-breathing infant eat and breathe, contact precautions limit spread of RSV on surfaces and hands, small frequent feedings maintain hydration despite respiratory effort, and oxygen saturation guides the need for supplemental oxygen. Antibiotics do not treat a viral infection, and routine chest physiotherapy has not been shown to help and may distress the infant.

items.stem: A parent asks how to reduce their infant's risk of developing middle ear infections. Which teaching should the nurse provide?
options: Feed the infant in an upright position and avoid propping the bottle
Clean inside the ear canals daily with cotton swabs
Lay the infant flat with a bottle at nap time
Give a daily low-dose antibiotic during the winter
items.rationale: Feeding upright and never propping the bottle keeps milk from pooling near the short, horizontal eustachian tubes of infancy, which is how feeding-related otitis media develops; avoiding secondhand smoke and breastfeeding also lower risk. Cotton swabs can injure the canal without preventing middle ear infection, flat bottle feeding increases risk, and antibiotics are not used for routine prevention.

items.stem: A nurse is caring for a 7-year-old having an acute asthma exacerbation. Which change in assessment findings requires the most immediate action?
options: Loud expiratory wheezing throughout the lung fields
Wheezing that has become faint with markedly decreased breath sounds
Frequent episodes of dry coughing
A respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute
items.rationale: Wheezing requires air movement, so a chest that grows quiet during an exacerbation signals severe obstruction and impending respiratory failure rather than improvement, and it demands immediate intervention. Audible wheezing, coughing, and an elevated respiratory rate all show the child is still moving air and, while they need treatment, they are less ominous findings.

items.stem: A nurse reinforces teaching with the parents of a child with cystic fibrosis. Which components belong in the daily plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Give pancreatic enzymes with all meals and snacks
Provide a high-calorie, high-protein diet
Restrict salt in the child's diet
Perform airway clearance therapy every day
Give supplemental fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K)
Limit the child's daily fluid intake
items.rationale: Thick secretions block the pancreatic ducts, so enzymes must accompany every meal and snack for digestion, a high-calorie, high-protein diet offsets malabsorption and the work of breathing, daily airway clearance mobilizes thick pulmonary mucus, and fat-soluble vitamins are replaced because fat absorption is impaired. Children with cystic fibrosis lose extra salt in sweat and need liberal salt and fluids, so restriction of either is harmful.

items.stem: A nursing student asks which congenital heart defect causes cyanosis. Which defect should the nurse identify?
options: Ventricular septal defect
Patent ductus arteriosus
Atrial septal defect
Tetralogy of Fallot
items.rationale: Tetralogy of Fallot combines a ventricular septal defect with pulmonary stenosis, an overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy, allowing deoxygenated blood to shunt right to left into the systemic circulation and produce cyanosis. Ventricular and atrial septal defects and a patent ductus arteriosus are acyanotic defects because their higher left-sided pressures shunt already-oxygenated blood left to right.

items.stem: An infant with tetralogy of Fallot suddenly becomes deeply cyanotic and irritable while crying (a hypercyanotic "tet" spell). Place the nursing actions in the order they should be performed.
options: Administer morphine sulfate as prescribed
Administer 100% oxygen by face mask
Place the infant in a knee-to-chest position
Give an intravenous fluid bolus as prescribed
items.rationale: The knee-to-chest position comes first because it increases systemic vascular resistance, which reduces the right-to-left shunt and sends more blood through the lungs. Oxygen is then applied to improve saturation, morphine calms the infant and relaxes the spasm of the right ventricular outflow tract, and fluids support preload if the spell persists.

items.stem: A 5-week-old infant has forceful projectile vomiting of non-bile-stained formula immediately after feedings, then acts eager to feed again. The nurse palpates a small olive-shaped mass in the right upper abdomen. Which condition do these findings suggest?
options: Intussusception
Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis
Hirschsprung disease
Gastroesophageal reflux
items.rationale: Projectile nonbilious vomiting shortly after feeds, persistent hunger, and a palpable olive-shaped mass are the hallmark triad of pyloric stenosis, in which the hypertrophied pyloric muscle obstructs gastric emptying; repeated vomiting also risks metabolic alkalosis. Intussusception causes episodic pain and currant-jelly stools, Hirschsprung disease presents with failure to pass meconium and distention, and reflux produces effortless rather than projectile spitting up.

items.stem: A nurse assesses a 9-month-old with suspected intussusception. Which stool finding is characteristic of this condition?
options: Ribbon-like stools
Clay-colored stools
Stools resembling red currant jelly
Frothy, foul-smelling fatty stools
items.rationale: When one segment of bowel telescopes into another, the compressed, ischemic mucosa sheds blood and mucus that mix into stools resembling red currant jelly. Ribbon-like stools suggest the narrowed segment of Hirschsprung disease, clay-colored stools point to biliary obstruction, and fatty stools occur with malabsorption such as cystic fibrosis.

items.stem: An infant returns to the unit after surgical repair of a cleft lip. Which intervention should the nurse include in postoperative care?
options: Position the infant prone to promote drainage of secretions
Offer a pacifier to soothe the infant between feedings
Apply soft elbow immobilizers to both arms
Clean the suture line by rubbing it firmly with gauze
items.rationale: Protecting the suture line is the priority after cleft lip repair, so soft elbow immobilizers keep the infant's hands away from the incision while being removed periodically for skin checks. Prone positioning would press the incision into the bedding, pacifiers and other objects in the mouth stress the repair, and the suture line is cleansed gently as prescribed, never rubbed.

items.stem: A nurse in the newborn nursery reviews assessments. Which finding is most consistent with Hirschsprung disease?
options: Passage of meconium within the first 12 hours of life
No passage of meconium within the first 48 hours of life
Projectile vomiting immediately after each feeding
Stools that resemble red currant jelly
items.rationale: In Hirschsprung disease a segment of colon lacks ganglion cells and cannot relay peristalsis, so stool cannot pass; failure to pass meconium within 48 hours, abdominal distention, and bilious vomiting are the classic newborn presentation. Meconium passage in the first hours is normal, projectile vomiting suggests pyloric stenosis, and currant-jelly stools indicate intussusception.

items.stem: A nurse assesses a 7-month-old brought in with vomiting and diarrhea for 2 days. Which findings indicate dehydration? Select all that apply.
options: A sunken anterior fontanel
Fewer wet diapers than usual
Absence of tears when crying
A bulging, tense anterior fontanel
Dry mucous membranes
Capillary refill of 2 seconds
items.rationale: Volume loss in an infant shows as a sunken fontanel, decreased urine output, absent tears, and dry mucous membranes, often accompanied by tachycardia and poor skin turgor. A bulging fontanel suggests increased intracranial pressure rather than fluid loss, and capillary refill of 2 seconds or less is a normal finding.

items.stem: A toddler experienced a simple febrile seizure. Which statement by the parent indicates that discharge teaching was effective?
options: I will hold him tightly during a seizure to stop the shaking.
I will place a spoon in his mouth so he cannot bite his tongue.
I will turn him onto his side and move nearby objects away.
Daily antibiotics will keep him from having more seizures.
items.rationale: During any seizure the child is placed side-lying to keep the airway clear and the area around him is cleared to prevent injury. Restraining a seizing child or placing objects in the mouth causes harm, and antibiotics have no role because simple febrile seizures result from a rapid rise in temperature, are usually brief and benign, and are not reliably prevented even by antipyretics.

items.stem: A 3-year-old with Kawasaki disease is receiving intravenous immune globulin and aspirin. Which assessment is the nurse's highest priority during and after treatment?
options: Renal function and urine output trends
Cardiovascular status, including signs of heart failure
Blood glucose levels before meals
Signs of increased intracranial pressure
items.rationale: Kawasaki disease inflames medium-sized vessels, and its most serious complication is coronary artery aneurysm, so monitoring cardiac status and echocardiogram follow-up take priority; immune globulin given early lowers this risk. Renal, glucose, and neurologic monitoring are routine care but do not address the life-threatening coronary involvement that defines this disease.

items.stem: A community health nurse screens children for lead exposure. Which child is at highest risk for lead poisoning?
options: A toddler living in a 1960s home with chipping paint
An 8-year-old living in newly built housing
A toddler whose home uses municipal water tested annually
A preschooler who recently enrolled in a new child care center
items.rationale: Homes built before 1978 may contain lead-based paint, and toddlers are the highest-risk group because normal hand-to-mouth behavior leads them to ingest paint chips and contaminated dust; routine blood lead screening is recommended around ages 1 and 2. New construction, tested water supplies, and modern child care facilities are unlikely lead sources.

items.stem: A parent telephones the clinic after finding their alert 3-year-old with an open bottle of adult vitamins, several of which are missing. Which instruction should the nurse give first?
options: Give syrup of ipecac to induce vomiting
Offer a large glass of milk to dilute the tablets
Call the poison control center right away
Watch the child at home for any symptoms
items.rationale: For any suspected ingestion in a child who is awake and breathing, the poison control center is contacted first because it provides substance-specific guidance; adult vitamins often contain iron, which can be highly toxic to young children. Inducing vomiting is no longer recommended and can worsen injury, milk is not a reliable antidote, and waiting for symptoms delays treatment.

items.stem: A 9-year-old with type 1 diabetes reports feeling shaky and sweaty before lunch and appears pale but is alert. Place the nursing actions in the order they should be performed.
options: Give 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, such as 4 ounces of juice
Recheck the blood glucose after 15 minutes
Check the capillary blood glucose level
Provide a snack containing complex carbohydrate and protein
items.rationale: Shakiness, sweating, and pallor suggest hypoglycemia, which is confirmed first with a glucose check in an alert child. Treatment follows the 15-15 rule: give 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes and repeat if the level is still low, then provide a complex carbohydrate and protein snack to keep the glucose from falling again before the next meal.

items.stem: A nurse in the emergency department assesses an injured infant and toddler brought in by caregivers. Which findings should raise suspicion of physical abuse? Select all that apply.
options: Bruises on the torso in multiple stages of healing
A caregiver explanation inconsistent with the injury
A spiral femur fracture in a 3-month-old who cannot walk
Small bruises over the shins of an active 4-year-old
A delay of 2 days in seeking care for a significant burn
Flat blue-gray patches across an infant's buttocks
items.rationale: Bruises of different ages on protected areas like the torso, histories that do not match the injury, fractures requiring twisting force in a child who is not yet mobile, and unexplained delays in seeking care are recognized indicators of inflicted injury, and nurses are mandated reporters of reasonable suspicion. Shin bruises on an active preschooler are typical accidental findings, and blue-gray patches (slate-gray macules) are a normal skin variant, not bruising.

items.stem: A school-age child with sickle cell disease is admitted in vaso-occlusive crisis with severe leg pain. Which interventions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Administer intravenous fluids as prescribed
Give opioid analgesics on a scheduled basis as prescribed
Apply cold packs to the painful extremities
Apply warm compresses to the painful areas
Encourage rest to reduce oxygen demand
Restrict oral fluid intake during the crisis
items.rationale: Vaso-occlusive crisis is treated with aggressive hydration to reduce blood viscosity and sludging of sickled cells, scheduled opioid analgesia because the pain is severe, warmth to promote vasodilation, and rest to lower oxygen demand; oxygen is added if the child is hypoxic. Cold application and fluid restriction are contraindicated because vasoconstriction and dehydration both promote further sickling.

items.stem: A nurse measures vital signs on a healthy 6-month-old during a well-child visit: apical pulse 128/min, respirations 32/min, and axillary temperature 37.0 C (98.6 F). What is the appropriate nursing action?
options: Document the findings as normal for this age
Notify the provider of the elevated heart rate
Recheck the respiratory rate after calming the infant
Apply a cooling blanket and recheck the temperature
items.rationale: Infants normally have much faster heart and respiratory rates than older children and adults; a pulse of 128/min and respirations of 32/min are well within the expected range for a 6-month-old. The axillary temperature is also normal, so the nurse simply documents the findings.

items.stem: A nurse reviews vital signs collected on the pediatric unit. Which findings should the nurse report to the provider? Select all that apply.
options: A sleeping 3-month-old with an apical pulse of 62/min
A crying 2-year-old with a heart rate of 150/min
A resting 2-week-old with a sustained respiratory rate of 72/min
A 9-year-old with a blood pressure of 148/96 mm Hg
A quiet 4-year-old with a respiratory rate of 24/min
A 16-year-old with a resting heart rate of 72/min
items.rationale: A pulse in the low 60s is bradycardia even for a sleeping young infant, a sustained resting respiratory rate above 60/min in a newborn signals respiratory distress, and 148/96 mm Hg is markedly hypertensive for a school-age child. Tachycardia in a crying toddler, a respiratory rate of 24/min in a preschooler, and a pulse of 72/min in an adolescent are all expected findings.

items.stem: A nurse prepares to administer otic drops to an 18-month-old with an ear infection. Place the steps in the order the nurse should perform them.
options: Pull the pinna down and back
Perform hand hygiene and verify the medication order
Keep the child lying with the treated ear up for several minutes
Warm the bottle of drops by rolling it between the hands
Instill the prescribed drops along the side of the ear canal
Position the child on the unaffected side with the affected ear up
items.rationale: After hand hygiene and verifying the order, the drops are warmed because cold solution in the ear causes pain and dizziness. The child is positioned with the affected ear up, and because this child is younger than 3 years the pinna is pulled down and back to straighten the canal before instilling the drops. Remaining on that side for a few minutes lets the medication reach the eardrum.

items.stem: A nurse teaches a parent how to give a liquid antibiotic to an 8-month-old at home. Which parent statement indicates a need for further teaching?
options: I will give the dose slowly with an oral syringe toward the cheek
I will stir the medicine into a full bottle of formula to hide it
I will hold the baby with the head raised while giving the dose
I will let the baby swallow between small amounts of the medicine
items.rationale: Medication should never be mixed into a full bottle, because the infant receives the complete dose only if the entire bottle is finished, and an unpleasant taste may cause the infant to refuse formula afterward. Using an oral syringe directed toward the side of the cheek, keeping the head elevated, and pausing so the infant can swallow are all correct techniques.

items.stem: A nurse prepares to give an intramuscular vaccine to a 4-month-old infant. Which injection site should the nurse select?
options: Deltoid muscle
Dorsogluteal muscle
Vastus lateralis muscle
Rectus femoris muscle
items.rationale: The vastus lateralis is the preferred intramuscular site in infants because it is a large, well-developed muscle away from major nerves and vessels. The deltoid is too small until the toddler years, and the dorsogluteal site is avoided in young children because the muscle is undeveloped before walking and the sciatic nerve lies nearby.

items.stem: A nurse plans care for a hospitalized preschooler using the principles of atraumatic care. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Perform painful procedures in the treatment room, not the bed
Apply a topical anesthetic cream before intravenous insertion
Encourage a parent to remain with the child during procedures
Tell the child that the needle stick will not hurt at all
Complete procedures quickly in the bed to avoid moving the child
Offer the child a realistic choice, such as which arm to use
items.rationale: Atraumatic care minimizes physical and psychological distress: the bed stays a safe place by moving painful procedures to a treatment room, topical anesthetics reduce needle pain, parental presence lowers anxiety, and small realistic choices give the child a sense of control. Telling a child a procedure will not hurt is dishonest and destroys trust, and performing painful procedures in the bed removes the sense of safety it should provide.

items.stem: A toddler has a peripheral intravenous line infusing in the hand. Which nursing action is most important to detect complications early?
options: Rely on the infusion pump alarm to signal infiltration
Assess the site hourly and compare it with the other hand
Cover the entire site with an opaque dressing to protect it
Check the site once each shift when hanging new fluids
items.rationale: Young children cannot reliably report pain at an intravenous site, so the nurse must inspect it at least hourly, comparing the extremity with the opposite side for swelling, coolness, or redness. Pump alarms often continue to infuse into infiltrated tissue without alarming, and any protective covering must still allow the insertion site to be seen.

items.stem: The parent of an infant with a large ventricular septal defect asks why the baby keeps developing respiratory infections. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
options: The defect lets extra blood flow into the lungs, which promotes infection
The defect sends unoxygenated blood to the body, weakening immunity
The heart squeezes the airways because it is enlarged on the left
Frequent infections are unrelated to the heart defect at this age
items.rationale: A ventricular septal defect shunts blood from the higher-pressure left ventricle to the right ventricle, increasing pulmonary blood flow. The congested pulmonary circulation predisposes the infant to recurrent respiratory infections and symptoms of heart failure. It is not a cyanotic defect, so systemic desaturation is not the mechanism.

items.stem: A nurse auscultates the heart of an infant with a patent ductus arteriosus. Which finding is characteristic of this defect?
options: A pericardial friction rub at the lower sternal border
A continuous machine-like murmur
Muffled heart tones with a narrow pulse pressure
A midsystolic click at the apex
items.rationale: A patent ductus arteriosus produces a characteristic continuous murmur often described as machine-like, heard through systole and diastole as blood flows from the aorta into the pulmonary artery. Bounding peripheral pulses and a widened pulse pressure commonly accompany it. Friction rubs, muffled tones, and clicks point to other cardiac problems.

items.stem: A nurse assesses a child with suspected coarctation of the aorta. Which set of findings supports this diagnosis?
options: Blood pressure higher in the legs than the arms with flushed feet
Equal blood pressures in all extremities with a loud murmur
Blood pressure higher in the arms than the legs with weak femoral pulses
Cyanosis of the upper body with clubbing of the fingers
items.rationale: Coarctation narrows the aorta, usually near the ductus arteriosus, so pressure is elevated proximal to the narrowing and reduced distal to it. The classic picture is upper-extremity blood pressure notably higher than lower-extremity pressure, with weak or absent femoral pulses and cool lower extremities. Older children may also report leg cramping with activity.

items.stem: A nursing student reviews the anatomy of tetralogy of Fallot. Which defects make up this condition? Select all that apply.
options: Atrial septal defect
Ventricular septal defect
Pulmonary stenosis
Overriding aorta
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Right ventricular hypertrophy
items.rationale: Tetralogy of Fallot consists of four defects: a ventricular septal defect, pulmonary stenosis that obstructs right ventricular outflow, an aorta that overrides the septal defect, and right ventricular hypertrophy that develops from pumping against the stenosis. An atrial septal defect and left ventricular hypertrophy are not components.

items.stem: A nurse prepares to give the scheduled dose of digoxin to a 5-month-old with heart failure. The apical pulse, counted for a full minute, is 82/min. What should the nurse do?
options: Give the dose and recheck the pulse in 30 minutes
Give half of the prescribed dose and document the pulse
Withhold the dose and notify the provider
Delay the dose until the infant is crying, then give it
items.rationale: Before every digoxin dose the apical pulse is counted for one full minute, and in an infant the dose is typically withheld and the provider notified if the rate is below about 90 to 110 beats/min, because bradycardia is an early sign of toxicity. A nurse never independently halves a prescribed dose, and giving the drug despite bradycardia risks serious dysrhythmia.

items.stem: A nurse assesses a 3-month-old for early signs of heart failure. Which findings support this concern? Select all that apply.
options: Sweating on the scalp and forehead during feedings
Falling asleep after taking only a small amount of formula
Weight gain that falls below the expected curve
A resting respiratory rate of 68/min
A sunken anterior fontanel
An apical pulse of 88/min while awake
items.rationale: For an infant, feeding is exercise, so heart failure first appears as diaphoresis with feeds, tiring before the feeding is finished, poor weight gain, tachypnea, and tachycardia. A sunken fontanel suggests dehydration rather than heart failure, and an awake heart rate of 88/min in a young infant is bradycardic, not the tachycardia expected with failure.

items.stem: An 8-year-old is admitted with fever, migrating joint pain, and a new heart murmur three weeks after a sore throat. Which laboratory result supports a diagnosis of rheumatic fever?
options: A positive Monospot test
An elevated antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer
A decreased erythrocyte sedimentation rate
An elevated serum lipase level
items.rationale: Rheumatic fever is an inflammatory disease that follows inadequately treated group A streptococcal pharyngitis, and an elevated ASO titer documents the recent streptococcal infection. Diagnosis combines this evidence with major and minor clinical criteria such as carditis and polyarthritis. Inflammatory markers like the sedimentation rate rise rather than fall.

items.stem: A child recovering from rheumatic fever with carditis is being discharged. Which parent statement shows correct understanding of long-term management?
options: Antibiotics can stop once the joint pain has fully resolved
My child will need regular penicillin injections for years, even when feeling well
We only need to treat future sore throats if a fever develops
A repeat episode is unlikely, so no follow-up is needed
items.rationale: Children who have had rheumatic fever, especially with carditis, receive long-term prophylaxis, classically monthly intramuscular benzathine penicillin G, to prevent recurrent streptococcal infection and further heart valve damage. Prophylaxis continues for years regardless of how well the child feels, because each recurrence increases the risk of permanent cardiac injury.

items.stem: The parent of a child with asthma asks what it means when the peak flow reading falls in the yellow zone of the asthma action plan. Which response by the nurse is correct?
options: Asthma is well controlled, so continue the usual daily medicines
Symptoms are worsening, so give the quick-relief inhaler as the plan directs
This is a medical emergency, so call 911 right away
The controller medicine can be stopped for the rest of the day
items.rationale: The yellow zone, generally 50 to 79 percent of the personal best peak flow, signals caution: symptoms are flaring and the child should use the prescribed quick-relief bronchodilator and follow the step-up instructions on the action plan. Green means good control, and red, below 50 percent, is the emergency zone requiring immediate treatment and urgent care.

items.stem: A nurse teaches a school-age child to use a metered-dose inhaler with a spacer. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Breathe in slowly and deeply through the mouthpiece
Shake the inhaler and insert it into the spacer
Hold the breath for about 10 seconds
Press the canister once to release one puff into the spacer
Breathe out all the way, turning the head away from the spacer
Close the lips tightly around the spacer mouthpiece
items.rationale: The inhaler is shaken and attached to the spacer first, then the child exhales completely so the next breath can be a full, slow inhalation. After sealing the lips on the mouthpiece, one puff is released into the spacer, the child inhales slowly and deeply, and a 10-second breath-hold lets the medication settle in the airways. Only one puff at a time should ever be sprayed into a spacer.

items.stem: A school nurse responds to a 9-year-old who begins wheezing and coughing during recess. Place the actions in the order the nurse should perform them.
options: Reassess breathing and peak flow after the treatment
Have the child stop the activity and sit upright
Notify the parents and document the episode
Give the quick-relief inhaler with a spacer as the asthma action plan directs
Activate emergency medical services if breathing does not improve
items.rationale: Stopping the activity and sitting the child upright eases the work of breathing, and the quick-relief bronchodilator from the action plan is then given without delay. The nurse reassesses the response, escalates to emergency services if the child does not improve or moves into the red zone, and then completes parent notification and documentation.

items.stem: A nurse teaches the parents of a child with cystic fibrosis about pancreatic enzyme replacement. Which statement indicates the teaching was effective?
options: We will give the enzymes at bedtime so they work overnight
We will give the enzymes with every meal and every snack
We can crush the enzyme beads into hot cereal to hide them
We can skip the enzymes on days without greasy foods
items.rationale: Pancreatic enzymes replace what the blocked pancreatic ducts cannot deliver, so a dose must accompany all food, including snacks, taken within about 30 minutes of starting to eat. The enteric-coated beads must not be crushed or chewed, though capsules may be opened and sprinkled on a small amount of soft acidic food such as applesauce. Enzymes taken without food, or food taken without enzymes, leaves fat and protein unabsorbed.

items.stem: A nurse counsels the family of a school-age child with cystic fibrosis about nutrition. Which diet should the nurse recommend?
options: Low-fat, low-sodium diet with fluid restriction
High-calorie, high-protein diet with liberal salt
Standard-calorie diet with extra simple sugars
High-fiber, low-protein diet with potassium supplements
items.rationale: Children with cystic fibrosis lose calories through malabsorption and burn extra energy breathing, so they need a high-calorie, high-protein diet, with fat permitted because enzymes are taken with food. Because large amounts of sodium are lost in sweat, salty snacks and added salt are encouraged, especially in hot weather or with exercise.

items.stem: A nurse reinforces home care teaching for the family of a child with cystic fibrosis. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Use the airway clearance vest every day, even when the child feels well
Give pancreatic enzymes whenever the child eats meals or snacks
Provide a diet high in calories and protein
Offer extra fluids and salty snacks during hot weather
Limit dietary fat to reduce the number of stools
Perform airway clearance only when the child sounds congested
items.rationale: Daily airway clearance, such as high-frequency chest wall oscillation with a vest, prevents mucus stasis and must continue even during well periods. Enzymes with all food, a high-calorie high-protein diet, and replacement of the salt and fluid lost in sweat are core management. Fat is not restricted when enzymes are taken, and skipping airway clearance until congestion appears allows infection to take hold.

items.stem: A nurse plans the morning routine for a hospitalized child with cystic fibrosis. Place the care activities in the correct sequence.
options: Give pancreatic enzymes as the child begins breakfast
Assist the child to huff cough and expectorate loosened mucus
Administer the nebulized bronchodilator
Apply the high-frequency chest wall oscillation vest
items.rationale: The bronchodilator is given first to open the airways so that vest therapy can mobilize secretions effectively. Huff coughing then clears the loosened mucus, and airway clearance is completed before eating because the vibration and coughing can trigger vomiting on a full stomach. Enzymes are given as the meal starts so nutrients can be absorbed.

items.stem: A nurse in the neonatal unit identifies which infant as being at greatest risk for developing bronchopulmonary dysplasia?
options: A term infant treated briefly for transient tachypnea
An infant born at 26 weeks requiring weeks of mechanical ventilation and oxygen
A term infant of a mother with gestational diabetes
A 38-week infant who received phototherapy for jaundice
items.rationale: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia is a chronic lung disease of prematurity caused by injury to immature lungs from prolonged mechanical ventilation and high oxygen concentrations. The extremely preterm, ventilator-dependent infant is at greatest risk. These infants later need supplemental oxygen, careful nutrition for growth, and protection from respiratory infections such as respiratory syncytial virus.

items.stem: A nurse provides discharge teaching after a child has tympanostomy tubes placed for recurrent otitis media. Which parent statement indicates correct understanding?
options: He can never go swimming while the tubes are in place
He will wear earplugs for swimming if the surgeon recommends them
The tubes will stay in his ears permanently
We should pull a tube out ourselves if we see it loosening
items.rationale: Many surgeons allow swimming after tube placement but may recommend earplugs to keep water out of the middle ear, so parents should follow the provider's specific instructions. The tubes usually fall out on their own within about 6 to 12 months, and parents should simply notify the provider if a tube comes out rather than manipulating it themselves.

items.stem: A nurse monitors a 6-year-old during the first hours after a tonsillectomy. Which finding requires immediate notification of the provider?
options: The child reports a sore throat rated 4 out of 10
The child swallows frequently while dozing
Dark brown flecks are seen in the emesis basin
The child refuses to eat solid food
items.rationale: Frequent or continuous swallowing after tonsillectomy is the classic early sign of bleeding from the surgical site, because the child swallows the trickling blood; restlessness, tachycardia, and vomiting bright red blood are other warning signs. Throat pain is expected, old dark blood in small amounts is not alarming, and solid food is not required in the early postoperative period.

items.stem: A nurse gives discharge instructions to the parents of a child who had a tonsillectomy. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Do not let the child drink through a straw
Offer cool liquids that are not red or brown in color
Watch for bleeding about 5 to 10 days after surgery, when the scabs slough
Give acetaminophen as prescribed for throat pain
Encourage citrus juices to promote healing
Give aspirin if the pain medicine is not working
items.rationale: Straws create suction that can dislodge clots, and red or brown liquids make vomited blood impossible to recognize, so both are avoided. Bleeding risk returns around days 5 to 10 when the healing membrane sloughs, and acetaminophen is the preferred analgesic. Citrus juices irritate the raw surgical site, and aspirin is avoided because it increases bleeding and carries a risk of Reye syndrome.

items.stem: A nurse admits a 12-month-old returning from surgical repair of a cleft palate. Which item should the nurse remove from the bedside?
options: A pacifier clipped to the crib sheet
A small open drinking cup
Soft elbow immobilizers
The cardiorespiratory monitor
items.rationale: After cleft palate repair, nothing firm may enter the mouth because sucking on or contact with objects such as pacifiers, straws, spoons, or tongue blades can disrupt the suture line. An open cup is the preferred way to give fluids, and soft elbow immobilizers are used as needed to keep the child's hands away from the mouth while allowing periodic supervised removal.

items.stem: A nurse teaches the parents of a newborn with an unrepaired cleft palate about feeding. Which approach should the nurse recommend?
options: Feed the infant lying flat to reduce fatigue
Use a specialized bottle with a one-way valve and feed upright
Thicken all feedings and give them through a small spoon
Limit burping so the feeding is not interrupted
items.rationale: An infant with a cleft palate cannot generate normal suction, so specialized bottles with one-way valves or squeezable bodies deliver milk with minimal effort. Feeding in an upright position reduces the flow of milk into the nasal cavity, and frequent burping is needed because these infants swallow large amounts of air.

items.stem: A nurse teaches the parent of a 2-month-old with gastroesophageal reflux. Which parent statement indicates the teaching was understood?
options: I will hold her upright for about 30 minutes after each feeding
I will give larger feedings so she can go longer between bottles
I will lay her flat on her stomach right after she eats
I will switch her to low-fat formula to reduce the spitting up
items.rationale: Keeping the infant upright for 20 to 30 minutes after feeding uses gravity to keep formula in the stomach, and smaller, more frequent feedings, sometimes thickened as directed by the provider, reduce reflux episodes. Large feedings distend the stomach and worsen reflux, and although prone positioning improves reflux, infants must still sleep supine to reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome.

items.stem: A nurse reviews food choices with the parents of a child newly diagnosed with celiac disease. Which foods should the nurse teach the family to avoid? Select all that apply.
options: Plain rice cereal
Wheat toast with jam
A malted milk drink
Corn tortillas with cheese
Rye crackers
Vegetable soup made with pearl barley
items.rationale: Celiac disease requires strict elimination of gluten, the protein in wheat, rye, and barley; malt is made from barley, so malted drinks and malt-flavored cereals also contain gluten. Rice and corn are gluten-free grains and are safe staples for children with this condition.

items.stem: The parents of a child with celiac disease report that symptoms have resolved after several months without gluten. Which response by the nurse is appropriate?
options: You can slowly add wheat back and watch for symptoms
The gluten-free diet must continue for life, even without symptoms
Gluten is only harmful during periods of active diarrhea
Your child has outgrown the disease and may eat normally
items.rationale: Celiac disease is a permanent immune-mediated intolerance to gluten; symptom resolution means the diet is working, not that the disease is gone. Continued gluten exposure, even without obvious symptoms, damages intestinal villi and raises the risk of growth failure, nutrient deficiencies, and long-term complications, so the diet is lifelong.

items.stem: A nurse teaches the parents of an infant with a temporary colostomy created during surgery for Hirschsprung disease. Which observation should the parents report immediately?
options: The stoma appears deep red and moist
A small amount of blood appears when cleaning the stoma
The stoma has turned a dusky, grayish color
Soft stool collects in the pouch several times a day
items.rationale: A healthy stoma is deep red, moist, and may bleed slightly when cleaned because its surface is vascular mucosa. A dusky, gray, or purple stoma indicates compromised blood supply and possible necrosis, which is an emergency requiring immediate evaluation. Regular passage of soft stool into the pouch is the expected function of the ostomy.

items.stem: A 10-year-old awaiting an appendectomy has been guarding the right lower abdomen and rating pain 8 out of 10. The child suddenly announces that the pain is gone. What should the nurse do first?
options: Document that the pain has resolved spontaneously
Offer clear liquids since the child feels better
Notify the provider immediately
Assist the child to ambulate in the hallway
items.rationale: Sudden relief of pain in a child with appendicitis suggests the appendix has ruptured, releasing the pressure that was causing pain. Peritonitis follows, so the provider must be notified immediately. The child remains on nothing-by-mouth status for surgery, and the apparent improvement must never be documented as recovery.

items.stem: A nurse teaches the parent of a preschool-age girl who has had repeated urinary tract infections. Which prevention measures should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Avoid bubble baths
Teach her to wipe from front to back
Dress her in snug nylon underwear
Encourage water during the day and voiding every 3 to 4 hours
Teach her to hold urine until she gets home from preschool
Choose cotton underwear
items.rationale: Bubble baths and harsh soaps irritate the urethra, and wiping back to front carries bowel bacteria toward the urinary meatus, so both are corrected. Good fluid intake with regular, complete voiding flushes bacteria out of the bladder, and breathable cotton underwear keeps the perineum dry. Nylon traps moisture and urinary retention lets bacteria multiply, so both increase infection risk.

items.stem: A child with vesicoureteral reflux is prescribed a daily low-dose antibiotic. The parent asks why an antibiotic is needed when the child has no infection. Which explanation by the nurse is best?
options: It keeps the urine sterile so backflow cannot carry infection to the kidneys
It strengthens the valve between the bladder and the ureters
It dissolves the scar tissue that is blocking urine flow
It prevents the reflux from becoming painful during voiding
items.rationale: In vesicoureteral reflux, urine flows backward from the bladder into the ureters and kidneys, so any bladder infection can ascend and scar the kidneys. Low-dose prophylactic antibiotics keep the urine free of bacteria while the child grows, because mild reflux often resolves as the ureteral valves mature. The medication does not repair the valve or remove scar tissue.

items.stem: A nurse assesses a preschooler admitted with nephrotic syndrome. Which findings should the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
options: Periorbital edema that is worse on waking
Tea-colored urine
Urine that appears frothy in the diaper
Massive proteinuria on dipstick testing
Severely elevated blood pressure
Recent weight gain with abdominal distention
items.rationale: Nephrotic syndrome causes heavy urinary protein loss, which makes the urine frothy, drops serum albumin, and drives fluid into the tissues, producing periorbital and dependent edema, ascites, and weight gain. Blood pressure is typically normal or only mildly changed. Tea-colored urine and marked hypertension are hallmarks of acute glomerulonephritis instead.

items.stem: A 4-year-old receiving daily high-dose prednisone for nephrotic syndrome is due for the varicella vaccine. Which action by the nurse is correct?
options: Give the vaccine now to protect the immunosuppressed child
Give half the vaccine dose and complete it after the steroids end
Defer the vaccine until the corticosteroid course is finished
Give the vaccine only if the child has a sibling in school
items.rationale: Varicella vaccine contains live attenuated virus, and live vaccines are withheld during high-dose corticosteroid therapy because the suppressed immune system may allow the vaccine strain to cause disease. The vaccine is deferred until an adequate interval after the steroids are completed, while inactivated vaccines may still be given. Splitting a vaccine dose is never appropriate.

items.stem: A 7-year-old is admitted with acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis: tea-colored urine, periorbital edema, and a blood pressure of 128/86 mm Hg. Which assessment is the priority during hospitalization?
options: Daily head circumference measurement
Frequent blood pressure monitoring
Hourly capillary glucose checks
Range-of-motion testing of the joints
items.rationale: Acute glomerulonephritis reduces glomerular filtration, causing fluid retention and hypertension that can rise abruptly and lead to hypertensive encephalopathy with seizures. Frequent blood pressure monitoring, along with daily weights and strict intake and output, is therefore the priority. Glucose and joint assessments are unrelated to this condition.

items.stem: A toddler is admitted with a newly diagnosed Wilms tumor and is scheduled for surgery. Which intervention should the nurse include in the plan of care?
options: Post a sign above the bed stating that the abdomen must not be palpated
Measure the abdominal mass with a tape measure every shift
Encourage the parents to massage the abdomen to ease discomfort
Apply warm compresses to the flank to reduce swelling
items.rationale: A Wilms tumor is an encapsulated kidney tumor, and any palpation or manipulation of the abdomen can rupture the capsule and seed cancer cells throughout the abdomen. A visible reminder not to palpate protects the child from well-meaning staff and family. Handling and bathing are done gently until the tumor is removed.

items.stem: A nurse reviews the workup of a toddler with an abdominal mass. Which finding suggests neuroblastoma rather than Wilms tumor?
options: A smooth mass confined to one side of the abdomen
A mass that crosses the midline with elevated urinary catecholamines
Painless swelling first noticed during a diaper change
A mass discovered before 5 years of age
items.rationale: Neuroblastoma arises from sympathetic nervous system tissue, often in the adrenal gland, typically presents as an irregular mass that crosses the abdominal midline, and secretes catecholamines detectable as elevated urinary vanillylmandelic and homovanillic acid. A Wilms tumor is usually a smooth, firm mass confined to one flank. Both occur in young children and may be found incidentally by caregivers.

items.stem: A newborn is diagnosed with hypospadias, and the parents ask about circumcision before discharge. Which information should the nurse provide?
options: Circumcision should be done now to prevent future infections
Circumcision is delayed because the foreskin may be used in the surgical repair
Circumcision is required by law before hypospadias repair
Circumcision has no relationship to the hypospadias repair
items.rationale: In hypospadias the urethral opening is on the underside of the penis, and surgical correction, usually performed in the first year of life, often uses the foreskin tissue to reconstruct the urethra. Circumcision is therefore deferred until the repair is complete so the tissue remains available.

items.stem: The parents of a 9-month-old with an undescended right testis (cryptorchidism) ask what will happen next. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
options: The testis always descends on its own by 2 years of age
Surgical correction is usually performed around 1 year of age if it has not descended
Treatment can safely wait until puberty begins
No treatment is needed because one descended testis is enough
items.rationale: Spontaneous descent rarely occurs after about 6 months of age, so orchiopexy is typically performed between roughly 6 and 12 months. Leaving the testis in the warmer abdominal environment damages sperm-producing cells and increases the lifelong risk of testicular cancer, and an undescended testis is also harder to examine for masses later in life.

items.stem: A school-age child with type 1 diabetes plans to join an after-school soccer team. Which instruction should the nurse give the child and parents?
options: Skip the afternoon insulin dose on practice days
Eat an extra carbohydrate snack before prolonged practice
Avoid drinking fluids during practice to prevent cramping
Withdraw from the team because exercise is too risky
items.rationale: Exercise increases glucose uptake by muscles, so an additional 15 to 30 grams of carbohydrate before sustained activity helps prevent hypoglycemia, and glucose should be monitored because lows can occur hours after exercise ends. Insulin is adjusted only as directed by the provider, never simply skipped, and regular exercise is encouraged as part of diabetes management.

items.stem: A nurse reviews sick-day management with the parents of a child who has type 1 diabetes. Which parent statement indicates correct understanding?
options: I will stop the insulin while she has no appetite
I will keep giving insulin and check her glucose and urine ketones frequently
I will wait to check her glucose until she can eat a full meal
I will give only half the insulin whenever she vomits once
items.rationale: Illness triggers stress hormones that raise blood glucose, so insulin is never stopped during sickness even when the child eats poorly. Glucose is checked every few hours, urine ketones are monitored, and sugar-containing fluids are offered if intake is poor, with the provider called for persistent vomiting, moderate to large ketones, or inability to keep fluids down.

items.stem: A school nurse is called for a 7-year-old with type 1 diabetes who is shaky, sweaty, and pale before lunch. Place the actions in the order the nurse should perform them.
options: Recheck the blood glucose after 15 minutes
Check the blood glucose with a glucometer
Provide a snack with protein and complex carbohydrate once the level is normal
Give 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate, such as 4 ounces of juice
Repeat the fast-acting carbohydrate if the level remains low
items.rationale: Because the child is alert, the nurse first confirms hypoglycemia with a glucose check, then gives 15 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate. The level is rechecked in 15 minutes and the carbohydrate repeated if it remains low, following the rule of 15. Once the glucose is normal, a snack with protein and complex carbohydrate prevents the level from dropping again before the next meal.

items.stem: A child with growth hormone deficiency is prescribed daily somatropin injections. Which instruction should the nurse give the parents?
options: Give the subcutaneous injection at bedtime
Give the injection only on days the child seems tired
Massage the site vigorously after each injection
Stop the injections once height catches up to peers
items.rationale: Growth hormone is normally secreted in pulses during sleep, so giving the daily subcutaneous dose at bedtime mimics the natural pattern. Doses are given consistently every day with rotated sites, and therapy continues for years under endocrine supervision, typically until growth plates close, rather than stopping when height improves.

items.stem: A 6-year-old girl with precocious puberty is starting monthly leuprolide injections. Which point is most important for the nurse to emphasize with the parents?
options: She should be given more household responsibility to match her appearance
Continue to treat her according to her actual age, not her physical development
She should be moved to a classroom with older children
Discussion of body changes should be avoided so she does not worry
items.rationale: A child with precocious puberty looks older than her years, but her cognitive, social, and emotional development match her chronological age, so expectations, dress, and activities should fit a typical 6-year-old. Parents should also give simple, honest explanations of body changes, because silence increases anxiety. Leuprolide pauses pubertal progression while treatment continues.

items.stem: A 20-month-old is diagnosed with iron-deficiency anemia. Which information from the diet history most likely explains the anemia?
options: The child eats eggs several mornings a week
The child drinks about 32 ounces of whole milk daily
The child snacks on dry iron-fortified cereal
The child dislikes citrus fruits and juices
items.rationale: Excessive milk intake is the classic cause of iron-deficiency anemia in toddlers: milk is low in iron, it fills the child so iron-rich solid foods are refused, and large volumes interfere with iron absorption. Milk should generally be limited to about 16 to 24 ounces per day, with iron-rich foods making up the difference.

items.stem: A nurse teaches the parents of a toddler starting liquid oral iron supplements. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Offer the iron with orange juice or another vitamin C source
Give the iron with a full glass of milk to protect the stomach
Expect the stools to look dark green or black
Give the liquid through a straw or syringe placed past the front teeth
Store the bottle locked and out of the child's reach
Stop the iron as soon as the child seems less pale
items.rationale: Vitamin C enhances iron absorption, while milk and other calcium sources block it. Dark green-black stools show the iron is being taken, and directing the liquid past the teeth with a straw or syringe prevents staining of the enamel. Iron is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in young children, so it must be locked away, and the full prescribed course is completed to rebuild iron stores even after the child looks better.

items.stem: A school-age child with sickle cell disease is admitted in a vaso-occlusive crisis with severe leg pain. Which interventions should the nurse implement first?
options: Apply ice packs to the painful areas and restrict fluids
Give prescribed opioid analgesia and start intravenous hydration
Begin active range-of-motion exercises to improve circulation
Place the child in a knee-to-chest position and give oxygen
items.rationale: The priorities in vaso-occlusive crisis are aggressive pain control, usually with scheduled intravenous opioids, and hydration to reduce blood viscosity and sludging of sickled cells. Cold causes vasoconstriction and worsens sickling, so warmth, not ice, is applied, and the child needs rest rather than exercise during the acute crisis.

items.stem: A nurse assesses a 2-year-old with sickle cell disease. Which finding indicates a life-threatening complication requiring emergency intervention?
options: Sudden pallor and listlessness with a rapidly enlarging left-sided abdominal mass
Swelling of the hands and feet with irritability
Yellow tint to the sclera noticed over several weeks
A hemoglobin level near the child's usual baseline
items.rationale: Sudden pallor, lethargy, and a rapidly enlarging spleen signal splenic sequestration, in which a large portion of the blood volume pools in the spleen and hypovolemic shock can develop within hours. This is an emergency requiring rapid volume support and transfusion. Painful swelling of the hands and feet and mild scleral icterus are common, non-emergent findings in sickle cell disease.

items.stem: A nurse teaches the family of a child with sickle cell disease how to reduce the risk of vaso-occlusive crises. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Encourage fluids throughout the day, with extra in hot weather
Apply ice packs promptly to any painful, swollen joint
Avoid travel to high-altitude locations
Give the daily prophylactic penicillin as prescribed
Keep pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccinations up to date
Restrict fluids in the evening to prevent bedwetting
items.rationale: Generous hydration keeps blood viscosity low and is the cornerstone of crisis prevention, while high altitude lowers oxygen tension and can trigger sickling. Because the spleen loses function early, daily prophylactic penicillin and current immunization against encapsulated organisms protect against overwhelming infection. Ice is avoided because cold vasoconstriction promotes sickling, and fluids are never restricted, even at night.

items.stem: The parents of a school-age child with severe hemophilia A ask which activities are appropriate. Which activities should the nurse encourage? Select all that apply.
options: Swimming
Tackle football
Golf
Bicycling while wearing a helmet and pads
Wrestling
Walking and hiking on marked trails
items.rationale: Regular exercise strengthens the muscles that protect joints, so noncontact activities such as swimming, golf, walking, and helmeted bicycling are encouraged. Contact and collision sports like tackle football and wrestling carry a high risk of traumatic bleeding, including joint and intracranial hemorrhage, and are avoided.

items.stem: A child with hemophilia A bumps a knee at home, and the joint becomes swollen and painful. Place the actions the nurse teaches the family in the order they should be performed.
options: Apply a cold pack wrapped in a cloth to the knee
Have the child stop all activity immediately
Elevate the affected leg above heart level
Administer the prescribed factor VIII replacement
Immobilize the knee with a splint in a comfortable position
items.rationale: Activity stops at once so the bleeding is not worsened, and factor VIII replacement is given as early as possible because replacing the missing clotting factor is what actually stops a hemarthrosis. The joint is then rested and immobilized, cold is applied to promote vasoconstriction, and elevation above the heart reduces blood flow into the joint, completing the rest-ice-compression-elevation approach.

items.stem: A child receiving chemotherapy for leukemia is at the expected nadir, with an absolute neutrophil count of 400/mm3. Which precautions should the nurse implement? Select all that apply.
options: Place the child in a private room
Avoid rectal temperatures and suppositories
Remove fresh flowers and live plants from the room
Screen visitors and restrict anyone with signs of illness
Offer fresh salad and unpeeled raw fruit at meals
Schedule daily group play in the unit playroom
items.rationale: At the nadir the neutrophil count is at its lowest and any organism can cause overwhelming infection, so the child is protected with a private room, careful visitor screening, and removal of flowers and plants that harbor mold and bacteria. Rectal procedures are avoided because they can tear fragile mucosa and introduce bacteria. Raw unpeeled produce and group play in shared spaces expose the child to unnecessary pathogens during this period.

items.stem: A child receiving chemotherapy has developed painful oral mucositis. Which mouth care instruction should the nurse give?
options: Clean the mouth with a soft sponge swab and rinse with saline
Brush vigorously with a firm toothbrush after every meal
Rinse twice daily with an alcohol-based mouthwash
Use lemon-glycerin swabs to freshen the mouth
items.rationale: Chemotherapy damages rapidly dividing mucosal cells, so the mouth is cleaned gently with a soft sponge swab or very soft brush and rinsed with bland solutions such as normal saline. Firm brushes traumatize the tissue and can cause bleeding, while alcohol mouthwashes and lemon-glycerin swabs dry, burn, and further irritate the ulcerated mucosa.

items.stem: The parent of a child receiving maintenance chemotherapy asks about influenza protection for the family this fall. Which response by the nurse is correct?
options: The child should receive the live nasal spray flu vaccine
The child may receive the inactivated injectable flu vaccine, and household members should be vaccinated too
No one in the household should receive any flu vaccine this year
The child needs no flu vaccine because chemotherapy prevents infection
items.rationale: Children on chemotherapy may receive inactivated vaccines such as the injectable influenza vaccine, although the response may be blunted; live vaccines, including the nasal spray, are contraindicated during immunosuppression. Vaccinating household members with inactivated vaccines creates a protective cocoon around the child and is strongly encouraged.

items.stem: A nurse prepares to give an oral liquid medication to a 6-month-old infant. Place the steps in the order the nurse should perform them.
options: Place the syringe tip along the inside of the infant's cheek
Verify the order and perform hand hygiene
Cuddle and comfort the infant after the dose is finished
Hold the infant in a semi-upright position on the lap
Draw up the measured dose in an oral syringe
Give small amounts, allowing the infant to swallow each one
items.rationale: After verifying the order and performing hand hygiene, the nurse measures the dose accurately in an oral syringe. Holding the infant semi-upright reduces the risk of aspiration, and directing the syringe along the inside of the cheek in small increments lets the infant swallow safely between amounts. Comforting the infant afterward ends the experience positively, consistent with atraumatic care.

items.stem: A 5-year-old is admitted with varicella (chickenpox). Which transmission-based precautions should the nurse implement?
options: Droplet precautions with a surgical mask when within 3 feet
Contact precautions only, using a gown and gloves
Airborne and contact precautions in a negative-pressure room
Standard precautions, because the child is afebrile
items.rationale: Varicella spreads by airborne droplet nuclei and by direct contact with vesicle fluid, so the child needs an airborne infection isolation room plus contact precautions, and only immune staff should provide care. Droplet precautions alone do not stop airborne spread, contact precautions alone ignore the respiratory route, and standard precautions are insufficient regardless of fever.

items.stem: A nurse provides discharge teaching to the parent of a 6-year-old with varicella who will recover at home. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Apply a heating pad to itchy areas to soothe the skin
Keep the child home until every lesion has crusted over
Give acetaminophen rather than aspirin for fever
Trim the fingernails short and consider soft mittens at night
Scrub the lesions daily with an antibacterial cleanser
Offer lukewarm oatmeal baths and calamine lotion for itching
items.rationale: The child remains contagious until all vesicles have crusted, aspirin is avoided because of its link with Reye syndrome, short nails and mittens limit scratching and secondary bacterial infection, and tepid oatmeal baths with calamine ease pruritus. Heat increases itching through vasodilation, and scrubbing lesions breaks the vesicles, inviting infection and scarring.

items.stem: A nurse assesses a 3-year-old with a 3-day history of high fever, cough, runny nose, and red watery eyes. The nurse notes tiny white spots on a red base on the buccal mucosa opposite the molars. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
options: Rubeola (measles)
Hand-foot-and-mouth disease
Scarlet fever
Oral candidiasis (thrush)
items.rationale: Koplik spots, small bluish-white lesions on the buccal mucosa, appear during the measles prodrome along with the classic cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis, 1 to 2 days before the maculopapular rash begins at the hairline.
