Hand-foot-and-mouth disease causes painful vesicles on the tongue and palate with lesions on the palms and soles, scarlet fever produces a strawberry tongue and sandpaper rash, and thrush produces white plaques without this febrile respiratory prodrome.

items.stem: A parent walks into a pediatric clinic carrying a 4-year-old who is unimmunized, has a high fever, and has a blotchy red rash spreading downward from the hairline. Place the nurse's actions in the order they should be performed.
options: Notify the local public health department of the suspected case
Place a surgical mask on the child and move the family out of the waiting area immediately
Identify other patients and staff who shared the waiting room for exposure follow-up
Escort the family to an airborne infection isolation room or a private room with the door closed
Assign a caregiver with documented measles immunity to complete the assessment
items.rationale: Measles is one of the most contagious airborne diseases and the virus lingers in room air for up to 2 hours, so the very first action is to mask the child and remove the family from the shared space, then place them in a negative-pressure room. Only staff with documented immunity should provide care. Suspected measles is immediately reportable, and the health department then works with the clinic to identify everyone who was exposed and offer post-exposure vaccine or immune globulin.

items.stem: A 15-year-old with mumps reports new, severe pain and swelling of one testicle on the fifth day of illness. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Reassure the adolescent that this is unrelated to mumps and will resolve without treatment
Prepare the adolescent for emergency surgical exploration
Instruct the adolescent to apply warm compresses and walk frequently
Explain that this is a known complication, notify the provider, and apply ice packs with scrotal support
items.rationale: Orchitis develops in a portion of post-pubertal males with mumps, usually 4 to 8 days after parotid swelling; care is supportive with ice, a scrotal support, analgesics, and rest, and the provider is informed. Dismissing the symptom is inaccurate, mumps orchitis is not treated surgically (although torsion would be ruled out if the picture were unclear), and warmth and activity worsen the swelling and pain.

items.stem: A 6-year-old is diagnosed with rubella (German measles). The child's aunt, who is 10 weeks pregnant, asks whether she can help care for the child at home. What is the nurse's best response?
options: "Rubella is a mild illness, so caring for the child is safe as long as you wash your hands."
"You should avoid contact with the child during the contagious period because rubella can cause serious birth defects."
"You can care for the child if you wear a mask for the first day of the rash."
"Rubella is only dangerous to a pregnancy during the third trimester."
items.rationale: Rubella is mild in children but is teratogenic; infection during the first trimester carries the highest risk of congenital rubella syndrome with deafness, cataracts, and heart defects. A pregnant person without documented immunity should stay away from the child for about 7 days after the rash appears and have her immune status checked. Hand hygiene or a mask for a single day does not protect against a droplet-spread virus during the contagious period, and the danger is greatest early in pregnancy, not late.

items.stem: A 3-month-old is admitted with pertussis (whooping cough). Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Maintain droplet precautions until the infant has completed 5 days of antibiotic therapy
Administer the prescribed macrolide antibiotic such as azithromycin
Place the infant on a cooling blanket to shorten the paroxysmal stage
Recommend prophylactic antibiotics for all household contacts regardless of immunization status
Encourage the parents to bring the infant's unimmunized 2-year-old sibling to visit
Keep suction and oxygen at the bedside and monitor pulse oximetry continuously
items.rationale: Pertussis spreads by droplets and remains contagious until 5 days of effective antibiotics; macrolides are first-line treatment and are also given to household contacts because vaccine immunity wanes. Young infants can develop apnea, cyanosis, and thick mucus plugs during coughing paroxysms, so airway equipment and continuous monitoring are essential. Cooling blankets have no role, and an unimmunized toddler must not be exposed to a contagious infant.

items.stem: A parent calls the clinic because their 7-year-old woke up with bright red cheeks that look "slapped" and a lacy pink rash on the arms. The child feels well and had a mild cold last week. The parent asks whether the child can attend school. Which response is correct?
options: "The child may attend school; once this rash appears, the child is no longer contagious."
"Keep the child home until the rash has completely faded."
"Keep the child home for 5 days and start the prescribed antibiotic."
"Bring the child in today for an urgent strep test."
items.rationale: Erythema infectiosum (fifth disease, parvovirus B19) is contagious during the mild prodrome before the rash; by the time the slapped-cheek and lacy reticular rash appear, the child no longer sheds the virus and may attend school. The rash may fade and reappear for weeks with heat or sunlight, the illness is viral so antibiotics are useless, and strep testing is not indicated for this classic picture. Pregnant contacts should be told about the exposure because the virus can affect the fetus.

items.stem: A 14-month-old had 3 days of fever near 39.5 C (103.1 F) with no other findings. This morning the fever broke and a pink, blanching rash appeared on the trunk. The child is playful. Which explanation should the nurse give the parent?
options: "The rash suggests an allergic reaction to the fever medicine."
"This is measles, and the child needs to be seen immediately."
"The child likely has scarlet fever and needs a throat culture."
"This pattern is typical of roseola; the rash means the illness is ending."
items.rationale: Roseola (human herpesvirus 6) classically causes several days of abrupt high fever in an otherwise well-appearing infant or toddler, followed by a rose-pink macular rash on the trunk that appears as the fever resolves. A drug rash would not follow this predictable timeline, measles presents with cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis and a rash that starts at the hairline during high fever, and scarlet fever produces a sandpaper rash with pharyngitis.

items.stem: A 6-year-old is diagnosed with scarlet fever and started on oral penicillin. The child has a fine, rough red rash on the trunk and a red tongue with prominent papillae. Which statement by the parent indicates a need for further teaching?
options: "My child can return to school after 24 hours on the antibiotic if the fever is gone."
"The skin on the fingers and toes may peel as the rash fades."
"I can stop the antibiotic as soon as the rash disappears."
"I should replace my child's toothbrush after a day or two on the antibiotic."
items.rationale: Scarlet fever is group A streptococcal pharyngitis with a toxin-mediated sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue; the full 10-day antibiotic course must be completed even after symptoms resolve to prevent rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis. Returning to school after 24 hours of antibiotics without fever is standard, desquamation of the hands and feet is expected during recovery, and replacing the toothbrush removes a reservoir for reinfection.

items.stem: A nurse in a child-care setting teaches staff about hand-foot-and-mouth disease after two toddlers are diagnosed. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
options: Children with the illness should be given aspirin for mouth pain
The illness is caused by a virus, so antibiotics are not helpful
Children must be kept home until all blisters on the hands and feet have healed
Cold fluids and soft foods are better tolerated than citrus juices and salty foods
Careful hand hygiene after diaper changes is essential because the virus is shed in stool for weeks
items.rationale: Hand-foot-and-mouth disease is caused by coxsackievirus and other enteroviruses, spreads through respiratory secretions, blister fluid, and feces, and is managed with cold bland fluids, analgesia, and frequent disinfection of toys and surfaces. Exclusion is based on fever, drooling, or inability to participate rather than on the presence of blisters, and aspirin is never given to children with viral illness because of Reye syndrome.

items.stem: A school nurse examines a 5-year-old with clustered lesions around the nose and mouth that have ruptured and formed honey-colored crusts. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Apply a warm compress to loosen the crusts and send the child back to class
Wash the hands, put on gloves, and cover the lesions before contacting the parent
Advise the parent that the lesions are viral and will resolve on their own
Send the child home with instructions to scrub the lesions with alcohol
items.rationale: Honey-colored crusts are the hallmark of impetigo, a highly contagious bacterial skin infection caused by staphylococci or streptococci and spread by direct contact, so contact precautions and covering the lesions come first, followed by referral for topical or oral antibiotics. The child should not return to class untreated, impetigo is bacterial rather than viral, and alcohol scrubbing is painful and does not treat the infection.

items.stem: A school nurse reviews the morning's visits. Based on common exclusion guidelines, which children may remain at school today? Select all that apply.
options: A 7-year-old with bacterial conjunctivitis who began antibiotic eye drops 24 hours ago and has no drainage
A 9-year-old with a round scaly patch of ringworm on the forearm that is covered and being treated with antifungal cream
A 6-year-old with live head lice found during a routine check who is otherwise well
A 5-year-old with untreated impetigo lesions on the chin that are oozing
A 4-year-old with hand-foot-and-mouth disease who is drooling, feverish, and refusing to drink
An 8-year-old with the lacy rash of fifth disease who feels well
items.rationale: A child with bacterial conjunctivitis may return after 24 hours of antibiotics, covered and treated ringworm is not a reason for exclusion, current guidance allows a child with live lice to finish the school day and return after treatment, and fifth disease is no longer contagious once the rash appears. A child with untreated, weeping impetigo is excluded until 24 hours of antibiotic therapy, and a child who is febrile, drooling, and unable to drink cannot participate and needs care at home.

items.stem: A nurse instructs a parent on collecting a specimen to check a 4-year-old for pinworms using the tape test. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Press the sticky side of clear cellophane tape against the skin around the anus
Wake the child early in the morning before bathing or using the toilet
Place the tape sticky side down on a glass slide or in a clean bag and bring it to the clinic
Spread the buttocks apart with gloved hands
Wash hands thoroughly and repeat on 3 consecutive mornings if the first test is negative
items.rationale: Female pinworms migrate to the perianal skin overnight to lay eggs, so the sample is collected first thing in the morning before the child bathes or has a bowel movement, which would remove the eggs. The buttocks are spread, the sticky tape is pressed against the perianal folds, and the tape is placed on a slide for microscopy. Because egg laying is intermittent, up to 3 morning collections may be needed before the test is considered negative.

items.stem: A 5-year-old is diagnosed with pinworms (enterobiasis) and prescribed a single dose of an anthelmintic to be repeated in 2 weeks. Which additional instruction should the nurse give the family?
options: The child must stay home from school until the second dose is given
Pets in the home should be treated by a veterinarian
All household members should be treated at the same time
The family should discard all of the child's toys
items.rationale: Pinworm eggs spread easily on hands, bedding, and surfaces, and household members are usually infected without symptoms, so treating everyone simultaneously and repeating in 2 weeks prevents reinfection; hot-water laundering of bedding and underwear and morning showers also help. School exclusion is not required, pinworms infect only humans so pets are not involved, and toys need washing rather than disposal.

items.stem: A parent whose 8-year-old was found to have head lice tells the nurse, "I am so embarrassed; I keep my house very clean." Which statements should the nurse include in the response? Select all that apply.
options: "Soak your child's head in kerosene overnight to smother the lice."
"Head lice spread by head-to-head contact and are not a sign of poor hygiene."
"Apply the pediculicide as directed and repeat the treatment in about 7 to 9 days to kill newly hatched lice."
"Shave your child's head to prevent the infestation from returning."
"Wash bedding, hats, and recently worn clothing in hot water and dry on high heat."
"Seal stuffed animals that cannot be washed in a plastic bag for about 2 weeks."
items.rationale: Lice infest clean and dirty hair alike and spread mainly through direct contact; treatment includes a pediculicide applied per the label with a second application 7 to 9 days later to kill nymphs that hatch after the first treatment, laundering items in hot water, and bagging unwashable items so any remaining lice die. Kerosene is flammable and toxic, and shaving the head is unnecessary and distressing for the child.

items.stem: A nurse teaches a parent how to treat a child's head lice with over-the-counter 1% permethrin creme rinse. Place the steps in the correct order.
options: Apply the permethrin to the damp hair and scalp and leave it in place for 10 minutes
Rinse the product out with warm water over a sink rather than in the tub
Use a fine-toothed nit comb on the wet hair to remove nits, working section by section
Shampoo the hair with a regular shampoo without conditioner and towel dry
Repeat the application in 7 to 9 days to kill lice that hatch after the first treatment
items.rationale: Permethrin creme rinse is applied to hair that has been washed with plain shampoo (conditioner coats the hair shaft and blocks the product) and towel dried, left on for 10 minutes, then rinsed at a sink to limit skin exposure. Nit combing removes eggs that the product does not kill, and a second application 7 to 9 days later kills nymphs that hatched after the first treatment.

items.stem: A nurse reviews a clinic's list of infants entering their first RSV season. Which infant is the most appropriate candidate for monthly palivizumab injections?
options: A 4-month-old born at 28 weeks gestation who required oxygen for chronic lung disease of prematurity
A healthy 2-month-old born at 39 weeks whose sibling attends daycare
A 6-month-old born at 36 weeks with a small ventricular septal defect that closed on its own
A 10-month-old who recovered from RSV bronchiolitis last winter
items.rationale: Palivizumab is a monoclonal antibody reserved for infants at highest risk of severe RSV disease, such as those born very preterm with chronic lung disease requiring treatment or those with hemodynamically significant congenital heart disease, and is given monthly through the RSV season. Healthy term infants, late preterm infants without lung or heart disease, and infants who already had RSV do not meet the criteria, although the newer long-acting antibody nirsevimab is offered more broadly to infants in their first season.

items.stem: A 4-year-old is due for the second doses of MMR and varicella vaccines. The child's 9-year-old brother is receiving chemotherapy for leukemia. Which action by the nurse is correct?
options: Defer both vaccines until the brother completes chemotherapy
Give MMR but withhold varicella because of the brother's immune status
Give inactivated versions of both vaccines instead
Administer both vaccines to the 4-year-old as scheduled
items.rationale: Healthy household contacts of immunocompromised people should receive MMR and varicella vaccines, because vaccine viruses are almost never transmitted and immunizing contacts shields the vulnerable child from wild-type disease. The only precaution is to avoid close contact if the vaccinated child develops a vesicular rash after varicella vaccine. Deferral leaves both children at risk, MMR virus is not transmitted from vaccinees at all, and no inactivated forms of these vaccines exist.

items.stem: A nurse in a pediatric clinic prepares to administer scheduled immunizations. Which children can receive their vaccines today? Select all that apply.
options: A 12-month-old presenting for the first doses of MMR and varicella vaccines
A 2-month-old with a runny nose and a temperature of 37.6 C (99.7 F) who is feeding well
An 11-year-old presenting for the first dose of HPV vaccine
A 6-month-old presenting for a first influenza vaccine in October
A 4-year-old who has taken high-dose corticosteroids for 3 weeks and is due for MMR
A 15-month-old who had anaphylaxis after the first dose of DTaP and is due for the fourth dose
items.rationale: MMR and varicella are first given at 12 to 15 months, a minor illness with low-grade fever is not a reason to delay vaccines, HPV vaccination is routinely started at 11 to 12 years (and may begin at 9), and yearly influenza vaccine is recommended for everyone 6 months and older. High-dose systemic steroids for 2 weeks or more suppress immunity and contraindicate live vaccines until therapy has been stopped for at least a month, and anaphylaxis to a previous dose is an absolute contraindication to further doses of that vaccine.

items.stem: A parent tells the nurse they gave their 4-year-old, who has influenza, a "baby aspirin" for fever. Which teaching point is the priority?
options: "Aspirin is fine as long as you give it with food to protect the stomach."
"Aspirin should not be given to children with viral illnesses because it is linked to Reye syndrome, a serious brain and liver disorder."
"Low-dose aspirin is safe in children, but adult-strength tablets are not."
"You may alternate aspirin with ibuprofen every 3 hours to keep the fever down."
items.rationale: Salicylate use during influenza or varicella is associated with Reye syndrome, which causes acute encephalopathy and fatty liver failure; acetaminophen or ibuprofen (for children older than 6 months) are the appropriate antipyretics. Giving aspirin with food, using a smaller dose, or alternating it with another drug does not remove the risk, and the parent should watch for persistent vomiting, lethargy, or confusion.

items.stem: A nurse teaches the parent of a 2-year-old how to manage a fever of 39 C (102.2 F) at home. Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Dress the child lightly and keep the room comfortably cool
Sponge the child with cold water and rubbing alcohol to bring the fever down quickly
Offer fluids frequently to prevent dehydration
Dose acetaminophen or ibuprofen by the child's weight, not age
Bundle the child in blankets to "sweat out" the fever
Call the provider if the child becomes hard to wake, has a stiff neck, or develops a rash that does not blanch
items.rationale: Fever is managed for comfort with light clothing, extra fluids, and weight-based doses of acetaminophen or ibuprofen, and parents need to know the warning signs of serious infection. Cold water and alcohol sponging cause shivering, which raises core temperature, and alcohol can be absorbed through the skin and inhaled; if sponging is used at all it should be with tepid water after an antipyretic. Bundling traps heat and can push the temperature higher.

items.stem: A nurse in the emergency department assesses four children with vomiting and diarrhea. Which child should the nurse evaluate first?
options: A 2-year-old who is fussy, has slightly dry lips, and drank 4 ounces of oral rehydration solution in the past hour
A 5-year-old who vomited twice this morning and has a moist mouth and normal skin turgor
An 8-month-old who is limp, has a capillary refill of 4 seconds, and has had no wet diaper in 10 hours
A 10-year-old who reports thirst and has had three loose stools today
items.rationale: Lethargy, prolonged capillary refill, and markedly decreased urine output indicate severe dehydration with early hypovolemic shock, which requires immediate isotonic fluid boluses. The toddler with mild signs who is tolerating oral rehydration, the well-hydrated 5-year-old, and the thirsty but otherwise stable school-age child can be managed with oral rehydration and are lower priority.

items.stem: A nurse coaches a parent whose 18-month-old has mild dehydration from gastroenteritis and is vomiting intermittently. Place the parent's actions in the correct order.
options: Gradually increase the volume of solution as the child keeps it down
Offer 1 to 2 teaspoons (5 to 10 mL) of oral rehydration solution every 2 to 3 minutes with a spoon or syringe
Resume the child's usual age-appropriate diet once rehydrated
If the child vomits, wait about 10 minutes and then restart with small amounts
Confirm signs of mild dehydration such as fewer wet diapers, dry mouth, and lack of tears
items.rationale: The parent first confirms mild dehydration, then begins oral rehydration in very small, frequent amounts, which are absorbed even when the child is vomiting; a brief pause after emesis and then restarting keeps the parent from abandoning oral therapy. Volumes are increased as tolerated, and once the child is rehydrated, usually within 4 hours, a normal diet is resumed because early feeding shortens the illness. Rehydration solution replaces juice and sports drinks, whose sugar load worsens diarrhea.

items.stem: A 7-year-old with epilepsy begins having a generalized tonic-clonic seizure while sitting in a chair in the playroom. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
options: Ease the child to the floor and place something soft under the head
Insert a padded tongue blade between the teeth to protect the tongue
Turn the child onto the side once the jerking movements allow
Restrain the arms and legs to prevent injury
Note the time the seizure started and observe the movements
Move furniture and toys away from the child
items.rationale: During a seizure the nurse protects the child from injury by lowering them to the floor, cushioning the head, clearing the area, and positioning them on the side so secretions drain, while timing and observing the event for the provider. Nothing is ever placed in the mouth because it can break teeth or obstruct the airway, and restraining the limbs can cause fractures or muscle injury.

items.stem: A school nurse responds to a 10-year-old with a known seizure disorder who is having a generalized tonic-clonic seizure in the hallway. The child's seizure action plan includes intranasal midazolam for seizures lasting longer than 5 minutes. Place the nurse's actions in order.
options: Give the intranasal midazolam when the seizure reaches 5 minutes, as the plan directs
Turn the child onto the side and check breathing as the jerking subsides
Note the time, move objects away, and cushion the child's head
Document the event and notify the parents and provider
Stay with the child, reorient them as they wake, and allow them to rest
items.rationale: Immediate care is protecting the child and timing the event; when the seizure passes the 5-minute threshold, the rescue benzodiazepine is given per the action plan because prolonged seizures can become status epilepticus. As movements stop, the side-lying position protects the airway, and the nurse remains with the drowsy, confused child through the postictal period. Documentation and notification follow once the child is safe; emergency services are called if the seizure does not respond to the rescue medication.

items.stem: A 12-year-old has a vagus nerve stimulator implanted for seizures that have not responded to medication. Which statement by the child's parent indicates correct understanding of the device?
options: "If I see a seizure starting, I can pass the magnet over the device to trigger an extra stimulation."
"The stimulator replaces the seizure medication, so we can stop the daily doses."
"My child should avoid all physical activity now that the device is in place."
"The device will keep my child from ever having another seizure."
items.rationale: The vagus nerve stimulator delivers programmed intermittent stimulation, and swiping the supplied magnet over the generator during an aura or at seizure onset delivers an on-demand pulse that may shorten or abort the seizure. It is an add-on therapy, so antiepileptic drugs continue, it reduces seizure frequency rather than eliminating seizures, and normal activity with the usual seizure precautions is encouraged. Hoarseness or throat tingling during stimulation is a common side effect.

items.stem: A 6-year-old with intractable epilepsy is started on a ketogenic diet. Which instruction should the nurse give the parents?
options: "Offer plenty of fruit and whole grains to keep the diet balanced."
"You can loosen the diet on weekends as long as it is followed on school days."
"Stop the diet immediately if your child's urine tests positive for ketones."
"Check labels on liquid medicines, vitamins, and toothpaste for hidden sugars, which can break ketosis and trigger seizures."
items.rationale: The ketogenic diet is a strictly measured high-fat, very-low-carbohydrate regimen that forces the body to burn ketones, which reduces seizures in many children; even small amounts of carbohydrate in liquid medications, chewable vitamins, or flavored toothpaste can interrupt ketosis. Fruits and grains are carbohydrate sources that are tightly limited, the diet cannot be relaxed on weekends, and urinary ketones are the expected sign that the diet is working. A dietitian supervises the diet and prescribes vitamin and mineral supplements.

items.stem: A nurse assesses a 5-month-old brought to the emergency department for fever and irritability. Which findings suggest bacterial meningitis in this infant? Select all that apply.
options: A tense, bulging anterior fontanelle while the infant is calm and upright
A high-pitched cry that worsens when the infant is picked up
Nuchal rigidity with a positive Kernig sign
Poor feeding with vomiting
A sunken fontanelle with decreased skin turgor
Purple, nonblanching spots spreading on the trunk and legs
items.rationale: In infants, meningitis produces nonspecific signs: a bulging fontanelle from raised intracranial pressure, a high-pitched cry with paradoxical irritability (crying more when held), poor feeding, vomiting, and lethargy; a petechial or purpuric rash suggests meningococcal disease and is an emergency. Nuchal rigidity and the Kernig and Brudzinski signs are unreliable before 12 to 18 months because of the immature nervous system, and a sunken fontanelle points to dehydration rather than meningitis.

items.stem: A 3-year-old is admitted with suspected meningococcal meningitis. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Obtain a detailed immunization history from the parents
Place the child in droplet precautions in a private room
Arrange prophylactic antibiotics for the child's daycare classmates
Dim the lights and provide a quiet environment
items.rationale: Meningococcal disease spreads through respiratory droplets, so isolating the child in a private room under droplet precautions is the first action, maintained until the child has received 24 hours of effective antibiotics, which are started as soon as cultures are drawn. Close contacts, including household members and daycare contacts, receive prophylaxis such as rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone, and reducing light and noise helps with photophobia, but neither precedes protecting others from exposure.

items.stem: A 4-month-old had a ventriculoperitoneal shunt placed 6 weeks ago for hydrocephalus. Which finding reported by the parent most strongly suggests shunt malfunction?
options: The infant sleeps for 4-hour stretches at night
A slight bump can be felt over the shunt valve behind the ear
The head circumference has increased rapidly and the soft spot feels full and tense
The infant spits up a small amount after some feedings
items.rationale: In an infant whose sutures are still open, shunt failure lets cerebrospinal fluid reaccumulate, producing a rapidly enlarging head, a bulging fontanelle, dilated scalp veins, vomiting, irritability or lethargy, and downward deviation of the eyes ("sunsetting"); the provider must be notified immediately. Sleeping through the night, a palpable valve, and small spit-ups are normal. In older children with fused sutures, malfunction presents instead with headache, vomiting, and behavior change.

items.stem: A 9-year-old whose ventriculoperitoneal shunt was revised 3 weeks ago is admitted with a 2-day history of headache, vomiting, a temperature of 39.2 C (102.6 F), and redness along the shunt tubing on the neck. Which conclusion should the nurse draw?
options: The findings suggest shunt infection, which is most common in the first months after placement or revision
The findings are consistent with a viral illness unrelated to the shunt
The findings indicate the child has outgrown the shunt and needs routine lengthening
The findings represent normal postoperative healing
items.rationale: Fever with redness or tenderness along the shunt tract, combined with signs of increased intracranial pressure such as headache and vomiting, points to shunt infection, which usually appears within the first 1 to 2 months after surgery and often requires shunt removal, external drainage, and IV antibiotics. In a school-age child with closed sutures, headache, vomiting, sleepiness, and declining school performance are the signs of malfunction. A viral illness would not explain erythema along the tubing, and neither outgrowing the shunt nor normal healing causes fever and tract inflammation.

items.stem: A newborn with a myelomeningocele is awaiting surgical closure. Which interventions should the nurse include in preoperative care? Select all that apply.
options: Keep the infant prone with the hips slightly flexed
Cover the sac with a sterile dressing moistened with normal saline and change it as prescribed
Diaper the infant snugly to keep the area clean
Measure the head circumference daily and assess the fontanelles
Use latex-free gloves and supplies for all care
Hold the infant supine in the caregiver's arms during feedings
items.rationale: Before closure, the exposed neural sac is protected from rupture, drying, and contamination by keeping the infant prone, which also keeps stool away from the lesion, and by covering it with a moist sterile saline dressing; head circumference is monitored because hydrocephalus often develops, and latex-free care starts at birth because these children have a very high rate of latex allergy. A diaper presses on and contaminates the sac, and holding the infant supine risks pressure and rupture; feedings are given with the infant prone or side-lying with the head turned.

items.stem: A 7-year-old with spina bifida who performs clean intermittent catheterization is scheduled for orthopedic surgery. Which intervention is most important for the nurse to include in the plan?
options: Restrict the child's fluids for 24 hours before the procedure
Apply a warm blanket to the lower extremities to promote sensation
Encourage a high-protein meal the night before surgery
Ensure that all equipment used, including catheters and gloves, is latex free
items.rationale: Children with spina bifida have repeated mucosal exposure to latex through catheterizations and surgeries, and a large proportion develop latex sensitivity that can cause anaphylaxis; latex-free supplies, an allergy alert, and awareness of cross-reacting foods such as bananas, kiwi, and avocado are essential. A 24-hour fluid restriction would harm a child who catheterizes, heat applied to insensate limbs risks burns, and diet does not address the primary safety concern.

items.stem: A 3-year-old with spastic cerebral palsy is admitted for a scheduled procedure. Which nursing action best supports this child during hospitalization?
options: Feed the child in a supine position to reduce the risk of choking
Ask the parents about the child's routines, communication cues, and positioning devices, and build them into care
Limit visits from the therapy team so the child can rest
Postpone play activities because the child cannot participate at an age-appropriate level
items.rationale: Parents are the experts on a child with cerebral palsy; using the child's home routines, adaptive equipment, and preferred ways of communicating reduces stress and maintains function, and the interdisciplinary therapy team continues during the stay. Children with spastic cerebral palsy are fed upright with the head in midline and the jaw supported to prevent aspiration, and play is adapted to the child's abilities rather than withheld.

items.stem: A nurse observes a 4-year-old boy rise from the floor by first turning onto his hands and knees, then pushing his hands against his shins and thighs to "walk" up his legs to a standing position. Which condition does this finding suggest?
options: Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Developmental dysplasia of the hip
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis
Cerebral palsy
items.rationale: The Gower sign, using the hands to climb up the legs when rising from the floor, reflects proximal weakness of the pelvic girdle and is a classic early sign of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, along with a waddling gait, frequent falls, and enlarged calves from fatty infiltration. Hip dysplasia causes limping and leg-length inequality, juvenile arthritis causes joint swelling and morning stiffness, and cerebral palsy causes spasticity or abnormal tone rather than progressive weakness.

items.stem: A nurse assesses a 3-month-old during a well-child visit. Which finding should prompt evaluation for developmental dysplasia of the hip?
options: Feet that turn inward when the infant is held upright
Bowed legs when the infant's legs are extended
Asymmetric thigh and gluteal skin folds with limited abduction of one hip
A soft click when the knees are flexed
items.rationale: Uneven thigh and gluteal folds, restricted hip abduction, and apparent shortening of the femur on the affected side (Galeazzi sign) are classic findings of hip dysplasia; the Ortolani and Barlow maneuvers are most useful in the first 2 to 3 months, before the hip becomes fixed. Mild in-toeing and physiologic bowing are normal in infants, and benign knee clicks are common and unrelated to the hip.

items.stem: A nurse teaches parents how to care for their 6-week-old who was just fitted with a Pavlik harness for developmental dysplasia of the hip. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Keep the harness on continuously, giving sponge baths, unless the provider allows removal
Adjust the straps at home whenever the infant seems uncomfortable
Place a cotton undershirt and knee socks under the straps to protect the skin
Check the skin under the straps several times a day for redness or breakdown
Use a diaper that fits under the straps and change it without removing the harness
Apply lotions and powders under the straps to keep the skin soft
items.rationale: The Pavlik harness holds the hips flexed and abducted so the femoral head can seat in the acetabulum, and it is generally worn 23 to 24 hours a day for several weeks; only the provider adjusts the straps as the infant grows. A shirt and socks under the straps, frequent skin checks, and diapering beneath the harness prevent skin breakdown, while lotions and powders trap moisture and cause irritation.

items.stem: A 2-week-old is beginning serial casting (Ponseti method) for bilateral clubfoot. Which statement by the parent indicates that teaching has been effective?
options: "The casts will stay on for 3 months, and then the feet will be fixed."
"The casts are only needed if our baby starts walking with a limp."
"We should check the toes once a day for warmth and color."
"We will return each week to have the casts changed as the feet are gradually corrected."
items.rationale: The Ponseti method involves gentle manipulation and a new long-leg cast about every week for 5 to 8 weeks, often followed by a heel-cord release and a brace worn for months to years to prevent recurrence. Treatment begins in the newborn period when tissues are most pliable, not after walking begins, and parents check the toes at every diaper change for swelling, coolness, dusky color, or reduced movement, which signal a cast that is too tight.

items.stem: A 13-year-old girl with idiopathic scoliosis and a 30-degree curve is prescribed a thoracolumbosacral orthosis (TLSO). Which statement by the adolescent indicates correct understanding of the treatment?
options: "The brace will straighten my spine completely if I wear it while I sleep."
"I need to wear the brace about 18 to 23 hours a day and take it off only for bathing and swimming."
"I only need to wear the brace when my back hurts."
"I can stop wearing the brace once I turn 14."
items.rationale: Bracing does not correct an existing curve; it slows or halts progression while the skeleton is still growing, and its effectiveness depends directly on hours worn, so the brace is worn nearly full time and removed only briefly for hygiene and swimming. Pain is not the trigger for wearing it, and bracing continues until skeletal maturity is documented on radiographs, not until a birthday. The nurse assesses the skin under the brace, suggests a thin cotton shirt underneath, and addresses body image and peer concerns.

items.stem: A 5-year-old falls from a climbing structure, and a radiograph shows a fracture that bends and cracks one side of the radius without breaking through the bone. The parent asks why this type of fracture happens in children. Which explanation is accurate?
options: "Children's bones are more flexible and have a thicker outer covering, so they often bend and splinter rather than snap."
"Children's bones are more brittle than adults' bones, so they break more easily."
"This fracture means your child probably has a bone disease that weakens the bones."
"The break happened because the bone was already fractured before the fall."
items.rationale: A greenstick fracture is unique to children because their bones are more porous and pliable and have a thick periosteum, allowing one cortex to bend while the other breaks. Pediatric bones heal faster than adult bones, but injuries through the growth (epiphyseal) plate need careful follow-up because they can disturb future bone growth. A single greenstick fracture after a fall does not indicate bone disease or a prior fracture.

items.stem: A school nurse performs scoliosis screening on a 12-year-old. Place the steps in the order the nurse should perform them.
options: Ask the child to bend forward at the waist with knees straight and arms hanging loosely toward the floor
Have the child stand straight with the shirt removed, feet together, and arms at the sides
Refer the child to the provider for radiographic evaluation if asymmetry is found
Look along the back for a rib hump or lumbar prominence on one side
Observe from behind for uneven shoulder height, scapular prominence, or asymmetric waist creases
items.rationale: Screening starts with a standing inspection for shoulder, scapula, and hip asymmetry, then the Adams forward bend test, in which a rib hump on one side indicates vertebral rotation, the most sensitive sign of a structural curve; visible asymmetry or a scoliometer reading of 7 degrees or more warrants referral for a standing radiograph. Screening is done during the early adolescent growth spurt, when curves are most likely to progress.

items.stem: A 5-month-old is brought to the emergency department by a caregiver who reports the infant "rolled off the couch." Radiographs show a spiral fracture of the femur. Which action by the nurse is the priority?
options: Reassure the caregiver that this injury is common in infants who are learning to roll
Provide home safety teaching and discharge the infant after casting
Follow the facility's protocol for suspected child abuse, including a skeletal survey and a report to child protective services
Confront the caregiver with the discrepancy between the story and the injury
items.rationale: A spiral femur fracture in an infant who cannot yet walk requires a twisting force that a short fall onto a couch does not produce, and a history that does not fit the injury or the child's developmental ability is a red flag for inflicted trauma. The nurse is a mandated reporter and ensures the child's safety with a skeletal survey to find fractures of different ages, careful documentation, and a report; the infant is not discharged to the same environment until the situation is evaluated. Reassurance and safety teaching ignore the risk, and confrontation can escalate the situation and compromise the investigation.

items.stem: A 6-year-old is admitted with a 3-day history of fever, refusal to bear weight on the right leg, and localized tenderness and warmth over the distal femur after a puncture wound to the thigh the previous week. Which nursing action is most important during the first day of treatment?
options: Encourage passive range of motion of the affected leg every 2 hours
Administer analgesics only when the child rates the pain as severe
Restrict fluids to prevent swelling at the infection site
Obtain blood cultures before starting the prescribed IV antibiotics
items.rationale: Acute osteomyelitis in children usually spreads through the blood or follows a wound and is most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus; identifying the organism from blood cultures or bone aspirate before the first antibiotic dose guides the prolonged IV-to-oral course that lasts several weeks. The limb is rested and immobilized during the acute phase because movement increases pain and can spread infection, pain is managed on a schedule rather than only when severe, and fluids and nutrition are increased to support healing.

items.stem: A 9-year-old with juvenile idiopathic arthritis reports that her knees and wrists are stiff and sore for about an hour each morning. Which suggestion by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: "Stay in bed until the stiffness goes away, and skip physical education class."
"Take a warm bath or shower on waking and do gentle range-of-motion exercises before school."
"Apply ice packs to the joints for 20 minutes before getting up."
"Wear splints on the wrists and knees all day to keep the joints from moving."
items.rationale: Morning stiffness is characteristic of juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and warmth followed by gentle movement loosens the joints, preserves range of motion, and lets the child take part in school and appropriate physical activity, which maintains muscle strength and prevents contractures. Prolonged rest worsens stiffness and function, cold is more useful for acutely swollen joints than for morning stiffness, and splints are worn at night or during rest rather than to immobilize joints all day. Scheduled NSAIDs, often given with breakfast, also reduce morning symptoms.

items.stem: A nurse helps a parent choose toys for a 2-year-old and a 7-year-old who share a playroom. Which teaching point is most important?
options: "Any toy or toy part that fits through a toilet-paper tube is a choking hazard for the 2-year-old and must be kept out of reach."
"Toys labeled for ages 3 and up are fine for the 2-year-old as long as an adult is nearby."
"Balloons are a safe alternative to small toys for the toddler."
"The 7-year-old's building sets with small pieces can be stored on the floor for easy access."
items.rationale: Children younger than 3 explore by mouthing objects and have narrow airways, so small parts, marbles, button batteries, magnets, and pieces that fit through a 1.25-inch cylinder are choking hazards, and the older sibling's small-piece toys must be stored where the toddler cannot reach them. Age labels reflect safety testing rather than intelligence, and latex balloons are a leading cause of toy-related choking deaths.

items.stem: A nurse is feeding a 7-month-old in the hospital when the infant suddenly cannot cough, cry, or breathe after a piece of cracker enters the mouth. Place the nurse's actions in the correct order.
options: Turn the infant face up on the forearm with the head lower than the trunk
Deliver up to 5 back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of the hand
Lay the infant face down along the forearm, supporting the jaw, with the head lower than the chest
Give up to 5 chest thrusts with two fingers on the lower half of the breastbone
Repeat the cycle until the object is expelled or the infant becomes unresponsive, then begin CPR
items.rationale: For a conscious choking infant who cannot make sounds, the rescuer alternates 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts while keeping the head lower than the body so gravity assists expulsion; abdominal thrusts are not used in infants because of the risk of liver injury. The cycle continues until the airway clears or the infant loses consciousness, at which point CPR begins and the mouth is checked for a visible object before each set of breaths. Blind finger sweeps are never performed.

items.stem: A nurse presents a drowning-prevention program to parents of toddlers. Which points should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Empty buckets, wading pools, and bathtubs immediately after use
Install a four-sided fence with a self-latching gate that completely separates the pool from the house
Inflatable arm floats can substitute for adult supervision in shallow water
Stay within arm's reach of a toddler during baths and around any water
A toddler who has completed swimming lessons no longer needs constant supervision
items.rationale: Toddlers can drown silently in only a few inches of water, so emptying containers, isolation fencing around pools, and touch supervision are the key measures, along with caregiver CPR training. Air-filled floats are toys that give a false sense of security, and swimming lessons reduce but never eliminate risk, so constant close supervision is still required.

items.stem: A 2-year-old is brought to the clinic with burns on both feet and lower legs that end in a sharp, even line just above the ankles, with no splash marks. The caregiver states the child "stepped into the tub before I checked the water." Which interpretation should guide the nurse's actions?
options: The burn pattern is consistent with the history and requires only wound care and bathing safety teaching
The burns indicate a sunburn that occurred while the child was outdoors barefoot
The symmetric, sharply demarcated pattern suggests forced immersion and must be reported as suspected abuse
The pattern is typical of a child who pulled a pot of hot liquid from the stove
items.rationale: Immersion burns have a "stocking" or "glove" distribution with clear, uniform lines and no splash marks because the limb was held still in hot water; a child who steps into hot water accidentally jerks the foot out, producing irregular, asymmetric burns with splash marks. Spill or pull-down burns form an arrow-shaped pattern that is deepest at the top and tapers downward, and sunburn does not produce a sharp horizontal line. Suspicious burns are reported and the child is protected while wound care is provided.

items.stem: A nurse teaches a group of parents about bicycle safety for school-age children. Which statement by a parent indicates correct understanding?
options: "A helmet is only needed when my child rides on busy streets."
"Once a helmet has been in a crash, it is fine to keep using it if the shell looks intact."
"My child can wear the helmet tilted back so the forehead is uncovered and it feels less hot."
"The helmet should sit level on the head and cover the forehead, with the straps snug enough that it does not move."
items.rationale: A properly fitted helmet greatly reduces the risk of serious head injury and should sit level, about two finger widths above the eyebrows, with the side straps forming a V under the ears and the chin strap allowing no more than one finger width of slack. Helmets are needed on every ride because most crashes happen close to home, the foam liner is damaged in a crash even when the shell looks fine so the helmet must be replaced, and a tilted helmet leaves the forehead unprotected. Parents should model helmet use themselves.

items.stem: A 16-year-old being interviewed alone tells the nurse, "I'll tell you what is going on, but you can't tell my parents." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: "I promise that nothing you tell me will ever be shared with anyone."
"What you share stays between us unless I learn that you or someone else is in danger of serious harm; then I would need to involve others to keep you safe."
"I cannot keep anything from your parents because you are a minor."
"Let's wait and talk about this when your parents are back in the room."
items.rationale: Adolescents are more likely to disclose risky behavior and seek care when confidentiality is assured, and in most jurisdictions minors can confidentially access care for sexual health, substance use, and mental health concerns. Confidentiality has limits, however: suicidal or homicidal intent, abuse, or another serious threat to safety must be acted on, so the nurse explains those limits up front instead of promising absolute secrecy. Refusing confidentiality or deferring to the parents shuts down the conversation.

items.stem: A 20-month-old was admitted 2 days ago. Each time the parent leaves the room, the toddler screams, clings to the crib rails, and cannot be comforted by staff. The parent asks whether they should sneak out while the child is distracted. Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "This protest is a normal reaction to separation at this age. Tell your child you are leaving and when you will return, and leave a familiar object with them."
"Slipping out quietly while your child is playing is the kindest approach."
"The crying means your child is not adjusting; we may need to sedate them."
"Your child will settle faster if you limit your visits to once a day."
items.rationale: Toddlers experience separation anxiety intensely, and the protest phase of crying, clinging, and rejecting strangers is expected; if separation continues it can progress to despair (withdrawal) and then detachment, which is easily mistaken for adjustment. Parents should say goodbye honestly and leave a transitional object, because sneaking out destroys trust and heightens anxiety. Sedation is not a treatment for normal protest, and rooming-in or frequent visits are encouraged rather than restricted.

items.stem: A 4-year-old scheduled for a tonsillectomy tells the nurse, "I have to get my throat cut because I yelled at my sister." Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: "That is not why you are here. Let's talk about something else."
"Sometimes bad things happen when we yell at people, but you will be fine."
"Having surgery is not a punishment. Your tonsils are sick, and the doctor is going to fix them so your throat feels better."
"Ask your parents to explain why you need surgery."
items.rationale: Preschoolers think magically and egocentrically, so they often believe illness or procedures are punishment for misbehavior; the nurse corrects this directly in simple, concrete words and replaces threatening terms such as "cut" with neutral language. Dismissing the concern leaves the guilt in place, agreeing that bad things follow yelling reinforces the misconception, and deferring to the parents misses the moment. Preschoolers are prepared shortly before a procedure with play and are told what they will see, hear, and feel.

items.stem: A 15-year-old hospitalized for 3 weeks after a motor vehicle crash has a large facial scar and an external fixator on one leg. The adolescent refuses visitors, keeps the lights off, and says, "Everyone at school is going to stare at me." Which nursing intervention is most appropriate?
options: Tell the adolescent that appearance is not important compared with being alive
Ask the parents to stay at the bedside continuously to keep the adolescent company
Restrict phone use so the adolescent can focus on physical recovery
Acknowledge the concern, encourage contact with close friends by phone or video, and involve the adolescent in decisions about care and appearance
items.rationale: Adolescents are forming their identity and rely heavily on peer acceptance, so changes in appearance and separation from friends are the greatest stressors of hospitalization; validating feelings, maintaining peer connections, offering choices, and promoting independence support coping. Minimizing the concern is dismissive, constant parental presence does not replace peers and may feel intrusive to a teen seeking autonomy, and removing the phone cuts off the peer support the adolescent needs most.

items.stem: A nurse prepares a 7-year-old for a lumbar puncture scheduled later that day. Which approach is most appropriate for this age?
options: Wait until the child is in the treatment room so there is less time to worry
Use a doll and the actual equipment to show what will happen, explain what the child will feel, and let the child ask questions and practice the curled position
Tell the child that the procedure will not hurt so the child stays calm
Give a detailed explanation of spinal anatomy and the medical reasons for the test
items.rationale: School-age children think concretely, want to know how and why, and cope better when given honest information ahead of time with a demonstration on a doll and a chance to handle equipment, rehearse, and ask questions; this therapeutic play lowers anxiety and increases cooperation. Preparing only at the last moment removes the chance to build coping skills, false promises of no pain destroy trust, and abstract anatomy lectures are beyond a 7-year-old's understanding.

items.stem: A client on an inpatient unit says, "I just found out my wife filed for divorce. I have no idea what to do now." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?
options: "Why do you think she decided to file for divorce?"
"This sounds overwhelming. Tell me more about what you are going through."
"Try not to worry — these things usually work out for the best."
"If I were you, I would focus on your health before dealing with that."
items.rationale: Reflecting the client's feelings and inviting elaboration keeps the focus on the client and encourages expression. "Why" questions put clients on the defensive, false reassurance dismisses real concerns, and giving advice blocks the client's own problem-solving.

items.stem: A preceptor observes a new nurse talking with an anxious preoperative client. Which statement by the new nurse should the preceptor identify as nontherapeutic?
options: "You seem more tense than you were this morning."
"Don't worry — the surgeons here are excellent, and everything will be fine."
"Tell me what concerns you most about the surgery."
"It sounds like you are saying the anesthesia frightens you."
items.rationale: Telling the client not to worry is false reassurance: it minimizes the client's feelings and cuts off further discussion, and the nurse cannot guarantee the outcome. Making observations, asking open-ended questions, and restating are all therapeutic techniques that encourage the client to keep talking.

items.stem: A client with major depression tells the nurse, "Sometimes I feel like it would be easier if I just weren't here anymore." What is the nurse's best response?
options: "You have so many reasons to keep living."
"Are you thinking about killing yourself?"
"Let's talk about something more pleasant to take your mind off it."
"Everyone feels discouraged now and then."
items.rationale: A statement like this requires a direct, matter-of-fact question about suicidal ideation so the nurse can assess intent, plan, and means. Asking directly does not plant the idea; it communicates that the topic is safe to discuss. The other responses minimize or change the subject and shut down a critical safety assessment.

items.stem: A client hospitalized after a suicide attempt has been withdrawn and tearful for a week. This morning the client is smiling, gives a treasured watch to a roommate, and tells the nurse, "I've finally figured out how to fix everything." How should the nurse interpret this behavior?
options: The antidepressant has reached a therapeutic level.
The client may have decided on a plan to complete suicide.
The client is ready for less frequent observation.
The client has developed effective coping skills and the crisis has passed.
items.rationale: A sudden lift in mood, giving away valued possessions, and statements about having "a solution" are classic warnings that a client has decided on suicide and now feels at peace with the plan. Returning energy early in treatment can also give a depressed client the ability to act. Observation should be increased, not relaxed.

items.stem: A client admitted after a suicide attempt is placed on suicide precautions. Which actions should the nurse implement? Select all that apply.
options: Remove belts, shoelaces, razors, and glass items from the client's belongings.
Check the client's mouth to confirm each oral medication dose is swallowed.
Assign the client to a private room at the far end of the hallway.
Observe the client at the ordered frequency, such as one-to-one or every 15 minutes.
Avoid mentioning suicide so the client does not get new ideas.
Provide plastic utensils and count them when meal trays are collected.
items.rationale: Restricting access to means (sharps, cords, glass, hoarded pills, utensils) and maintaining close, ordered observation are core suicide precautions, and mouth checks prevent cheeking medications for a later overdose. The client should be placed near the nurses' station where staff can see them, not isolated in a distant private room, and suicide should be discussed openly because direct assessment does not increase risk.

items.stem: A client with major depressive disorder sits alone, answers in short phrases, and has very little energy. Which nursing approach is most appropriate?
options: Encourage the client to join a large group activity to lift their mood.
Sit with the client for short, regularly scheduled periods, even in silence.
Cheerfully remind the client of all the positive things in their life.
Wait for the client to initiate interaction so their independence is respected.
items.rationale: Brief, consistent, scheduled contacts — including silent presence — communicate that the client has worth without demanding energy the client does not have. Severely depressed clients rarely initiate contact, large groups are overwhelming, and forced cheerfulness minimizes the client's feelings and can deepen guilt.

items.stem: A client experiencing acute mania paces the unit almost constantly and has lost 4 lb in three days. Which intervention best meets this client's nutritional needs?
options: Serve meals in the dining room so the client can socialize while eating.
Provide high-calorie, high-protein finger foods and drinks the client can carry while moving.
Teach the client the components of a balanced diet.
Require the client to remain seated at the table until the tray is finished.
items.rationale: Clients in acute mania are too hyperactive and distractible to sit for meals, so portable, calorie-dense foods and fluids they can consume while pacing best protect nutrition and hydration. Teaching cannot be absorbed during mania, forced sitting invites a power struggle, and a stimulating dining room increases distraction.

items.stem: During a community meeting, a client in the manic phase of bipolar disorder repeatedly interrupts, tells crude jokes, and grabs another client's snack. What is the nurse's best action?
options: Ask the group to decide on consequences for the client's behavior.
Calmly and firmly redirect the client out of the meeting to a quieter, low-stimulation activity.
Ignore the behavior so that it is not reinforced by attention.
Tell the client the behavior is childish and must stop immediately.
items.rationale: Manic clients cannot filter stimulation, so removing the client to a calmer setting with matter-of-fact, consistent limits protects the client's dignity and the rights of others. Group-imposed consequences and belittling comments are punitive and can escalate agitation, and ignoring intrusive behavior allows it to continue and disrupt the milieu.

items.stem: A client with schizophrenia tilts an ear toward the empty corner of the room and tells the nurse, "The voices are saying terrible things about me again." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "The voices aren't real, so do your best to ignore them."
"I don't hear any voices, but I can see that they seem very real and frightening to you."
"Let's figure out why the voices only bother you in this room."
"I'll ask the provider to increase your medication right away."
items.rationale: The nurse presents their own reality without arguing while validating that the experience feels real and distressing to the client — this builds trust and keeps communication open. Telling the client to ignore the voices dismisses the experience, "why" questions are nontherapeutic, and jumping to a medication change avoids the client's immediate feelings.

items.stem: A client with a persecutory delusion refuses lunch, stating, "The kitchen staff put poison in my food." Which nursing response is most appropriate?
options: "That can't be true — the kitchen staff have no reason to hurt you."
"You feel unsafe right now. I'll stay with you, and you may have food in unopened containers."
"If the food were poisoned, the other clients would already be sick."
"Tell me exactly how you think the poison was put into the food."
items.rationale: Arguing with or logically disproving a delusion only entrenches it and damages trust; the nurse instead acknowledges the underlying feeling of fear and offers a practical option — sealed, unopened food — that maintains nutrition. Asking the client to elaborate on the delusion focuses attention on the false belief and reinforces it.

items.stem: A client suddenly develops palpitations, trembling, shortness of breath, and a feeling of impending doom, crying, "Something terrible is happening to me!" Physical causes have been ruled out. What should the nurse do first?
options: Stay with the client and speak in short, simple, calm sentences.
Teach the client about the physiology of panic attacks.
Leave the client alone in a quiet room to reduce stimulation.
Ask the client to describe what triggered the attack.
items.rationale: A client in panic cannot be left alone — the nurse's calm presence and brief, concrete directions provide safety and help the anxiety subside. Perception is so narrowed during panic that teaching and exploring triggers are impossible; those interventions come later, once anxiety has decreased to a mild or moderate level.

items.stem: During discharge teaching, a client begins pacing and speaking rapidly, says, "I can only focus on one thing at a time," and cannot complete a simple menu form. The nurse should identify these findings as which level of anxiety?
options: Mild
Moderate
Severe
Panic
items.rationale: Severe anxiety greatly narrows the perceptual field: the client fixates on a single detail, cannot solve problems or learn, and shows marked physical agitation. Mild anxiety actually sharpens learning, moderate anxiety narrows focus but responds to redirection, and panic involves complete loss of rational thought with dread or immobility.

items.stem: A veteran is being evaluated eight months after returning from a combat deployment. Which findings support a diagnosis of posttraumatic stress disorder? Select all that apply.
options: Recurrent nightmares that replay the traumatic event
Feeling detached and estranged from family and friends
Refusing to drive because roadside debris triggers intense fear
An exaggerated startle response to loud noises
A continuously elevated mood with a decreased need for sleep
Repeated handwashing to neutralize intrusive thoughts
items.rationale: PTSD is characterized by re-experiencing (nightmares, flashbacks), avoidance of trauma reminders, negative changes in mood such as detachment, and hyperarousal including an exaggerated startle response, persisting more than one month after the trauma. Elevated mood with little need for sleep suggests mania, and compulsive handwashing points to obsessive-compulsive disorder.

items.stem: A newly admitted client with obsessive-compulsive disorder washes their hands dozens of times a day, causing skin breakdown, and arrives late to meals because of the ritual. Which initial nursing approach is best?
options: Interrupt the handwashing each time it begins to break the habit.
Build time for the ritual into the daily schedule while meeting the client's basic needs.
Explain to the client that the handwashing is irrational and unnecessary.
Restrict the client's access to the sink during mealtimes.
items.rationale: Rituals bind anxiety, so abruptly blocking them — physically or by argument — drives anxiety toward panic. Initially the nurse allows scheduled time for the ritual, protects skin and nutrition, and only later works with the client to gradually limit the behavior as therapy and medication take effect. The client already knows the ritual is irrational, so pointing this out only increases shame.

items.stem: A client with anorexia nervosa is admitted to an eating disorder unit at 70% of ideal body weight. Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.
options: Remain with the client during meals and for one hour afterward.
Weigh the client at the same time each day, in a gown, after voiding.
Allow the client to choose which days they will be weighed.
Set a reasonable time limit for finishing each meal.
Discuss calorie counts and food choices in detail during meals.
Monitor serum electrolytes and cardiac rhythm.
items.rationale: Supervision during and after meals prevents food disposal and purging, consistent weighing conditions prevent manipulation of weights, meal time limits keep eating from becoming an all-day power struggle, and electrolyte and cardiac monitoring detects the life-threatening effects of starvation and refeeding. Letting the client control the weighing schedule invites avoidance, and dwelling on food and calories during meals reinforces the disorder's obsessional focus.

items.stem: The family of a 79-year-old client with mild Alzheimer disease reports that over the past two days the client has become suddenly much more confused, drowsy during the day, agitated at night, and is now picking at the bedcovers. The nurse should recognize these changes as most consistent with which condition?
options: The expected gradual progression of dementia
Delirium, requiring prompt evaluation for an underlying cause such as infection
Normal age-related cognitive decline
Depression presenting as pseudodementia
items.rationale: An acute onset over hours to days, a fluctuating level of consciousness, and disturbed sleep-wake cycles are the hallmarks of delirium, which is often reversible once the cause — commonly infection, medications, dehydration, or hypoxia — is treated. Dementia progresses gradually over months to years with a clear level of consciousness, so a sudden change in a client with dementia should never be dismissed as disease progression.

items.stem: A hospitalized client with alcohol use disorder had their last drink shortly before admission. Place the manifestations of alcohol withdrawal in the order they typically appear, from earliest to latest.
options: Delirium tremens with disorientation, fever, and severe autonomic instability
Tremors, anxiety, diaphoresis, and a rising pulse and blood pressure
Generalized tonic-clonic withdrawal seizures
Vivid visual or auditory hallucinations while otherwise oriented
items.rationale: Early withdrawal (roughly 6-12 hours after the last drink) produces tremors, anxiety, and autonomic arousal; alcoholic hallucinosis follows at about 12-24 hours; withdrawal seizures peak around 24-48 hours; and delirium tremens, the life-threatening stage, typically emerges at 48-72 hours. Serial scoring with a tool such as the CIWA scale guides symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing to prevent progression.

items.stem: A client is brought to the emergency department with a respiratory rate of 6/min, pinpoint pupils, and minimal response to painful stimuli. A friend reports the client uses heroin. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Support ventilation and administer naloxone as prescribed.
Administer clonidine, because these findings indicate opioid withdrawal.
Place the client in a quiet, dark room and reassess in 30 minutes.
Give the client's usual opioid dose to reverse the symptoms.
items.rationale: Respiratory depression, pinpoint pupils, and a decreased level of consciousness form the classic opioid overdose triad, and the priority is airway and ventilation support with the antagonist naloxone. Withdrawal looks opposite — dilated pupils, yawning, rhinorrhea, cramping, and agitation — and is miserable but rarely life-threatening. Waiting or giving more opioid would allow fatal respiratory arrest.

items.stem: A student receives a failing exam grade, comes home, and yells at a younger sibling over a trivial issue. Which defense mechanism is the student demonstrating?
options: Projection
Displacement
Regression
Sublimation
items.rationale: Displacement transfers feelings aroused by one person or situation onto a safer, less threatening target — here, anger about the grade is redirected at the sibling. Projection attributes one's own unacceptable feelings to someone else, regression is a retreat to behavior of an earlier developmental stage, and sublimation channels unacceptable impulses into socially acceptable activities.

items.stem: A nurse in an urgent care clinic assesses an adult who reports falling at home. Which findings should raise the nurse's suspicion of intimate partner violence? Select all that apply.
options: Bruises in various stages of healing on the trunk and upper arms
An explanation of the injury that does not match its pattern or severity
A partner who refuses to leave the room and answers every question for the client
A delay of several days between the injury and seeking care
A single abrasion on the knee consistent with the reported fall
The client making steady eye contact while describing the injury
items.rationale: Injuries in multiple healing stages or in protected areas, stories inconsistent with the injury, a controlling partner who prevents private conversation, and delayed care-seeking are classic red flags for abuse. The nurse should arrange to interview the client alone and help develop a safety plan. An isolated injury that matches the history and normal eye contact are not, by themselves, indicators of violence.

items.stem: A client admitted involuntarily to a psychiatric unit after threatening a family member calmly refuses the prescribed oral antipsychotic and is not threatening anyone. What is the nurse's best action?
options: Administer the medication by injection, because the admission is involuntary.
Honor and document the refusal, because the client retains the right to refuse treatment.
Tell the client that refusing will lengthen the commitment.
Mix the medication into the client's food without telling the client.
items.rationale: Involuntary admission restricts the right to leave, but the client remains legally competent and keeps civil rights, including the right to refuse medication, unless there is an immediate danger to self or others or a court has ordered treatment. Forcing an injection or hiding medication in food constitutes battery, and threatening a longer commitment is coercion.

items.stem: A client on a psychiatric unit is escalating — pacing, clenching fists, and shouting at staff. Place the nurse's interventions in order from least restrictive to most restrictive.
options: Offer a prescribed PRN calming medication.
Apply physical restraints with a provider's order.
Use a calm voice to verbally de-escalate and acknowledge the client's feelings.
Move the client to a quieter area with decreased stimulation.
Place the client in seclusion with a provider's order.
items.rationale: Law and standards require using the least restrictive intervention that keeps everyone safe: verbal de-escalation first, then reducing environmental stimulation, then offering PRN medication, with seclusion and finally physical restraint reserved for imminent danger after less restrictive measures fail. Behavioral restraint or seclusion requires a time-limited provider order (never PRN), a face-to-face evaluation within one hour, and continuous monitoring, and it must end as soon as the client regains control.

items.stem: A client with schizophrenia spends most of the day in bed, shows little facial expression, and has stopped bathing or starting conversations. Which nursing approach is most appropriate for these symptoms?
options: Establish a structured daily routine with simple, achievable expectations.
Wait until the client expresses interest before offering any activities.
Explain that other clients will avoid the client if hygiene does not improve.
Enroll the client in several stimulating group activities each day.
items.rationale: Avolition, flat affect, and social withdrawal are negative symptoms, and they respond best to structure, patience, and small realistic goals that build success without overwhelming the client. Waiting for initiative ignores the illness process, shaming the client is nontherapeutic, and a heavy activity schedule exceeds the client's current capacity.

items.stem: The nurse is planning care for a client with schizophrenia. Which manifestations should the nurse identify as positive symptoms? Select all that apply.
options: Hearing a voice that narrates the client's actions
A fixed belief that government agents have implanted a tracking device
Absence of facial expression when discussing emotional topics
Speech containing invented words that have meaning only to the speaker
Loss of motivation to bathe or dress
Inability to feel pleasure in previously enjoyed activities
items.rationale: Positive symptoms are additions to normal experience: hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized speech such as neologisms. Flat affect, avolition, and anhedonia are negative symptoms — losses of normal function that tend to respond less dramatically to antipsychotic medication.

items.stem: A client with schizophrenia is pacing, glancing toward the corner of the room, and whispering. The client tells the nurse, "The voices are back and they are very loud tonight." Which response is the priority?
options: Engage the client in a card game to provide distraction.
"What are the voices telling you to do?"
"The voices are a symptom of your illness and are not real."
Administer the next scheduled dose of the antipsychotic early.
items.rationale: The priority is to assess the content of the hallucinations, because command hallucinations may direct the client to harm self or others, and safety measures depend on knowing what the voices are saying. Distraction and reality-orientation may come later, and medications are not given early without an order or an assessment.

items.stem: A client with schizophrenia refuses lunch, stating, "The staff are putting poison in my food because they want me dead." Which response by the nurse is best?
options: "It must be frightening to believe you are in danger. You are safe here."
"Why would the staff want to poison you?"
"That cannot be true — the trays come sealed from the kitchen."
"I will taste your food first to prove that it is safe."
items.rationale: Acknowledging the feeling behind the delusion without arguing about its content builds trust and reduces fear. Logical arguments cannot dislodge a fixed false belief, "why" questions sound accusatory, and tasting the food validates and reinforces the delusion.

items.stem: During an assessment, a client with acute psychosis says, "I need to take the cake, rake the lake, shake and bake for goodness sake." The nurse should document this speech pattern as which finding?
options: Word salad
Neologisms
Clang associations
Echolalia
items.rationale: Clang associations are words linked by rhyme or similar sound rather than by meaning. Word salad is a jumble of unrelated words with no logical connection, neologisms are invented words meaningful only to the speaker, and echolalia is the repetition of words spoken by another person.

items.stem: A client with catatonia remains motionless for hours, allows limbs to be positioned by others, and has not eaten or had fluids since admission the previous day. Which nursing intervention is the priority?
options: Monitor intake closely and provide assistance with fluids and feeding.
Encourage the client to verbalize the reasons for refusing to move.
Leave the client undisturbed until spontaneous movement returns.
Place the client in a seclusion room to decrease environmental stimulation.
items.rationale: A client who is immobile and not eating or drinking is at immediate risk for dehydration and malnutrition, so meeting physiologic needs is the priority; immobility also demands range-of-motion exercises and repositioning to prevent complications. Clients with catatonia often remain aware of their surroundings, so care should be explained even when the client does not respond, and neither insight-oriented questioning nor seclusion addresses the physical risk.

items.stem: A client with schizophrenia who has stopped oral medication after every discharge is switched to a monthly long-acting injectable antipsychotic. Which statement by the client indicates understanding of the new regimen?
options: "Since the shot lasts a month, I will not need follow-up appointments anymore."
"I still need to return every four weeks to receive my injection."
"The injection will cure my schizophrenia if I get it long enough."
"I can get the shot only during months when I hear voices."
items.rationale: Depot antipsychotics improve adherence by replacing daily pills, but the benefit depends on returning at the scheduled interval for each injection and for ongoing monitoring. The medication controls symptoms rather than curing the illness, and it must be continued even when the client feels well.

items.stem: A client taking clozapine telephones the clinic reporting a fever of 101.2°F (38.4°C), a sore throat, and feeling "wiped out." Which instruction by the nurse is correct?
options: "Take acetaminophen and rest; call back if you are not better in three days."
"Come in today for blood work, and do not take another dose until the provider reviews the results."
"This is a common, harmless effect during the first months of treatment."
