WBC rise to 14,800/mm3 with 9% bands
items.rationale: Fever with tachycardia, oliguria, a climbing white count with bandemia, and a subtle change in mentation on postoperative day 2 together suggest a developing systemic infection and must be reported promptly. Well-controlled incisional pain and scant serosanguineous drainage from an approximated incision are expected findings at this stage of recovery.

items.stem: For each finding, specify whether it is consistent with an expected postoperative course or with a developing infection.
matrixRows: WBC increase from 11,200 to 14,800/mm3 with 9% bands
Serosanguineous drainage from an approximated incision
New warmth and spreading redness around the incision
Temperature 38.4 C with heart rate 102/min on day 2
Pain 4/10 relieved to 2/10 with scheduled analgesia
items.rationale: A rising leukocyte count with immature neutrophils (bands), periwound erythema and warmth, and fever with tachycardia on postoperative day 2 point toward infection rather than normal healing. Scant serosanguineous drainage and pain that responds to scheduled analgesia are anticipated after open abdominal surgery.

items.update: 0900: Lactate 2.2 mmol/L. Provider notified; blood cultures obtained from two sites as prescribed. Client now oriented to person only, with slowed speech. Family at bedside states, "She was not confused like this yesterday."
items.stem: Based on the trend in assessment data, which complication is the client at greatest risk for developing?
options: Atelectasis from shallow postoperative breathing
Sepsis progressing to septic shock
Paralytic ileus from anesthesia and opioids
Hemorrhage from the surgical anastomosis
items.rationale: The client has a likely intra-abdominal infection source plus fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, bandemia, rising lactate, oliguria, and acute confusion, which reflect early organ hypoperfusion from sepsis. Without rapid treatment this trajectory leads to septic shock. Atelectasis and ileus do not explain the confusion and lactate rise, and hemorrhage would produce a falling hemoglobin rather than these inflammatory markers.

items.update: 1130: BP 84/50 mm Hg (MAP 61), HR 118/min, RR 26/min, T 38.9 C (102.0 F), SpO2 91% on 2 L nasal cannula. Repeat lactate 4.2 mmol/L. Skin warm and flushed, capillary refill 4 seconds. Urine output 10 mL over the past hour. Client mumbling and difficult to arouse.
items.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess progress.
bowtieActions: Prepare to infuse a 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus as prescribed
Administer prescribed IV furosemide to improve urine output
Give prescribed broad-spectrum antibiotics now that cultures are drawn
Place the client flat in Trendelenburg position
Hold antibiotics until wound culture sensitivities result
items.rationale: Hypotension with warm, flushed skin, a lactate above 4 mmol/L, and an infectious source indicate septic shock. Sepsis bundles call for rapid crystalloid resuscitation at 30 mL/kg and broad-spectrum antibiotics as soon as cultures are obtained. MAP and serial lactate are the key markers of tissue perfusion used to judge whether resuscitation is working; diuretics and Trendelenburg positioning are not indicated and delaying antibiotics increases mortality.

items.update: 1200: Rapid response team at bedside. New prescriptions: 0.9% sodium chloride 30 mL/kg IV bolus, piperacillin-tazobactam IV now, oxygen titrated to keep SpO2 at 94% or greater, repeat lactate in 2 hours, hourly urine output, transfer to the ICU.
items.stem: Which actions will the nurse take at this time? Select all that apply.
options: Initiate the crystalloid bolus through a large-bore IV catheter
Increase oxygen and titrate to keep SpO2 at 94% or greater
Delay the antibiotic dose until the client arrives in the ICU
Recheck the lactate at the prescribed interval to trend perfusion
Ambulate the client in the hallway to prevent atelectasis
Continue hourly urine output measurement from the catheter
items.rationale: Rapid fluid resuscitation, supplemental oxygen, serial lactate measurement, and hourly urine output are core interventions and monitoring for septic shock. The first antibiotic dose is time critical and is given before transfer, not delayed. Ambulation is unsafe for a hypotensive client with depressed mental status.

items.update: 1600 (ICU): Fluid bolus and first antibiotic dose complete; norepinephrine infusing at a low dose. T 38.8 C (101.8 F), HR 96/min, RR 20/min, BP 104/58 mm Hg (MAP 73), SpO2 96% on 4 L nasal cannula. Lactate 2.1 mmol/L. Urine output 35 mL over the past hour. Client oriented to person and place and reports itching under the abdominal dressing.
items.stem: For each 1600 finding, specify whether it indicates the treatment plan has been effective, has been ineffective, or is unrelated to the treatment plan.
matrixRows: MAP increased from 61 to 73 mm Hg
Lactate decreased from 4.2 to 2.1 mmol/L
Urine output increased to 35 mL/hr
Temperature remains 38.8 C (101.8 F)
Itching under the abdominal dressing
items.rationale: A MAP above 65 mm Hg, a falling lactate, and urine output above 30 mL/hr show that perfusion is being restored, so resuscitation is working. The persistent fever shows the infection itself is not yet controlled and antibiotics need continued evaluation. Itching under the dressing does not reflect the response to shock treatment.

items.stem: Which findings are of immediate concern to the nurse? Select all that apply.
options: Chest pressure radiating to the jaw and left arm, rated 8/10
ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF
Cool, diaphoretic skin with nausea and vomiting
Temperature 37.0 C (98.6 F)
Chest pressure unrelieved by antacids taken at home
30 pack-year smoking history
items.rationale: Crushing chest pressure with radiation, diaphoresis, nausea, failure to respond to antacids, and ST elevation on the ECG are the classic cluster of acute coronary occlusion and demand immediate intervention. The normal temperature is not concerning, and the smoking history is a background risk factor rather than an acute cue.

items.stem: The nurse analyzes the 12-lead ECG together with the presentation. Which interpretation of the data is correct?
options: The changes reflect stable angina that will resolve with rest
ST elevation in the inferior leads indicates an evolving myocardial infarction requiring emergent reperfusion
Reciprocal ST depression shows the antacids are starting to work
The pattern represents early repolarization, a benign variant
items.rationale: ST-segment elevation in two or more contiguous leads (here II, III, and aVF, the inferior wall) with reciprocal depression indicates acute transmural injury from a blocked coronary artery. Stable angina resolves with rest and produces no ST elevation, and a benign variant would not present with ongoing crushing pain and diaphoresis.

items.update: 1035: Troponin I 0.9 ng/mL (elevated). Client vomits a second time and is increasingly anxious, asking, "Am I dying?" HR 98/min, BP 148/90 mm Hg, pain now 9/10.
items.stem: Which client problem is the priority at this time?
options: Anxiety related to fear of dying
Nausea related to vagal stimulation
Impaired myocardial tissue perfusion from coronary occlusion
Knowledge deficit related to cardiac risk factors
items.rationale: Every minute of coronary occlusion extends the zone of myocardial necrosis, so restoring perfusion takes priority over all other problems. The anxiety, nausea, and pain are consequences of the ischemia and improve once perfusion is restored; teaching about risk factors belongs in the recovery phase.

items.update: 1045: Provider confirms an acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction and activates the cardiac catheterization laboratory with a 90-minute door-to-balloon goal. Pain 9/10, BP 150/92 mm Hg, HR 100/min.
items.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess progress.
bowtieActions: Administer chewable aspirin 324 mg as prescribed
Prepare the client for emergent percutaneous coronary intervention
Schedule an exercise stress test for the morning
Apply a heating pad to the chest for comfort
Encourage ambulation in the room to promote circulation
bowtieParams: Continuous cardiac rhythm for ventricular dysrhythmias
Serial troponin levels and repeat 12-lead ECGs
Bowel sounds in all four quadrants
items.rationale: ST elevation with reciprocal changes, an elevated troponin, and unrelenting ischemic pain define a STEMI. Chewed aspirin blocks further platelet aggregation, and emergent PCI is the definitive reperfusion therapy when available within 90 minutes. Ischemic and reperfusing myocardium is electrically irritable, so the rhythm is watched continuously, and serial troponins with repeat ECGs track the evolution of the infarction.

items.update: 1050: Prescriptions received while the catheterization team assembles: chewable aspirin, IV heparin bolus per ACS protocol, sublingual nitroglycerin every 5 minutes up to 3 doses if systolic BP remains above 100 mm Hg, and continuous monitoring.
items.stem: For each intervention, specify whether it is anticipated or contraindicated for this client.
matrixRows: Give chewable aspirin 324 mg immediately
Administer sublingual nitroglycerin with blood pressure checks before each dose
Give pain medication by intramuscular injection
Administer the IV heparin bolus per ACS protocol
Give an IV beta-blocker if the heart rate falls below 50/min
Maintain continuous cardiac monitoring during transport to the catheterization lab
items.rationale: Aspirin, nitroglycerin with blood pressure verification, heparin, and uninterrupted monitoring are standard care for a client headed to emergent PCI. Intramuscular injections are avoided in anticoagulated clients because of hematoma risk and muscle trauma that can alter cardiac markers. Beta-blockers slow conduction and are withheld in bradycardia.

items.update: 1310: Client returns from the catheterization laboratory after drug-eluting stent placement in the right coronary artery. Right radial access site dressing dry and intact. BP 118/70 mm Hg, HR 74/min, RR 16/min, SpO2 98% on 2 L nasal cannula. Monitor shows sinus rhythm with ST segments returning toward baseline. Client states the chest pressure is completely gone.
items.stem: Which findings indicate to the nurse that reperfusion therapy was effective? Select all that apply.
options: Chest pain resolved to 0 out of 10
ST segments returning toward baseline on the monitor
Troponin level continuing to rise 4 hours after the procedure
Blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg with heart rate 74/min
Oozing of blood noted at the radial access site
Skin warm and dry with brisk capillary refill
items.rationale: Resolution of ischemic pain, normalization of the ST segments, stable hemodynamics, and warm well-perfused skin all show that coronary blood flow has been restored. Troponin routinely continues to rise for hours after infarction, so it does not measure procedural success, and access-site oozing is a complication to address, not evidence of effectiveness.

items.stem: For each finding at 0718, specify whether it requires immediate follow-up or is expected after hip arthroplasty.
matrixRows: Sudden dyspnea with respiratory rate 30/min
SpO2 of 86% on room air
Sharp chest pain that worsens with inspiration
Surgical site pain 3/10 with movement
Heart rate increase from 84 to 122/min
Small serosanguineous drainage on the hip dressing
items.rationale: Abrupt dyspnea, hypoxemia, pleuritic chest pain, and sudden tachycardia signal an acute cardiopulmonary event and cannot wait. Mild controlled surgical pain and scant serosanguineous drainage are normal findings on postoperative day 2.

items.stem: Which findings support the nurse's concern that the client is experiencing a pulmonary embolism? Select all that apply.
options: Sudden onset of dyspnea with pleuritic chest pain
SpO2 drop from 96% to 86% on room air
Refused enoxaparin and removed the compression devices
Serosanguineous drainage on the surgical dressing
Tachycardia of 122/min with a falling blood pressure
Docusate sodium scheduled twice daily
items.rationale: Recent orthopedic surgery already carries a high risk of venous thromboembolism, and missed anticoagulant prophylaxis plus absent mechanical compression raise it further. Sudden pleuritic pain, hypoxemia, tachycardia, and hypotension are the hallmark presentation of a clot obstructing the pulmonary circulation. The dressing drainage and stool softener are unrelated to this event.

items.update: 0725: Right calf noted to be swollen, warm, and tender compared with the left. Client increasingly anxious and states, "Something is really wrong, I can feel it."
items.stem: Based on the analysis of the data, which condition is the priority concern?
options: Fat embolism syndrome
Pulmonary embolism
Postoperative atelectasis
Panic attack related to uncontrolled pain
items.rationale: A unilateral swollen, tender calf points to a deep vein thrombosis as the embolic source, and the sudden hypoxemia, pleuritic pain, and hemodynamic changes fit a pulmonary embolism. Fat embolism typically follows long-bone fracture and presents with petechiae and confusion, atelectasis develops gradually with diminished breath sounds, and a panic attack does not cause an SpO2 of 86%.

items.update: 0730: Rapid response called. HR 128/min, RR 32/min, BP 98/64 mm Hg, SpO2 84% on room air. Client pale and apprehensive. Provider at the bedside; stat computed tomography pulmonary angiography prescribed.
items.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess progress.
bowtieActions: Apply oxygen and raise the head of the bed to high Fowler position
Anticipate an IV heparin bolus followed by a continuous infusion
Massage the swollen calf to relieve the tenderness
Position the client supine with both legs elevated
Encourage incentive spirometry every hour
bowtieParams: Oxygen saturation and work of breathing
aPTT results and signs of bleeding
items.rationale: Sudden hypoxemia, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, and a likely deep vein thrombosis after hip surgery point to pulmonary embolism. Immediate priorities are supporting oxygenation with upright positioning and supplemental oxygen, and halting clot propagation with IV heparin. The nurse then tracks gas exchange and anticoagulation safety; massaging the calf could dislodge more thrombus and supine leg elevation worsens the work of breathing.

items.update: 0755: Computed tomography pulmonary angiography confirms segmental emboli in the right lower lobe. Prescriptions: heparin 80 units/kg IV bolus then 18 units/kg/hr infusion, oxygen titrated to keep SpO2 at 92% or greater, continuous pulse oximetry, bed rest, aPTT 6 hours after the infusion starts.
items.stem: Which actions will the nurse take when implementing the heparin protocol? Select all that apply.
options: Verify the bolus dose and infusion rate with a second nurse
Obtain the aPTT 6 hours after the infusion starts as prescribed
Give the scheduled enoxaparin dose in addition to the infusion
Monitor for hematuria, bleeding gums, and new bruising
Confirm that protamine sulfate is available on the unit
Ambulate the client to the bathroom to prevent venous stasis
items.rationale: Weight-based heparin is a high-alert medication requiring an independent double check, scheduled aPTT monitoring to titrate the infusion, ongoing surveillance for bleeding, and ready access to protamine sulfate as the reversal agent. Adding enoxaparin would dangerously duplicate anticoagulation, and the client remains on bed rest during the acute phase.

items.update: 1400: Heparin infusing at the adjusted rate; aPTT 68 seconds (protocol goal 60 to 80 seconds). HR 92/min, RR 20/min, BP 116/70 mm Hg, SpO2 94% on 2 L nasal cannula. Client resting with the head of the bed elevated, rating chest pain 1/10 on deep inspiration. No bleeding noted at any site.
items.stem: Which finding best indicates to the nurse that treatment of the pulmonary embolism has been effective?
options: SpO2 of 94% with a respiratory rate of 20/min
aPTT result of 68 seconds
Client asking when lunch will arrive
No visible bruising at previous injection sites
items.rationale: The goal of treatment is restored gas exchange, so the climb in oxygen saturation with a normalizing respiratory rate is the best evidence of effectiveness. A therapeutic aPTT confirms the heparin dose is in range but does not by itself show that oxygenation has improved, and the absence of bruising reflects safety monitoring rather than resolution of the embolism.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the chart at 1005. Which findings require immediate follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Deep, rapid respirations at 32/min
Blood glucose 540 mg/dL
SpO2 99% on room air
Heart rate 124/min with blood pressure 98/60 mm Hg
Temperature 100.9 F (38.3 C)
pH 7.12 with bicarbonate 9 mEq/L
items.rationale: Kussmaul respirations, marked hyperglycemia, severe metabolic acidosis, and tachycardia with borderline hypotension signal diabetic ketoacidosis with significant volume depletion and require immediate intervention. The SpO2 of 99% is normal, and the low-grade fever, while worth noting as a possible illness trigger, is not an immediate threat compared with the acidosis and hypovolemia.

items.stem: The nurse analyzes the assessment data. The client's deep, rapid respirations are best interpreted as which of the following?
options: Anxiety-related hyperventilation that will resolve with reassurance
Primary respiratory alkalosis caused by a pulmonary embolism
Respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis (Kussmaul respirations)
Impending airway obstruction requiring immediate intubation
items.rationale: In DKA, ketoacid accumulation drives the pH down, and the lungs compensate by blowing off CO2 through deep, rapid Kussmaul respirations, reflected in the low PaCO2 of 24 mm Hg. This breathing pattern is compensatory and should not be suppressed; it will slow as the acidosis is corrected with fluids and insulin.

items.stem: Based on the current data, the nurse determines the client is at greatest immediate risk for which complication?
options: Hypoglycemia from prolonged fasting
Hypovolemic shock from osmotic diuresis and vomiting
Aspiration pneumonia from drowsiness
Diabetic peripheral neuropathy
items.rationale: Osmotic diuresis from severe hyperglycemia, combined with 2 days of vomiting, has produced marked fluid volume deficit, shown by the tachycardia, low-normal blood pressure, dry mucous membranes, and poor turgor. Untreated, this progresses to hypovolemic shock, making volume restoration the first priority of DKA management.

items.update: 1030: The emergency department provider evaluates the client and enters admission orders for management of diabetic ketoacidosis.
items.stem: For each provider prescription, specify whether it is Anticipated or Contraindicated for this client at this time.
matrixRows: 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L IV bolus over the first hour
Regular insulin IV infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hr after a bolus
Sodium bicarbonate IV bolus for a pH of 7.12
Continuous cardiac monitoring
Discontinue IV access and give rapid-acting insulin subcutaneously
items.rationale: Isotonic fluid resuscitation is the first step in DKA, followed by a continuous IV regular insulin infusion, and cardiac monitoring is essential because potassium shifts cause dysrhythmias. Bicarbonate is reserved for a pH below 6.9 because it can worsen intracellular acidosis and hypokalemia. Subcutaneous insulin is unreliable in a dehydrated, acidotic client, so the IV route is required.

items.update: 1300: Two hours into the insulin infusion. Glucose 310 mg/dL, pH 7.24, HCO3 13 mEq/L, potassium 3.2 mEq/L. Cardiac monitor shows flattened T waves and new U waves. Client reports leg cramps and generalized weakness. Urine output 60 mL/hr.
items.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.
bowtieActions: Administer IV potassium chloride as prescribed
Administer IV calcium gluconate to stabilize the myocardium
Anticipate holding the insulin infusion until potassium is replaced
Administer sodium polystyrene sulfonate as prescribed
Increase the insulin infusion rate to lower the glucose faster
bowtieParams: Cardiac rhythm on the continuous monitor
Bowel sounds in all four quadrants
items.rationale: This is the potassium trap of DKA: insulin and correction of acidosis drive potassium back into cells, so a level that was 5.6 on admission has fallen to 3.2, producing flattened T waves, U waves, cramps, and weakness. Potassium must be replaced, and because the level is below 3.3 mEq/L the insulin infusion is held until replacement begins, since continued insulin will drop it further. Serial potassium levels and continuous ECG monitoring track the response and detect life-threatening dysrhythmias.

items.update: 0500 the next day: Insulin infusion continues with dextrose and potassium added to IV fluids per protocol. Glucose 179 mg/dL, pH 7.33, HCO3 18 mEq/L, potassium 3.9 mEq/L, anion gap 13 mEq/L. Client is alert, respirations 16/min and unlabored, tolerating sips of clear liquids. During teaching, client states, "Next time I'm sick and not eating, I'll just stop my insulin again."
items.stem: For each finding, specify whether it indicates the client is Progressing as expected or Requires follow-up.
matrixRows: Anion gap decreased from 24 to 13 mEq/L
Alert with respirations 16/min and unlabored
Statement about stopping insulin during future illness
Blood glucose 179 mg/dL on the insulin protocol
Potassium 3.9 mEq/L with replacement infusing
items.rationale: The closing anion gap, resolving Kussmaul respirations, glucose in the target range, and normalized potassium all show the DKA is resolving as expected. The client's plan to stop insulin during illness is the knowledge gap that caused this admission: type 1 diabetics always need basal insulin, and sick-day rules call for continuing insulin, checking glucose and ketones frequently, and maintaining fluid intake. This statement requires focused teaching before discharge.

items.stem: The triage nurse reviews the 0910 documentation. Which findings require immediate follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Right facial droop with slurred speech
Symptom onset 40 minutes before arrival
Capillary glucose 118 mg/dL
Irregularly irregular heart rhythm
History of hyperlipidemia
Right arm drifting downward when raised
items.rationale: Facial droop, slurred speech, and arm drift are the classic FAST findings of acute stroke, and the recent, clearly established onset time makes the client a potential thrombolytic candidate, so every minute matters. The irregularly irregular rhythm suggests new atrial fibrillation, a likely embolic source. The normal glucose and the chronic hyperlipidemia do not require immediate action, although the glucose usefully rules out hypoglycemia as a stroke mimic.

items.stem: The stroke team is evaluating the client for IV thrombolytic (alteplase) therapy. Which piece of data is most important for the nurse to confirm when determining eligibility?
options: The client's age of 68 years
The client's history of hyperlipidemia
The capillary glucose of 118 mg/dL
The exact time the client was last known to be well
items.rationale: IV alteplase must be given within the approved window (up to 3 hours, or 4.5 hours for selected clients) from the time the client was last known to be well, so establishing that time precisely is the critical eligibility question. Here the spouse witnessed onset at 0830, giving a clear window. Age 68, hyperlipidemia, and a normal glucose do not exclude thrombolysis.

items.stem: After reviewing the CT and ECG results, the nurse recognizes the client's presentation is most consistent with which condition?
options: Hemorrhagic stroke from uncontrolled hypertension
Hypoglycemia mimicking a stroke
Acute ischemic stroke, likely embolic from new atrial fibrillation
Bell's palsy involving the facial nerve
items.rationale: The CT shows no hemorrhage, the glucose is normal, and the sudden focal deficits in a client with newly identified atrial fibrillation point to a cardioembolic ischemic stroke, since fibrillating atria form clots that embolize to the brain. Bell's palsy affects only the face and would not explain arm weakness or slurred speech of this pattern.

items.update: 0950: The provider determines the client meets criteria for IV alteplase and enters orders. Blood pressure remains 168/94 mm Hg.
items.stem: For each intervention, specify whether it is Anticipated or Contraindicated for this client receiving IV alteplase.
matrixRows: Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg IV: 10% as a bolus, remainder over 60 minutes
Neurologic assessments every 15 minutes during the infusion
Administer aspirin and subcutaneous heparin within the next 24 hours
Maintain blood pressure below 180/105 mm Hg
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter during the infusion
Keep the head of the bed elevated with the client on bed rest
items.rationale: The weight-based alteplase dose, every-15-minute neurologic checks, blood pressure control below 180/105, and bed rest with head-of-bed elevation are standard post-thrombolytic care. Antiplatelet and anticoagulant agents are withheld for 24 hours because they compound the bleeding risk, and invasive procedures such as urinary catheter insertion are avoided during and immediately after the infusion for the same reason.

items.update: 0955: Alteplase bolus given and infusion started. The client is transferred to the stroke unit on a cardiac monitor with the infusion running.
items.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting the complication the client is at highest risk for, 2 actions the nurse should take to reduce or detect it, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.
bowtieActions: Perform neurologic checks every 15 minutes and report any decline
Avoid IM injections, arterial punctures, and unnecessary venipuncture
Ambulate the client in the hallway every 2 hours
Insert a nasogastric tube now for medication administration
Massage the calves bilaterally each shift
bowtieParams: Level of consciousness and pupillary response
items.rationale: The most feared complication of thrombolytic therapy is intracranial hemorrhage, heralded by declining level of consciousness, severe headache, vomiting, pupil changes, or a sudden blood pressure surge, so frequent neurologic checks and close blood pressure monitoring are essential. Minimizing punctures, IM injections, and invasive tubes reduces bleeding sites while the fibrinolytic effect persists. Ambulation and calf massage are inappropriate during the immediate post-alteplase period.

items.update: Next day, 1000 (24 hours post-alteplase): NIHSS score 3, down from 12. Speech is clear; right arm strength 4/5 with mild residual weakness. Blood pressure 148/82 mm Hg on the monitor. Repeat CT head shows no hemorrhage. Swallow screen passed.
items.stem: Which findings indicate the alteplase therapy was effective? Select all that apply.
options: NIHSS score decreased from 12 to 3
Speech is clear and easily understood
Blood pressure of 148/82 mm Hg
Right arm strength improved to 4/5
Repeat CT head shows no hemorrhage
Client remains on the cardiac monitor
items.rationale: Effectiveness of thrombolysis is measured by recovery of the neurologic deficits it was given to reverse: the falling NIHSS score, cleared speech, and improved arm strength all show reperfusion of the ischemic territory. The absence of hemorrhage on CT and the current blood pressure reflect safety and supportive management rather than the drug's therapeutic effect, and continued cardiac monitoring is an intervention, not an outcome.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the admission data at 1105. Which findings require immediate follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Black, tarry stools for 2 days
Ibuprofen 800 mg three times daily
SpO2 97% on room air
Standing blood pressure 88/58 mm Hg with heart rate 122/min
Hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL, down from 13.9 g/dL
History of osteoarthritis
items.rationale: Melena indicates digested blood from an upper GI source, the orthostatic drop with compensatory tachycardia shows the blood loss is hemodynamically significant, and the hemoglobin has fallen nearly 6 g/dL from baseline. High-dose ibuprofen is the probable cause and must be identified and stopped. The oxygen saturation is acceptable, and the arthritis itself is not an acute concern.

items.stem: The nurse analyzes the laboratory results. The BUN of 42 mg/dL with a creatinine of 1.0 mg/dL is best interpreted as:
options: Acute kidney injury caused by NSAID use
Poor oral fluid intake over the past week
Digestion and absorption of blood proteins from an upper GI bleed
A normal finding for a 62-year-old client
items.rationale: A disproportionately elevated BUN with a normal creatinine is characteristic of upper GI bleeding: blood in the gut is digested and its protein absorbed, raising the BUN, and hypovolemia adds a prerenal component. NSAID nephropathy or dehydration alone would typically raise the creatinine as well, and a BUN of 42 mg/dL is not normal at any age.

items.stem: Based on the analysis, the nurse determines the client is at greatest immediate risk for which complication?
options: Hypovolemic shock from ongoing blood loss
NSAID-induced acute kidney injury
Slowly progressive iron-deficiency anemia
Anxiety-related tachycardia
items.rationale: The client is already orthostatic and tachycardic, which reflects roughly 15% or more circulating volume loss; if the bleeding continues, decompensated hypovolemic shock with organ hypoperfusion is the immediate life threat. Renal injury and chronic anemia are real but slower concerns, and tachycardia here is compensatory, not psychogenic.

items.update: 1120: Client vomits 300 mL of coffee-ground emesis and becomes more lethargic. Lying blood pressure now 92/56 mm Hg, heart rate 128/min, respirations 24/min. Skin cool, pale, and clammy; capillary refill 4 seconds.
items.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.
bowtieActions: Insert two large-bore IV catheters and infuse 0.9% sodium chloride as prescribed
Obtain a type and crossmatch and prepare to transfuse packed red blood cells
Administer an oral iron supplement now
Give the scheduled ibuprofen dose for abdominal discomfort
Assist the client to ambulate to the bathroom for a stool specimen
bowtieParams: Blood pressure and heart rate trends
items.rationale: Coffee-ground emesis on top of melena, with worsening hypotension, tachycardia, and cool clammy skin, indicates hypovolemic shock from continuing upper GI hemorrhage. Priorities are rapid volume access with two large-bore IVs and crystalloid, and readying crossmatched blood for transfusion. Vital sign trends and hourly urine output are the most direct bedside measures of perfusion; oral iron, further NSAIDs, and ambulating an unstable client are unsafe or irrelevant.

items.update: 1150: The provider prescribes 2 units of packed red blood cells, a pantoprazole IV infusion, and NPO status with GI consultation for endoscopy. 1210: The blood bank releases the first unit of packed red blood cells.
items.stem: Which actions should the nurse take when administering the first unit of packed red blood cells? Select all that apply.
options: Verify the blood product and client identity with a second registered nurse at the bedside
Obtain a complete set of vital signs immediately before starting the transfusion
Prime the blood tubing with lactated Ringer's solution
Remain with the client for the first 15 minutes of the transfusion
Plan to infuse the unit over 6 hours to prevent fluid overload
Prime the blood tubing with 0.9% sodium chloride
items.rationale: Safe transfusion requires two-nurse verification at the bedside, baseline vital signs, and staying with the client for the first 15 minutes, when acute hemolytic reactions are most likely to appear. Only 0.9% sodium chloride is compatible with blood; lactated Ringer's contains calcium and can cause clotting in the line. Each unit must be completed within 4 hours, and this hypovolemic client needs the volume promptly.

items.update: 1600: Both units of packed red blood cells have infused without reaction, and the pantoprazole infusion continues. Endoscopy is scheduled for this evening.
items.stem: For each 1600 finding, specify whether it indicates the interventions were Effective, Ineffective, or are Unrelated to the treatment of the GI bleed.
matrixRows: Blood pressure 118/72 mm Hg lying, with no orthostatic drop
Heart rate 84/min
Hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL on repeat testing
New large melenic stool containing dark clots at 1615
Client reports ongoing stiffness of both knees
items.rationale: Restoration of a normal blood pressure without orthostasis, resolution of the tachycardia, and a rising hemoglobin show the volume and blood replacement are working. A new large melenic stool with clots suggests bleeding may be continuing and must be reported before endoscopy. Chronic knee stiffness reflects the underlying osteoarthritis and is unrelated to the bleeding or its treatment.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the admission assessment at 0820. Which findings require immediate follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Blood pressure 172/114 mm Hg on repeat measurement
Headache unrelieved by acetaminophen with visual "spots"
Fetal heart rate baseline of 140/min with moderate variability
Right upper quadrant pain rated 6/10
Deep tendon reflexes 3+ with 1 beat of ankle clonus
Temperature 37.1 C (98.8 F)
items.rationale: Severe-range blood pressure, an unrelenting headache with visual changes, right upper quadrant pain, and hyperreflexia with clonus are signs of severe preeclampsia with rising central nervous system irritability and hepatic involvement. These cues signal a client at risk of imminent eclampsia and must be reported and acted on immediately. An FHR baseline of 140/min with moderate variability and a normal temperature are reassuring findings.

items.stem: For each finding, click to specify whether the finding is consistent with severe preeclampsia or is an expected change of normal pregnancy.
matrixRows: Blood pressure 172/114 mm Hg
Platelet count 98,000/mm3
AST 88 units/L
Mild ankle edema at the end of the day
Urinary frequency without pain or burning
Persistent headache with visual disturbances
items.rationale: Severe-range blood pressure, thrombocytopenia, elevated liver enzymes, and cerebral symptoms are defining features of preeclampsia with severe features and raise concern for developing HELLP syndrome. Dependent ankle edema and urinary frequency are common, benign changes of late pregnancy caused by venous compression and pressure of the gravid uterus on the bladder.

items.stem: Based on the analysis of the assessment data, the nurse determines the client is at highest risk for which complication?
options: Iron-deficiency anemia
Eclamptic seizure
Gestational diabetes mellitus
Preterm premature rupture of membranes
items.rationale: Worsening cerebral signs, including headache, visual changes, and hyperreflexia with clonus, indicate central nervous system irritability, the strongest predictor of progression to an eclamptic seizure. A seizure threatens the maternal airway, oxygenation, and uteroplacental perfusion, making it the priority risk. The other complications are not supported by this client's data.

items.update: 0845: Provider prescribes magnesium sulfate 4 g IV over 20 minutes, then 2 g/hr continuous infusion; labetalol 20 mg IV push for sustained BP of 160/110 mm Hg or higher; seizure precautions; and betamethasone 12 mg IM. The nurse plans care before starting the infusion.
items.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the client is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess the client's progress.
bowtieActions: Initiate the magnesium sulfate infusion via pump as prescribed
Ensure calcium gluconate is immediately available at the bedside
Encourage frequent ambulation in the hallway
Keep the room brightly lit to facilitate assessments
Position the client supine with the head of the bed flat
bowtieParams: Deep tendon reflexes and respiratory rate
Bowel sounds in all four quadrants
Hourly urine output and serum magnesium levels
items.rationale: New-onset severe-range hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria, thrombocytopenia, elevated liver enzymes, and cerebral symptoms defines severe preeclampsia. Magnesium sulfate is given to prevent seizures, and its antidote, calcium gluconate, must be kept at the bedside. Because magnesium is excreted renally and depresses neuromuscular and respiratory function, the nurse monitors deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate, hourly urine output, and serum levels; a quiet, dimly lit room and lateral positioning are also indicated.

items.update: 1010: Magnesium sulfate infusing at 2 g/hr. The client is drowsy and slurring her words. RR 10/min, deep tendon reflexes absent, SpO2 93% on room air. Stat serum magnesium level 9.8 mg/dL.
items.stem: Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Administer calcium gluconate 1 g IV
Stop the magnesium sulfate infusion
Obtain a stat 12-lead electrocardiogram
Notify the provider of the magnesium level
items.rationale: Absent reflexes, a respiratory rate below 12/min, and a serum level of 9.8 mg/dL indicate magnesium toxicity, so the first action is to stop the source by discontinuing the infusion. Calcium gluconate is then administered as the antidote, oxygen is applied, and the provider is notified. Performing any other action while the infusion continues would deepen respiratory and cardiac depression.

items.update: 1130: Magnesium infusion stopped at 1012; calcium gluconate 1 g IV administered at 1015; oxygen applied. No seizure activity has occurred. The nurse reassesses at 1130.
items.stem: Which findings indicate that the interventions have been effective? Select all that apply.
options: Respiratory rate 16/min with SpO2 98%
Deep tendon reflexes 2+ without clonus
Urine output 15 mL over the past hour
Client alert and states the headache has improved
Blood pressure 148/92 mm Hg
New report of epigastric pain rated 8/10
items.rationale: Return of a normal respiratory rate and oxygen saturation, 2+ reflexes, an alert sensorium with an improving headache, and a blood pressure below the severe range show that the toxicity has resolved and the disease is controlled without progression to eclampsia. Urine output of 15 mL/hr is oliguria, and new severe epigastric pain suggests hepatic capsule distention; both findings would require further intervention.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 0230 assessment. Which findings require immediate follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Fundus boggy and 1 cm above the umbilicus
Peripad and underpad saturated within 15 minutes
Heart rate increase from 84/min to 118/min
Placenta delivered intact at 0210
Report of dizziness with pale, cool skin
Second stage of labor lasting 12 minutes
items.rationale: A boggy, elevated fundus, rapid pad saturation with clots, a rising pulse with falling blood pressure, and dizziness with pale, cool skin are hallmarks of early postpartum hemorrhage with developing hypovolemia. Tachycardia is often the earliest vital sign change because healthy postpartum clients compensate before the blood pressure falls. An intact placenta and a short second stage are documentation of completed events, not cues requiring action.

items.stem: The nurse analyzes the assessment data. Which condition is the most likely source of the bleeding?
options: Cervical or vaginal laceration
Retained placental fragments
Uterine atony
Disseminated intravascular coagulation
items.rationale: A uterus that is boggy and firms only with massage indicates atony, the most common cause of early postpartum hemorrhage; this client's risk factors include grand multiparity, precipitous labor, and a macrosomic infant that overdistended the uterus. A laceration classically produces a steady trickle of bright red blood despite a firm fundus, and the placenta was inspected and delivered intact. The presence of clots shows the blood is coagulating normally.

items.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting the complication the client is at highest risk for developing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess the client's progress.
bowtieActions: Perform firm fundal massage until the uterus contracts
Assist the client to a warm shower to promote relaxation
Increase the oxytocin infusion rate as prescribed
Encourage early ambulation to promote uterine drainage
Withhold all uterotonic medications until laboratory results return
bowtieParams: Quantified blood loss and vital signs every 15 minutes
Bowel sounds in all four quadrants
items.rationale: Ongoing uterine atony with heavy bleeding places the client at highest risk for hypovolemic shock, already signaled by tachycardia, hypotension, and pale, cool skin. Fundal massage is the first-line intervention to stimulate contraction, and increasing the oxytocin infusion sustains uterine tone. Progress is judged by whether the fundus remains firm and by trending quantified blood loss and vital signs.

items.update: 0245: Fundus remains boggy despite massage; bladder palpable above the symphysis pubis. Quantified blood loss now 900 mL. Provider at the bedside; new prescriptions received.
items.stem: For each potential intervention, click to specify whether the intervention is anticipated or contraindicated for this client.
matrixRows: Administer carboprost tromethamine 250 mcg IM
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter to empty the bladder
Place the client in high Fowler position
Infuse a 500-mL bolus of lactated Ringer solution
Encourage the client to walk to the bathroom to void
Administer tranexamic acid 1 g IV as prescribed
items.rationale: Carboprost and tranexamic acid are second-line pharmacologic treatments for atony with ongoing hemorrhage, a distended bladder displaces the uterus and prevents contraction so catheterization is anticipated, and a crystalloid bolus restores circulating volume. Sitting the client upright reduces cerebral perfusion during hypovolemia, and ambulating a hypotensive, tachycardic client risks syncope and injury.

items.update: 0300: Carboprost given at 0250. Fundus firms with massage but relaxes when massage is stopped. Quantified blood loss 1,100 mL. BP 88/54 mm Hg, HR 128/min; client increasingly drowsy. A second IV line has been placed, and 2 units of packed red blood cells are on the way from the blood bank.
items.stem: Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Document the findings and reassess in 15 minutes
Apply oxygen at 10 L/min via nonrebreather mask while continuing uterine massage
Offer oral fluids to help restore circulating volume
Ask the client to rate her pain using a numeric scale
items.rationale: The client is showing progressive hypovolemic shock, so the priority is supporting oxygen delivery to vital organs while controlling the source of loss with continued uterine massage. High-flow oxygen maximizes the carrying capacity of the remaining red cells until blood is transfused. Waiting 15 minutes, offering oral fluids, and assessing pain do not address the immediate threat.

items.update: 0400: Client received bimanual compression by the provider, 1 unit of packed red blood cells, and a total of 1,500 mL lactated Ringer solution. The nurse reassesses at 0400.
items.stem: Which findings indicate that the interventions have been effective? Select all that apply.
options: Fundus firm, midline, at the level of the umbilicus
Peripad with scant lochia rubra over the past hour
Blood pressure 104/66 mm Hg with heart rate 96/min
Steady trickle of bright red blood from the vagina
Urine output 40 mL over the past hour via catheter
Capillary refill 5 seconds with cool extremities
items.rationale: A firm midline fundus, scant lochia, a recovering blood pressure with a falling heart rate, and urine output above 30 mL/hr show that uterine tone has been restored and perfusion is improving. A continued trickle of bright red blood would suggest an unrepaired laceration or ongoing loss, and delayed capillary refill with cool extremities indicates persistent poor peripheral perfusion; both would require further evaluation.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 1335 entries. Which findings require immediate follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Six contractions in a 10-minute window with a firm resting tone
Clear amniotic fluid noted at rupture of membranes
Recurrent late decelerations with slow return to baseline
Change in FHR variability from moderate to minimal
Cervical dilation of 5 cm at 41 weeks
Maternal heart rate of 88/min
items.rationale: More than 5 contractions in 10 minutes with a firm resting tone is tachysystole, which shortens the time the placenta can refill between contractions. Recurrent late decelerations with loss of moderate variability indicate the fetus is not tolerating the reduced uteroplacental blood flow. Clear amniotic fluid, 5-cm dilation, and a maternal heart rate of 88/min are expected findings.

items.stem: The nurse analyzes the fetal heart rate tracing. The pattern is most consistent with which physiologic cause?
options: Fetal head compression during contractions
Umbilical cord compression
Uteroplacental insufficiency
A normal fetal sleep cycle
items.rationale: Late decelerations begin after the peak of the contraction and recover slowly because oxygen transfer across the placenta cannot keep up with contraction demand, which is the definition of uteroplacental insufficiency, here worsened by oxytocin-induced tachysystole. Head compression causes early decelerations that mirror contractions, and cord compression causes abrupt variable decelerations. A fetal sleep cycle can reduce variability but does not produce recurrent late decelerations.

items.stem: Complete the diagram by selecting the condition the fetus is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess progress.
bowtieActions: Increase the oxytocin infusion to strengthen labor
Discontinue the oxytocin infusion
Perform a sterile vaginal examination every 15 minutes
Reposition the client onto her left side
Prepare for immediate amniotomy
bowtieParams: Contraction frequency and uterine resting tone
Maternal urine protein at each void
items.rationale: Recurrent late decelerations with minimal variability during tachysystole indicate fetal hypoxemia from impaired uteroplacental perfusion. Stopping the oxytocin removes the cause of the excessive uterine activity, and lateral positioning relieves aortocaval compression to improve placental blood flow. The nurse then tracks the FHR pattern and uterine activity to determine whether the fetus is recovering.

items.update: 1345: Oxytocin discontinued and client repositioned to the left side. Late decelerations continue with most contractions; contractions remain every 90 seconds. Provider notified and en route.
items.stem: Which additional interventions should the nurse implement? Select all that apply.
options: Administer an intravenous bolus of lactated Ringer solution
Apply oxygen at 10 L/min via nonrebreather mask
Ambulate the client in the hallway to promote fetal descent
Administer terbutaline 0.25 mg subcutaneously as prescribed for tachysystole
Apply fundal pressure with each contraction
Encourage sustained breath-holding and pushing with contractions
items.rationale: Intrauterine resuscitation continues with an IV fluid bolus to expand maternal circulating volume and oxygen to raise the maternal-fetal oxygen gradient. Because tachysystole persists after the oxytocin is stopped, terbutaline is given to relax the uterus and restore rest time between contractions. Ambulation is unsafe with an epidural and a Category II tracing, and fundal pressure or pushing at 5 cm would worsen fetal stress.

items.update: 1405: FHR baseline 155/min with absent variability and recurrent late decelerations, followed by a prolonged deceleration to 80/min lasting 3 minutes (Category III). Cervix remains 5 cm.
items.stem: Which action should the nurse take?
options: Continue current measures and reassess the tracing in 30 minutes
Notify the provider of the Category III tracing and prepare the client for cesarean birth
Restart the oxytocin infusion at half the previous rate
Coach the client to begin pushing with each contraction
items.rationale: Absent variability with recurrent late decelerations is a Category III tracing, which predicts abnormal fetal acid-base status and requires expeditious delivery when resuscitation fails. With an unfavorable cervix at 5 cm, cesarean birth is the fastest safe route, so the nurse communicates the tracing and readies the client for surgery. Waiting 30 minutes, restarting oxytocin, or pushing before complete dilation would each deepen fetal compromise.

items.update: 1415: Terbutaline given at 1350. Consent for cesarean birth signed; operating room team assembling. The nurse completes a final reassessment before transfer.
items.stem: For each 1415 finding, click to specify whether the finding indicates the intrauterine resuscitation measures have been effective or ineffective.
matrixRows: Contractions now 3 in 10 minutes with 90 seconds of rest between
Uterine resting tone soft between contractions
Recurrent late decelerations persist with most contractions
FHR variability remains absent
A second prolonged deceleration to 80/min lasting 2 minutes
items.rationale: Terbutaline and stopping the oxytocin corrected the uterine activity problem, shown by a normal contraction frequency and a soft resting tone. The fetal findings have not recovered: persistent late decelerations, absent variability, and a repeated prolonged deceleration show ongoing hypoxemia despite maximal intrauterine resuscitation. This combination confirms that proceeding with cesarean birth is the correct decision.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the admission notes, vital signs, and weights. Which findings require immediate follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Heart rate 178/min
Sunken anterior fontanelle
Breath sounds clear bilaterally
One scant wet diaper in the past 12 hours
Axillary temperature 37.9°C (100.2°F)
Capillary refill 4 seconds
items.rationale: Marked tachycardia, a sunken fontanelle, minimal urine output, and prolonged capillary refill all signal significant fluid volume deficit and impaired perfusion in an infant. Clear breath sounds are an expected finding, and a low-grade temperature is common with viral gastroenteritis and is not the immediate concern.

items.stem: For each assessment finding, specify whether the finding is most consistent with mild dehydration or severe dehydration.
matrixRows: Weight loss of approximately 10% of body weight
Capillary refill of 4 seconds
Slightly dry lips with a pink, moist tongue
Sunken fontanelle with listlessness
Alert infant who is easily consoled when held
items.rationale: Mild dehydration (3%-5% loss) produces subtle findings: slightly dry lips, normal alertness, and brisk perfusion. Severe dehydration (10% or more) produces weight loss near 10%, capillary refill longer than 3 seconds, a sunken fontanelle, and altered responsiveness. Classifying findings by severity guides whether oral or intravenous rehydration is appropriate.

items.stem: Based on the analysis of the findings, which complication poses the greatest immediate risk to this infant?
options: Aspiration pneumonia
Febrile seizure
Hypovolemic shock
Fluid volume overload
items.rationale: The infant already shows compensated shock: tachycardia, cool mottled extremities, and delayed capillary refill with a still adequate blood pressure. Infants decompensate rapidly because hypotension is a late sign, so hypovolemic shock is the priority hypothesis. Fever is low grade, and there is no current risk of aspiration or overload.

items.update: 0950: The provider examines the infant. Oral rehydration solution, 5 mL by syringe every 5 minutes, is attempted for 30 minutes. The infant vomits twice during the trial and becomes more listless, refusing further sips.
items.stem: Which prescription should the nurse anticipate next?
options: Continue oral rehydration solution at 5 mL every 5 minutes
Administer a 20 mL/kg intravenous bolus of 0.9% sodium chloride
Administer a 20 mL/kg intravenous bolus of dextrose 5% in water
Add potassium chloride to intravenous fluids before the infant voids
items.rationale: Oral rehydration is preferred for mild to moderate dehydration, but this infant has severe dehydration and has failed an ORT trial, so isotonic intravenous rehydration with 20 mL/kg of 0.9% sodium chloride is indicated. Dextrose 5% in water is hypotonic once metabolized and is never used for volume resuscitation. Potassium is withheld until urine output confirms renal function.

items.update: 1010: An intravenous catheter is placed in the left foot on the second attempt. Heart rate 182/min, extremities mottled to the knees, infant arouses only briefly to painful stimuli.
items.stem: Complete the diagram: identify the condition the infant is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor to assess progress.
bowtieActions: Administer the 20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride bolus as prescribed
Administer intravenous potassium chloride by rapid push
Offer full-strength apple juice between assessments
Maintain strict intake and output with diaper weights
Apply a cooling blanket for the low-grade temperature
items.rationale: Three days of gastrointestinal losses with 10% weight loss and signs of poor perfusion indicate hypovolemia from severe dehydration. The priority actions are rapid isotonic volume replacement and strict intake and output, including weighing diapers, to quantify ongoing losses. Heart rate with capillary refill and urine output (goal at least 1 mL/kg/hr in an infant) are the most direct indicators that circulating volume is being restored. Potassium is never given by rapid push.

items.update: 1830: The infant received two 20 mL/kg boluses of 0.9% sodium chloride and is now on maintenance dextrose 5% with 0.45% sodium chloride. The infant took 60 mL of oral rehydration solution over the last hour without vomiting. Repeat weight 7.9 kg.
items.stem: Which findings indicate that the rehydration therapy has been effective? Select all that apply.
options: Anterior fontanelle is soft and flat
Heart rate 128/min, down from 182/min
Capillary refill remains 4 seconds
Urine output 2.2 mL/kg/hr over the past 4 hours
Infant continues to refuse all oral fluids
Weight 7.9 kg, up from 7.4 kg on admission
items.rationale: A flattened fontanelle, a heart rate trending toward the normal infant range, urine output above 1 mL/kg/hr, and weight gain toward baseline all show that circulating volume has been restored. Capillary refill that is still 4 seconds and refusal of oral fluids would indicate the therapy has not yet met its goals and would require follow-up.

items.stem: The triage nurse reviews the notes, vital signs, and history. Which findings require immediate follow-up? Select all that apply.
options: Continuous drooling with refusal to swallow
Tripod positioning with the chin thrust forward
Weight of 16.5 kg
Inspiratory stridor with a muffled voice
Absence of Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccination
Skin warm and flushed
items.rationale: Drooling, tripod positioning, stridor with a muffled voice, and lack of Hib vaccination together form the classic picture of acute epiglottitis, a true airway emergency. The weight is appropriate for age, and warm flushed skin is expected with fever; neither changes the immediate plan.

items.stem: The nurse analyzes the cues. The abrupt onset of high fever, drooling, absence of cough, and tripod positioning are most consistent with which condition?
options: Viral laryngotracheobronchitis (croup)
Acute epiglottitis
Foreign-body aspiration
Peritonsillar abscess
items.rationale: Epiglottitis presents abruptly with high fever, drooling, dysphagia, distress, and stridor without a cough, typically in an underimmunized child. Croup develops gradually with a barky cough and low-grade fever, foreign-body aspiration is sudden but afebrile, and a peritonsillar abscess usually follows days of worsening sore throat in an older child.

items.stem: When prioritizing hypotheses, the nurse identifies which potential complication as the most urgent concern?
options: Febrile seizure from the rapidly rising temperature
Dehydration from refusal to swallow
Transmission of infection to household contacts
Sudden complete airway obstruction
items.rationale: The inflamed epiglottis can occlude the larynx completely and without warning, especially if the child cries or the throat is manipulated, and this would be immediately fatal without a secured airway. Dehydration, seizure risk, and household prophylaxis are real considerations but none threatens life within minutes the way obstruction does.

items.stem: The nurse plans care while awaiting the provider. For each intervention, specify whether it is anticipated or contraindicated for this child.
matrixRows: Examine the pharynx with a tongue blade
Allow the child to remain in a position of comfort on the caregiver’s lap
Notify the anesthesia and otolaryngology airway team
Place the child supine and restrain for immediate IV insertion
Have emergency intubation and tracheostomy equipment at the bedside
Obtain a throat culture before the airway is secured
items.rationale: Any instrumentation of the mouth or throat — a tongue blade exam or a throat swab — can trigger laryngospasm and complete obstruction, as can forcing the child supine or provoking crying with restraint and needle sticks. Anticipated care keeps the child calm and upright with the caregiver, mobilizes the team able to secure a surgical airway, and stages emergency airway equipment. Cultures are deferred until after intubation in the operating room.

items.update: 1800: The child becomes more anxious when staff approach. Stridor is now audible at rest, retractions are deepening, and SpO2 is 92% on room air. The airway team has been paged.
items.stem: Complete the diagram: identify the condition the child is most likely experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.
bowtieActions: Keep the child calm on the caregiver’s lap while the airway team assembles
Inspect the throat with a flashlight and tongue blade
Provide humidified oxygen by blow-by as the child tolerates
Obtain arterial blood gases immediately
Position the child supine and apply a strapped face mask
bowtieParams: Work of breathing and character of stridor
items.rationale: This is acute epiglottitis with impending obstruction, so the nurse minimizes stimulation by leaving the child with the caregiver and delivers oxygen in the least threatening way possible until the team can secure the airway in a controlled setting. Work of breathing, stridor, and oxygen saturation are the parameters that reveal deterioration first. Throat inspection, painful procedures, and forced positioning can precipitate complete obstruction.

items.update: Day 2, 0800: The airway was secured by endotracheal intubation in the operating room, where the epiglottis appeared cherry-red and grossly swollen. Blood cultures grew Haemophilus influenzae type b. The child has received 36 hours of IV ceftriaxone and remains sedated and intubated in the PICU. The team is evaluating readiness for extubation.
items.stem: Which finding best indicates to the nurse that the epiglottic swelling has resolved enough to consider extubation?
options: An audible air leak around the endotracheal tube when the cuff is deflated
Temperature decreased to 37.2°C (99.0°F)
The child moves all extremities during sedation vacations
Secretions suctioned from the tube are thin and clear
items.rationale: An air leak around the deflated cuff means air can pass between the tube and the airway wall, which shows the supraglottic edema has subsided enough to allow airflow around the tube — the key criterion for safe extubation in epiglottitis. Resolving fever, purposeful movement, and clear secretions are encouraging but do not directly measure airway caliber.

items.stem: The nurse reviews the 0200 findings. Which cues require immediate action? Select all that apply.
options: Respiratory rate 6/min with shallow breaths
SpO2 84% on room air
Pinpoint pupils bilaterally
Surgical dressing clean, dry, and intact
Arouses only briefly to sternal rub
Heart rate 64/min
items.rationale: A respiratory rate of 6/min, oxygen saturation of 84%, pinpoint pupils, and deep sedation unresponsive to voice are the classic triad-plus of opioid toxicity and demand immediate intervention. An intact dressing is a normal finding, and a heart rate of 64/min is acceptable and not the driver of the emergency.

items.stem: The nurse analyzes the cues, including the vital sign trend and the PCA pump history. The findings are most consistent with which condition?
options: Acute ischemic stroke
Postoperative hemorrhage with hypovolemia
Opioid-induced respiratory depression
Pulmonary embolism
items.rationale: Progressive slowing of respirations over 6 hours, pinpoint pupils, deep sedation, heavy PCA use with dosing by proxy, and untreated sleep apnea all point to opioid-induced respiratory depression. Hemorrhage produces tachycardia and falling pressure with pallor, pulmonary embolism produces tachypnea and tachycardia, and stroke does not explain pinpoint pupils with bradypnea in this context.

items.stem: Which potential outcome poses the greatest immediate risk and should drive the nurse’s next actions?
options: Aspiration of gastric contents
Respiratory arrest with hypoxic injury
Acute opioid withdrawal
Disruption of the surgical anastomosis
items.rationale: At 6 shallow breaths per minute with a saturation of 84%, the client is minutes from respiratory arrest, and hypoxic brain injury follows quickly once ventilation stops. Aspiration and anastomotic problems are secondary concerns, and withdrawal is a consideration only after naloxone is given, not a reason to withhold it.

items.update: 0205: The rapid response team arrives. The client remains minimally arousable with RR 6/min and SpO2 85% despite a jaw thrust and verbal and tactile stimulation.
items.stem: Complete the diagram: identify the condition the client is experiencing, 2 actions the nurse should take, and 2 parameters the nurse should monitor.
bowtieActions: Stop the PCA pump and support breathing with bag-valve-mask ventilation as needed
Administer diluted IV naloxone as prescribed, titrated to respiratory effort
Administer 50% dextrose IV push
Place the client flat and lower the head of the bed
Apply a non-rebreather mask and leave the room to notify the surgeon
items.rationale: The opioid source must be stopped and ventilation supported while diluted naloxone is titrated slowly to restore adequate breathing without precipitating severe pain and withdrawal. Respiratory rate and depth together with the sedation score are the parameters that show whether reversal is working, because sedation deepens before the respiratory rate falls. Dextrose treats hypoglycemia, which these cues do not support, and the nurse never leaves an unstable client.

items.update: 0215: After 0.4 mg of diluted naloxone IV given in increments over 2 minutes, the client opens his eyes and answers questions. RR 14/min, SpO2 95% on 2 L nasal cannula. He reports incisional pain 8/10. The provider is at the bedside writing new orders.
items.stem: Which action is most important for the nurse to include in the plan of care for the next several hours?
options: Resume the PCA at the previous settings once the client is fully awake
Maintain continuous observation with frequent respiratory and sedation assessments, anticipating repeat naloxone doses
Give the full remaining naloxone supply now to prevent any recurrence
Encourage the client to sleep undisturbed to recover from the event
items.rationale: Naloxone acts for roughly 30 to 90 minutes, while hydromorphone persists far longer, so sedation and respiratory depression commonly recur as the antagonist wears off; the client needs continuous monitoring and possibly repeated or infused naloxone. Resuming the PCA at unchanged settings recreates the overdose, stacking extra naloxone now causes severe pain and withdrawal without lasting protection, and undisturbed sleep would mask re-sedation.

items.update: 0300: Sixty minutes after naloxone, the nurse reassesses the client, who has been dozing intermittently between assessments.
items.stem: For each 0300 finding, specify whether it indicates an effective response to treatment or requires immediate follow-up.
matrixRows: Respiratory rate 14/min with regular, adequate depth
Awakens easily to voice and answers questions appropriately
Respiratory rate has drifted from 14/min to 8/min over the past 15 minutes
SpO2 88% while dozing after removal of the nasal cannula
Reports incisional pain 4/10 after a reduced-dose analgesic plan
items.rationale: Adequate respirations, easy arousability, and tolerable pain on a revised analgesic plan show the reversal and new regimen are working. A respiratory rate falling to 8/min and a saturation of 88% signal re-sedation as the naloxone wears off before the hydromorphone does, and both require immediate intervention, including another naloxone dose per orders.
